catalog.label: Base
catalog.description: Baseline security controls for PAN-OS firewalls.

controls.name: LDAP Server Profiles Require SSL/TLS
controls.description:
An LDAP bind carries the bind account's credentials. Without SSL/TLS they cross the network in the clear, and anyone on the path reads the account that can enumerate the directory.

ABSENT MEANS ON. `ssl` is IMPLICIT YES - measured 2026-09-09 by writing a profile without the key and opening it in the UI, where the box renders checked. So this fires only on an EXPLICIT `no`. Reading the key as "absent means off" would report every profile that has never been edited as cleartext.

EVERY QUERY CLAUSES ON `kind`. Six kinds share one table and the measured implicit values live on every row, so a query on this column alone would fire on kinds it means nothing for.

Applies to profiles used for administrator authentication, User-ID group mapping and GlobalProtect alike - the profile does not know what will reference it.
controls.rationale: A cleartext bind hands over the account that can read the whole directory.
controls.audit: Device > Server Profiles > LDAP > <profile> > Require SSL/TLS secured connection.
controls.remediation: Tick Require SSL/TLS secured connection, and pair it with port 636 and certificate verification (PAN-AAA-002) - encryption without verification still accepts any certificate presented.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: LDAP profiles with SSL/TLS explicitly off.

controls.name: LDAP Verify Server Certificate
controls.description:
Encryption without verification stops an eavesdropper and not an interceptor: the firewall will complete a TLS handshake with whatever presents itself, so a machine-in-the-middle collects the bind credentials and relays the session.

ABSENT MEANS OFF here, unlike its neighbour four lines up the same dialog. The Help says so outright - "Select this option (cleared by default)" - and the committed object omits it. So this fires on absence, and PAN-AAA-001 does not. Neighbouring checkboxes on one screen do not share a default.

EVERY QUERY CLAUSES ON `kind`. Six kinds share one table and the measured implicit values live on every row, so a query on this column alone would fire on kinds it means nothing for.

It fires whether or not SSL is on. A profile with neither has two things to fix and the remediation for this one is the same either way.
controls.rationale: TLS to an unverified server authenticates nothing.
controls.audit: Device > Server Profiles > LDAP > <profile> > Verify Server Certificate for SSL sessions.
controls.remediation: Import the CA that issued the directory server's certificate into the firewall certificate store, then tick Verify Server Certificate.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: LDAP profiles not verifying the server certificate.

controls.name: RADIUS Uses Strong Authentication Protocol
controls.description:
PAP sends the password obscured only by the shared secret, so anyone who learns the secret - or captures enough traffic - recovers credentials. CHAP removes that, and PEAP-MSCHAPv2 or EAP-TTLS put the whole exchange inside TLS with server-certificate validation.

TWO TIERS, and they are the corpus's own: CHAP is the MINIMUM and PEAP-MSCHAPv2 the PREFERRED. PAP reports at the control's `high`; CHAP reports `medium` through the second query below. Anything TLS-wrapped passes.

NO IMPLICIT VALUE IS NEEDED. `protocol` is refused at COMMIT if omitted, so a RADIUS profile that exists always states one - measured, not assumed.

EVERY QUERY CLAUSES ON `kind`. Six kinds share one table and the measured implicit values live on every row, so a query on this column alone would fire on kinds it means nothing for.
controls.rationale: The protocol decides whether a captured RADIUS exchange yields a password.
controls.audit: Device > Server Profiles > RADIUS > <profile> > Authentication Protocol.
controls.remediation: Move to PEAP-MSCHAPv2 or EAP-TTLS, which needs a certificate profile on the RADIUS profile so the server certificate is validated. CHAP is the floor, not the target.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: RADIUS profiles below the preferred protocol.

queries.name: Meets the minimum, misses the target
queries.short_description: CHAP - the corpus minimum, not its preferred.

controls.name: TACACS+ Profile Hardening
controls.description:
TACACS+ encrypts the body of its packets with the shared secret, but PAP still carries the password in a form recoverable by anyone holding that secret. CHAP is the corpus minimum and its preferred value both.

THE CORPUS NOTE'S WIRE FORM IS WRONG FOR THIS KIND. It says to write `<protocol><CHAP/></protocol>`; measured 2026-09-09, tacplus stores `protocol` as TEXT and refuses the element form - "tacplus -> <name> -> protocol is invalid". The RADIUS profile beside it does take the element form, and `action=complete` returns the same value list for both, so the schema oracle cannot tell them apart.

The enumeration measured on this platform is CHAP | PAP. The corpus mentions `auto` on 12.1; it is not offered here.

EVERY QUERY CLAUSES ON `kind`. Six kinds share one table and the measured implicit values live on every row, so a query on this column alone would fire on kinds it means nothing for.
controls.rationale: PAP inside TACACS+ is recoverable by anyone holding the shared secret.
controls.audit: Device > Server Profiles > TACACS+ > <profile> > Authentication Protocol.
controls.remediation: Set the protocol to CHAP. Pair it with use-single-connection and a per-device shared secret, and reach the TACACS+ server over the management network only.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: TACACS+ profiles using PAP.

controls.name: SAML IdP Certificate Validation Enabled
controls.description:
With validation off the firewall accepts a SAML assertion signed by anything. That is CVE-2020-2021, an authentication bypass: forge an assertion and become any user the IdP could have named.

ABSENT MEANS ON. `validate-idp-certificate` is IMPLICIT YES - measured by writing a profile without the key and opening it in the UI, where the box renders checked. So this fires only on an EXPLICIT `no`, which is somebody having turned it off. Reading absence as "off" would report every unedited SAML profile in an estate as bypassable.

EVERY QUERY CLAUSES ON `kind`. Six kinds share one table and the measured implicit values live on every row, so a query on this column alone would fire on kinds it means nothing for.

A bare saml-idp profile cannot exist: `certificate`, `entity-id`, `sso-url` and `sso-bindings` are all refused at commit if missing, so there is always an IdP certificate for this setting to validate.
controls.rationale: Validation off is an authentication bypass with a CVE attached.
controls.audit: Device > Server Profiles > SAML Identity Provider > <profile> > Validate Identity Provider Certificate.
controls.remediation: Tick Validate Identity Provider Certificate. It needs the IdP's signing certificate to be CA-issued and a certificate profile holding that CA; a self-signed IdP certificate is the case the CVE mitigation assumes.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: SAML profiles with IdP certificate validation explicitly off.

controls.name: SAML Message Signing Enforced
controls.description:
Signing the firewall's own authentication requests protects the outbound leg: without it an attacker can tamper with a request in flight. The corpus sets no MINIMUM here - certificate validation already covers the inbound assertion - so this is a preferred-value control and carries its preferred-gap severity.

ABSENT MEANS ON, measured the same way as PAN-AAA-008. Fires only on an explicit `no`.

EVERY QUERY CLAUSES ON `kind`. Six kinds share one table and the measured implicit values live on every row, so a query on this column alone would fire on kinds it means nothing for.

The signing certificate itself is configured on the authentication profile, not here, so a finding on this leaf is about the flag rather than about a missing certificate.
controls.rationale: An unsigned request leg is tamperable in flight.
controls.audit: Device > Server Profiles > SAML Identity Provider > <profile> > Sign SAML Message to IdP.
controls.remediation: Tick Sign SAML Message to IdP, and set a Certificate for Signing Requests on the authentication profile that uses this IdP.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: SAML profiles not signing messages to the IdP.

controls.name: Authentication Profile Allow Lists Scoped
controls.description:
An authentication profile's allow-list decides WHICH users may authenticate through it. Set to `all`, every user the method can reach is admitted - so on a profile bound to administrators, one directory-wide phishing success reaches the management plane.

SCOPED TO ADMINISTRATIVE PROFILES, which is the corpus's own scoping and the same ruling Jason gave for PAN-AUTH-020: "GlobalProtect, Captive Portal, and even unused authentication profiles are very much separate controls." A profile counts as administrative when something under `mgt-config/users` or `deviceconfig/system` names it - derived from the referrer walk PAN-AUTH-025 already performs, which is what turns "which profiles do administrators use" from an open question into a column.

THE SUBJECT IS THE PROFILE, not the administrator. PAN-AUTH-019 and 020 moved to the account because their assertions were about a person's exposure; this one is about a property OF the profile and the remediation is on the profile, so it stays here. Jason, 2026-09-09: the per-user ruling "is not a general rule. The other authentication profile controls should stay profile-centric."

`all` is not a value somebody chose - it is what the Add form leaves behind, and all nine profiles on the lab carry it. That is why the administrative clause is load-bearing rather than decorative: without it this fires on every authentication profile in every estate.
controls.rationale: An admin-bound profile open to the whole directory turns one phished user into management-plane access.
controls.audit: Device > Authentication Profile > <profile> > Advanced > Allow List, for each profile an administrator authenticates through.
controls.remediation: Replace `all` with the named administrator group, sourced through LDAP group mapping over a verified TLS connection (PAN-AAA-001 and 002). Where the profile serves both administrators and users, split it - the allow-list is the only thing separating them.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: Administrator-bound profiles whose allow list is `all`.

controls.name: Administrator MFA Delivered by RADIUS or SAML
controls.description:
An MFA server profile is the firewall's DIRECT integration with a vendor's API - Duo v2, Okta Adaptive, PingID or RSA SecurID - and the platform invokes it for END-USER authentication through Authentication Policy only. It is not invoked for administrator login to the web interface, and not for GlobalProtect.

So an authentication profile that an administrator authenticates through, carrying an MFA factor, does not give that administrator a second factor. It gives the configuration the APPEARANCE of one. That is the finding: not missing MFA, which is PAN-AUTH-019's subject, but MFA that is configured, visible in the UI, reported by every config audit as present, and silently ignored at the moment it would matter.

Three passages say so in different words. Guide p.221: "For remote user authentication to GlobalProtect portals and gateways and for administrator authentication to the Panorama and PAN-OS web interface, the firewall integrates with MFA vendors using RADIUS and SAML only." Help p.941 says the API integration enforces MFA "through Authentication policy for end-user authentication only (not for GlobalProtect authentication or administrator authentication)". Help p.839 says it of the Factors tab itself: "Although you can configure additional factors, they will not be enforced for these use cases." None of them was trusted alone: the same Help was measured wrong twice this month on the lockout fields. Measured 2026-09-10: an administrator bound to a profile whose one factor points at an unresolvable Duo host logged in instantly with the password alone.

ADMINISTRATIVE is the whole control. The identical profile serving Authentication Policy is correct configuration and must not fire - which is why the lab carries the pair, two profiles differing in nothing but whether an administrator is bound to one.
controls.rationale: Administrators appear to have a second factor and do not have one.
controls.audit: Device > Authentication Profile > <profile> > Factors, for each profile named under mgt-config/users or deviceconfig/system. Any MFA server profile listed there is inert for administrator login.
controls.remediation: Deliver the second factor through the first factor instead: point the profile's Type at a RADIUS server profile for the MFA vendor's RADIUS endpoint, or at a SAML IdP that enforces MFA. Then remove the Factors entry, which is doing nothing. Keep vendor-API MFA profiles for Authentication Policy, where they work.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: Administrator-bound profiles with additional factors enabled and at least one listed.

controls.name: Authentication Sequence Fallback Order Safe
controls.description:
An authentication sequence tries its profiles top to bottom until one succeeds, so a member whose method is `local-database` or `none` is a way in with a credential the firewall itself holds - reached whenever everything above it fails, including when the external servers are down or unreachable. On a sequence an ADMINISTRATOR authenticates through, that is a management-plane login that bypasses the identity system, and an attacker who can knock the external servers over can force it.

SCOPED TO ADMINISTRATIVE SEQUENCES, the corpus's own wording: "No admin-facing authentication sequence falls back to local-database." A sequence counts as administrative when something under `mgt-config/users` or `deviceconfig/system` names it - every administrative binding accepts a sequence, measured 2026-09-11, including both device-wide leaves, which REFUSE a local-database profile but accept a sequence containing one. The identical sequence behind captive portal is other people's control, and the lab carries the pair.

THE VENDOR RECOMMENDS THIS SHAPE. Help p.843: "Make the local authentication profile the last profile in the sequence so it's only used if all external authentication methods fail." The corpus excepts documented break-glass; whether it is documented is not in the configuration, so the control reports and the consultant decides.

`exit-sequence-on-failure` (implicit NO, measured) does not clear it: it stops the sequence when credentials match a profile and fail, and a server that does not answer is not a failed match.
controls.rationale: A local fallback on an administrator sequence is a login the identity system cannot revoke.
controls.audit: Device > Authentication Sequence - for each sequence named under an administrator account or Device > Setup > Management > Authentication Settings, list the profiles in order and each one's Type.
controls.remediation: Remove local-database profiles from administrator-facing sequences. Keep break-glass as a separate, documented local account with its own profile rather than a silent fallback inside every administrator's login path.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: Administrator-bound sequences with a local-database or none member.

controls.name: Unused AAA Server Profiles Removed (Hygiene)
controls.description:
A server profile nothing references is configuration debt: a live definition nobody audits, often pointing at an AAA server that was decommissioned, and one binding away from being used.

AN UNUSED CLAIM IS ONLY AS GOOD AS THE LIST OF HIDING PLACES, so the reference count comes from walking the WHOLE merged payload for `server-profile` rather than visiting known paths - the same walk PAN-AUTH-025 uses, and the same reason: a path an enumeration missed would report an in-use profile as unused, and the remediation here is deletion.

A reference from inside a vsys resolves to that vsys's profile of the name when one exists and to the shared one otherwise. Attributing it wrongly is two errors at once - the real profile reports unused and the same-named orphan reports in use.

This one does NOT clause on kind: an orphan is an orphan whatever it authenticates.
controls.rationale: An orphaned AAA profile is a live definition nobody is maintaining.
controls.audit: Device > Server Profiles - for each profile, search the configuration for its name.
controls.remediation: Delete the profile. PAN-OS refuses a delete that would break a reference and names the referring path, so a refusal is itself the answer to 'is this really unused'.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: Server profiles nothing on the appliance references.

controls.name: Enable Minimum Password Complexity Enforcement
controls.description:
The master switch for the password-complexity engine. While it is off, every individual requirement on the device is stored but not enforced - a device can show a 12-character minimum and accept a one-character password.

Measured 2026-09-03: absent means OFF, and enabling it through the UI writes ONLY the flag. The zeros shown on that form are rendered defaults, not stored values, so the easiest path through the GUI produces a policy that is switched on and requires nothing.
controls.rationale: Administrative passwords are the last barrier when every other control has been bypassed, and a firewall's administrator holds the policy that protects everything behind it.
controls.audit: Device > Setup > Management > Minimum Password Complexity > Enabled.
controls.remediation: Tick Enabled, and set the individual requirements in the SAME change - enabling alone leaves every requirement at zero.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: Default baseline query.

controls.name: Minimum Password Length
controls.description:
Enforces a floor on local administrator password length. The corpus minimum is 12 (CIS) and the preferred value 15 (DISA STIG).

The configurable range is 6 to 16, so a zero is reachable only by ABSENCE - a deliberate zero cannot be written. A stored 0 for this key therefore always means never configured.

These settings are INERT while password complexity is disabled - the device enforces none of them. That does not change this finding, which is true either way, but it does change the remediation: fixing this alone accomplishes nothing until PAN-AUTH-001 is also fixed.
controls.rationale: Administrative passwords are the last barrier when every other control has been bypassed, and a firewall's administrator holds the policy that protects everything behind it.
controls.audit: Device > Setup > Management > Minimum Password Complexity > Minimum Length.
controls.remediation: Set Minimum Length to at least 12; 15 where clients allow it. The maximum the device accepts is 16.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: Default baseline query.

controls.name: New Password Minimum Character Difference
controls.description:
Requires characters to change on rotation, stopping trivial increments like Password1 to Password2. Corpus minimum 3, preferred 8; this control asserts the preferred 8. Jason, 2026-09-14: the control asserts the corpus PREFERRED value, not the minimum - one check, at the stricter number. An assessor who sees the finding reduces its severity where the weaker value is justified.

An assessor who sees the finding reduces its severity where the weaker value is justified.

controls.name: Password Expiration Period
controls.description:
Bounds how long a leaked credential stays usable. The corpus minimum is 90 days and the preferred value 60; this control asserts the preferred 60. Jason, 2026-09-14: the control asserts the corpus PREFERRED value, not the minimum - one check, at the stricter number. An assessor who sees the finding reduces its severity where the weaker value is justified.

This is the one setting on this form where BOTH ENDS are wrong. Zero means passwords NEVER expire, and a large value means they expire too rarely - so the control fires on 0 and on anything above 60, and passes between 1 and 60. A less-than comparison would have passed a 365-day expiry and failed the preferred 60.

These settings are INERT while password complexity is disabled - the device enforces none of them. That does not change this finding, which is true either way, but it does change the remediation: fixing this alone accomplishes nothing until PAN-AUTH-001 is also fixed.
controls.rationale: Administrative passwords are the last barrier when every other control has been bypassed, and a firewall's administrator holds the policy that protects everything behind it.
controls.audit: Device > Setup > Management > Minimum Password Complexity > Required Password Change Period.
controls.remediation: Set Required Password Change Period to 60 days or fewer, and not to 0. Where MFA and breach monitoring are in place, review whether forced rotation is still the right policy for your standard - this control asserts the corpus preferred value.

controls.name: Disallow Post-Expiration Admin Logins
controls.description:
How many times an administrator may still log in after their password has expired. The secure value is ZERO, which is also the default - so this control fires only where somebody has deliberately allowed expired credentials to keep working.

The range is 0 to 3.

These settings are INERT while password complexity is disabled - the device enforces none of them. That does not change this finding, which is true either way, but it does change the remediation: fixing this alone accomplishes nothing until PAN-AUTH-001 is also fixed.

controls.audit: Device > Setup > Management > Minimum Password Complexity > Post Expiration Admin Login Count.
controls.remediation: Set Post Expiration Admin Login Count to 0. Before enforcing it, make sure a break-glass or console path exists - this setting can lock every administrator out of a device whose passwords have expired.

controls.name: Failed Login Attempts Before Lockout
controls.description:
Locks an administrator account after N consecutive failed logins, which is what stops online password guessing and spraying.

BOUNDED AT BOTH ENDS, and the low end is not what it looks like. The device accepts 0 to 10. A 0 does not mean 'strict' - it means LOCKOUT IS DISABLED ENTIRELY, so it is the worst value available rather than the best, and it is also the implicit value: measured 2026-09-04 on the unconfigured Authentication Settings form. A comparison written as 'more than 5 is a finding' passes every unconfigured device in an estate.

The corpus grades 'more than 10' as high; the device grammar is 0-10, so that band cannot be reached. The reachable grading is 0 (sentinel, high), 1-5 (passes), 6-10 (medium).
controls.rationale: Administrative access to the firewall is access to every policy behind it.
controls.audit: Device > Setup > Management > Authentication Settings > Failed Attempts.
controls.remediation: Set Failed Attempts to 5 or fewer; 3 is the common hardening target. Do not leave it at 0, which disables lockout. Pair it with a non-zero Lockout Time (PAN-AUTH-015) or a locked account releases immediately.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: Default baseline query.

queries.name: Severity: 6 to 10
queries.short_description: failed attempts before lockout 6 to 10 — reported medium.

controls.name: Admin Account Lockout Duration
controls.description:
How long a locked administrator account stays locked. The device accepts 0 to 60 minutes.

ZERO IS THE STRONGEST VALUE HERE, which is the opposite of PAN-AUTH-014 on the same screen, and the reason the two cannot share a shape. The PAN-OS field help states it outright: "A value of 0 (default) means the lockout applies until another administrator manually unlocks the account" - and, explicitly, that failed-attempts set with lockout-time left at 0 locks the user until a manual unlock. So 0 is stricter than any duration, not weaker, and reporting it as "below 30 minutes" would flag the most restrictive setting available as a weakness.

The finding is therefore the EXCLUDED MIDDLE: 1 to 29 minutes - long enough to have been set deliberately, short enough not to throttle a guessing attack. The corpus minimum is 15 and the preferred value 30, and the threshold is the preferred. Jason, 2026-09-14: the control asserts the corpus PREFERRED value, not the minimum - one check, at the stricter number. An assessor who sees the finding reduces its severity where the weaker value is justified. 0 is also the implicit value, so an untouched device does not fire this. That is correct: with failed-attempts also 0 nothing ever locks, and PAN-AUTH-014 is the control that says so.

There is no severity scale, and none is needed - a 29-minute window has nothing to grade inside it.
controls.rationale: Administrative access to the firewall is access to every policy behind it.
controls.audit: Device > Setup > Management > Authentication Settings > Lockout Time.
controls.remediation:
Set Lockout Time to at least 30 minutes; Palo Alto's own field help recommends 30 "to prevent continuous login attempts from a malicious actor", which is also the corpus preferred value this control asserts. The maximum is 60.

Leaving it at 0 is stronger still - the account holds until an administrator unlocks it - and is a legitimate choice. Understand the trade first: an attacker who can reach the login page can lock every administrator out and leave them there. Pair either choice with a non-zero Failed Attempts (PAN-AUTH-014), or nothing locks at all.

A locked account is released with `request authentication unlock-admin`; `show authentication locked-users` lists them.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: Default baseline query.

controls.name: Management Session Idle Timeout
controls.description:
Ends an idle GUI or CLI session, closing the window in which an unattended console can be used by whoever walks past it. The device accepts 1 to 1440 minutes, or 0.

BOUNDED AT BOTH ENDS. 0 means sessions NEVER time out and is a sentinel - worse than any large number, though a naive comparison ranks it as the best possible value.

The implicit value is 60, MEASURED rather than assumed: the unconfigured form labels the field '60 (default)' - 2026-09-04, PA-5220. That matters because it decides what an untouched device reports. At 60 it is a live session an hour after the administrator walked away, which is a finding; had the implicit value been 0 it would have been the sentinel instead, and a more serious one.
controls.rationale: Administrative access to the firewall is access to every policy behind it.
controls.audit: Device > Setup > Management > Authentication Settings > Idle Timeout.
controls.remediation: Set Idle Timeout to 10 minutes or fewer. Do not set 0, which disables the timeout entirely. The same screen's Max Session Time is a separate limit and does not substitute for this one.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: Default baseline query.

queries.name: Severity: 11 to 60
queries.short_description: minutes of idle time before logout 11 to 60 — reported medium.

controls.name: API Key Lifetime Configured
controls.description:
How long a generated API key stays valid. The device accepts 1 to 525600 minutes, or 0.

The floor is ANY non-zero lifetime, so this fires on one value: 0, meaning keys never expire. A stolen key is then permanent, and the only remedy is expiring every key at once. 0 is also the implicit value - measured 2026-09-04, where the form reads '0 (default)' - so every device that has not been configured fires this.

The corpus grades longer lifetimes too (over a day medium, over a week high), but those bands sit above the floor and are unreachable while the assertion is 'configured at all'. They are kept rather than trimmed, because the scale is the corpus author's and a later tightening of the floor would want them.
controls.rationale: Administrative access to the firewall is access to every policy behind it.
controls.audit: Device > Setup > Management > Authentication Settings > API Key Lifetime.
controls.remediation: Set API Key Lifetime to a non-zero value; 1440 minutes (24 hours) is the common target. Changing the lifetime or the master key INVALIDATES EXISTING KEYS - coordinate with whoever owns the automation before doing it.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: Default baseline query.

controls.name: Authentication Profile Failed-Attempt Lockout
controls.description:
Locks an account authenticated through this profile after N consecutive failures, extending brute-force protection to externally authenticated administrators.

BOUNDED AT BOTH ENDS, and the low end is the trap. The device accepts 0 to 10, and a 0 does not mean strict - it means UNLIMITED LOGIN ATTEMPTS. It is also the implicit value in normal operational mode, so a comparison written as 'more than 5 is a finding' passes every unconfigured profile in an estate.

A lockout-time of 0 does NOT disable this. The Web Interface Help says on p.840 that a non-zero Failed Attempts with Lockout Time 0 means the user is never locked out; that was MEASURED FALSE on 2026-09-04, three failed logins against a profile with failed-attempts 2 and lockout-time 0 locked the account until an administrator released it. The same wrong claim appears on p.707 about the device-admin lockout and was measured false there too. So this control asserts on failed-attempts alone.

Does not apply to SAML profiles: the Help prefixes both lockout fields '(All authentication types except SAML)'.

The query EXCLUDES SAML profiles rather than merely noting the exception, because a finding the platform cannot act on is a false positive. The lab has one - asdfasdf on pan-fw-111 - and it fired before the exclusion was added.
controls.rationale: Administrative access to the firewall is access to every policy behind it.
controls.audit: Device > Authentication Profile > <profile> > Advanced > Failed Attempts.
controls.remediation: Set Failed Attempts to 5 or fewer on the profile; 3 is the common hardening target. Do not leave it at 0, which permits unlimited guessing. Set a Lockout Time as well - 0 holds the account until an administrator releases it, which is stronger but is an availability decision.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: Lockout disabled, or a limit looser than 3 attempts.

queries.name: Severity: 4 to 5
queries.short_description: failed attempts before lockout 4 to 5 — reported low.

queries.name: Severity: 6 to 10
queries.short_description: failed attempts before lockout 6 to 10 — reported medium.

controls.name: Multi-Factor Authentication for Administrative Access
controls.description:
COMPLETE AS AN INTERVIEW QUESTION, not a config check. Jason, 2026-09-14: "This is not a config check, it needs to be handled via interview. Let's mark 020 as complete." It stays in the catalogue, inactive and generating no findings, so the question and the reason travel with the control. The interview: how does each administrator's login get a second factor - which RADIUS, SAML or Cloud Identity Engine policy enforces it, and are any administrators exempt? Deferred 2026-09-10 for the same reason: Jason: "PAN-AUTH-020 is not derived from the config, lock that decision in."

PAN-OS gives an administrator a second factor only through the FIRST factor - a RADIUS server, a SAML identity provider, or the Cloud Authentication Service - and none of the three records in the firewall's configuration whether MFA is enforced on the other side. The one factor the configuration DOES show, the Factors tab, is not enforced for administrators: measured 2026-09-10, oep-mfa-admin logged in with its password alone through a profile carrying an MFA factor (PAN-AAA-011 reports that trap). The Cloud Authentication `force-mfa` key records an operator's claim about the IdP, not a check.

So a pass here would credit MFA the configuration cannot see, and a failure would fire on administrators whose MFA lives on the server. Kept in the catalog, inactive, so the model, compiler and tests remain; the evidence belongs to the RADIUS/SAML/CIE side.

Requires a second factor on the path an ADMINISTRATOR authenticates by, so a stolen password alone cannot reach the management plane.

THE FINDING IS ABOUT A PERSON, NOT A PROFILE. This was first built over AuthenticationProfile and left inactive, because a profile row cannot say which administrators are exposed: two accounts on one appliance can sit behind different profiles, and the estate's profiles also serve GlobalProtect and Captive Portal, which are separate controls. Jason, 2026-09-08, ABOUT THIS CONTROL AND PAN-AUTH-019 SPECIFICALLY: "We generate findings per user, not per profile... A row is a specific user, and its values are the value checks." So it reports one finding per administrator, on the same row as that account's other findings.

THAT IS NOT A GENERAL RULE, and he said so on 2026-09-09: the other authentication profile controls stay profile-centric. PAN-AUTH-018 asserts something about a profile's own lockout configuration and its subject is the profile. What moves a control onto the account is that its assertion is about a PERSON'S exposure, which a profile row cannot express because two administrators on one appliance can sit behind different profiles.

IT RESOLVES THROUGH TWO BINDINGS. The per-account `mgt-config/users/entry/authentication-profile` wins; otherwise the device-wide `deviceconfig/system/authentication-profile` covers the account. `admin_mfa_enabled` is the resolved profile's flag.

NO PROFILE AT ALL FIRES. An administrator on the local database has no second factor, so a stolen password alone reaches the management plane - which is exactly what this asserts. It is a separate failure from PAN-AUTH-019 (the credential is local and unrevocable) and both report on the row, because one bad thing is not excused by another.

The device enforces a prerequisite that needs no encoding: `mfa-enable` is REJECTED unless the profile already references an MFA factor, so an enabled profile always has one. A SAML profile may carry MFA at the identity provider instead, which this cannot see - that is a downgrade the assessor makes.
controls.rationale: Administrative access to the firewall is access to every policy behind it.
controls.audit: Device > Administrators > <account> > Authentication Profile, then Device > Authentication Profile > <that profile> > Factors > Enable Additional Authentication Factors. Where the account names no profile, check Device > Setup > Management > Authentication Settings.
controls.remediation: Create an MFA server profile, add it as a factor on the authentication profile, then enable Multi Factor Authentication - in that order, because the device refuses the flag without a factor. SAML profiles may carry MFA at the identity provider instead, which this control cannot see.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: No second factor governs this administrator.

controls.name: External Authentication for Administrator Accounts
controls.description:
An administrator account is centrally authenticated only when BOTH halves hold: authentication reaches an external identity service, and no credential is stored on the device. This reports every account where either fails.

A BOUND PROFILE IS NOT EVIDENCE OF CENTRALIZATION. The method matters. On the lab, three of the four accounts that passed an earlier version of this control were reaching the firewall's OWN local user database through a profile - `oep-auth-lockout` and `oep-auth-hardened` are method `local-database`, and `aegis_auth_prof` names no method at all. A control titled for external authentication was passing accounts that do not use it. External means RADIUS, TACACS+, LDAP, Kerberos, SAML or Cloud.

A STORED CREDENTIAL STILL COUNTS EVEN WHERE A PROFILE IS BOUND. Measured 2026-09-08 as an A/B on one account: with its authentication profile unbound it authenticated; with the same password and the profile bound back a minute later it was refused, and the device logged the profile and its unreachable server. A per-account profile takes precedence and the local password is not tried. So the credential is unreachable while the binding holds - and it is still a secret that leaves with a configuration backup, and becomes live the moment somebody removes the profile. Latent, the way a password profile that weakens the global policy is a latent exemption. Jason, 2026-09-08: "mfa/external=yes and local phash=no".

BOTH CREDENTIAL KINDS COUNT. The corpus note names `phash` only; an SSH public key in the same config is exactly as local. pan-fw-111's `azureuser` carries no password at all and is a superuser reachable by a key nobody centrally holds.

The DEVICE-WIDE binding `deviceconfig/system/authentication-profile` is honoured when the account names no profile of its own, and it is a different mechanism from the per-account one. Measured 2026-09-08 with both device-wide leaves pushed at an unreachable server, two attempts two seconds apart: an account with NO credential was sent to the profile and timed out, while an account holding a stored password authenticated locally and the profile was never consulted for it. So it covers exactly the accounts that have no local credential - which is why resolving through it is right, and why an account holding a password is not excused by it.

`client-certificate-only` clears nothing. Web Interface Help p.825 scopes it to the web interface - "Use only client certificate authentication (web)" - and it neither replaces the stored credential nor centralizes the account.

This is a POSTURE control. A break-glass account is a legitimate reason for one of these to exist, and an assessor gives it; the control's job is to put every one of them in front of somebody, not to decide which are documented. That reading is reinforced by the other edge of the precedence measurement: when the AAA server is down, nobody bound to it per-account can log in at all.
controls.rationale: A credential that exists only on the device is one no joiner-mover-leaver process can reach.
controls.audit: Device > Administrators > <account> > Authentication Profile, then Device > Authentication Profile > <that profile> > Authentication > Type. Check the account's Password and SSH key while you are there.
controls.remediation: Bind the account to an authentication profile whose type is TACACS+, RADIUS, LDAP, Kerberos or SAML - not `local database` and not `none` - and then remove its local password and any public key. Removing the credential is the half that gets skipped, and it is the half that survives somebody unbinding the profile later. Where an account must stay local as break-glass, vault the credential offline, alert on its use, and record the decision.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: Not reached by an external identity service, or holding a device-stored credential.

controls.name: Default 'admin' Account Disabled or Replaced
controls.description:
`admin` is the username every PAN-OS device ships with and every password spray starts from. Named per-person accounts should carry day-to-day work, and the default account should be deleted or held as vaulted break-glass.

IT FIRES ON PRESENCE, AT THE CORPUS SEVERITY. Whether the password is still the factory one is not in the configuration - `phash` is a hash - so this cannot confirm the whole failure the severity describes. That is not a reason to soften it. The consultant can see the account, ask how it is held, and reduce the severity when it meets the control language; nothing downstream can raise a severity that arrived understated, so an understated one is the finding nobody looks at again.

Jason, 2026-09-08: "if an account with name 'admin' exists, it should be a critical finding. The consultant can then do the work to reduce the severity if it meets minimum control language. We can't account for that."

The corpus's `minimum_value_descr` and `preferred_value_descr` split this into a password check and a presence check, and the split does not survive contact with what a config read can see. Read the two together: the assertion is that the default account should not be sitting there.
controls.rationale: A universally known username is a free half of every credential-stuffing attempt.
controls.audit: Device > Administrators - is there an entry named `admin`, and do named superusers exist beside it?
controls.remediation: Create and TEST a named superuser first, then delete `admin`. Where it is kept as break-glass, vault the credential, bind login alerting to it, record the decision - and downgrade the finding, which is the assessor's call rather than the tool's.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: An account named admin exists.

controls.name: Limit Number of Superuser Accounts
controls.description:
Every superuser is a full-compromise path: the role can rewrite policy, read secrets, create further administrators and disable the logging that would show it. Day-to-day work belongs on least-privilege roles.

THE FINDING NAMES THE ACCOUNTS, NOT THE APPLIANCE. The assertion is about a count, but the remediation is per-account - somebody decides which of the seven get demoted - so each superuser reports, and they share one graded severity because they share one cause.

`superuser_cohort_size` is the appliance's superuser total written onto each superuser row, and 0 on every account holding another role. That is literally correct - a devicereader belongs to no superuser cohort - and it keeps every query on this control to ONE field, so a threshold is the only number in play. The graded severities are the two non-baseline queries below: 3 to 5 reports low, 6 to 10 reports medium, and anything above reports the control default.

Thresholds are the corpus's proposed baselines - 5 minimum, 2 preferred - and are pending sign-off.
controls.rationale: Superuser count is the size of the blast radius, and it only ever grows on its own.
controls.audit: Device > Administrators - count entries whose Administrator Type is Dynamic / Superuser.
controls.remediation: Move operators, auditors and automation onto custom admin roles scoped to what they do, and leave superuser to a named few plus break-glass. Demoting an account does not disturb how it authenticates.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: More than two superusers on this appliance.

queries.name: Severity: 3 to 5
queries.short_description: superuser accounts 3 to 5 — reported low.

queries.name: Severity: 6 to 10
queries.short_description: superuser accounts 6 to 10 — reported medium.

controls.name: Unused Authentication Profiles (Hygiene)
controls.description:
An authentication profile that nothing references is configuration debt. It authenticates nobody while it stays unreferenced, but it is a definition nobody is maintaining, and binding it later applies whatever it was left holding - often a stale AAA server, or no lockout at all.

AN UNUSED CLAIM IS ONLY AS GOOD AS THE LIST OF HIDING PLACES. The CLI grammar names eight referrer paths on a firewall: the two `deviceconfig/system` leaves, per-administrator `mgt-config/users`, captive portal, GlobalProtect portal and gateway, secure web gateway, and authentication objects. Rather than visit those eight, the normalizer walks the WHOLE merged payload for the two referrer keys - a path the grammar missed would otherwise make this control report an in-use profile as unused, which is the worst direction for a hygiene control to fail in. The grammar list is kept as a cross-check on the walk.

Four of the eight have been seen carrying a real reference and confirmed readable from merged config, and they cover all four structural shapes: an appliance-level container of entries, a device leaf, a vsys leaf, and a leaf nested inside a vsys entry. The four unseen paths reuse those shapes.

A REFERENCE RESOLVES BY SCOPE. A referrer inside a vsys resolves to that vsys's profile of the name when one exists and to the shared one otherwise, so the count lands on the definition actually in use rather than on a same-named neighbour.

Reported per appliance. A profile pushed from a template exists separately in each firewall's configuration, and referenced on one device but not another is two facts about two devices.
controls.rationale: An orphaned profile is a live definition nobody audits, one binding away from being in use.
controls.audit: Device > Authentication Profile - for each profile, search the configuration for its name.
controls.remediation: Delete the profile. PAN-OS refuses a delete that would break a reference and names the referring path in the error, so a refusal is itself the answer to 'is this really unused'. Where a profile is staged for work not yet done, record that rather than leaving it to be rediscovered.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: Profiles nothing on the appliance references.

controls.name: Password Profiles Do Not Weaken Global Policy (Hygiene)
controls.description:
A password profile OVERRIDES the global Minimum Password Complexity settings for the accounts it is applied to - Web Interface Help p.822 - so it is an exemption rather than another place the same values live. This asks whether the exemption is weaker than what it replaces.

THE COMPARISON IS NOT 'profile larger than global'. Zero is a sentinel on BOTH sides: 0 means the password never expires, which is the weakest setting available rather than the strictest. The corpus note says to flag any larger value, and the lab holds exactly the case that breaks: a profile with expiration-period 365 on a device whose global is 0. Numerically larger, semantically STRONGER, and flagging it would report a profile that improves the policy.

So a profile weakens the global policy when it never expires and the global does, or when both expire and the profile's period is longer. A global of 0 cannot be weakened by anything.

The comparison is stored on the row rather than expressed as a query, because the search layer compares a field to a LITERAL and this is the only control in the corpus needing field-to-field. Both operands are kept as columns so the conclusion can be checked rather than taken.

The corpus also asks to flag the ACCOUNTS assigned such a profile. That needs the administrator model and is enrichment for the remediation, not part of the assertion - a profile that weakens policy is a latent exemption whether or not anyone holds it today. Note the platform will not let one be assigned to an account using local database authentication.
controls.rationale: An exemption nobody audited is how a hardened policy stops applying to the accounts that matter.
controls.audit: Device > Password Profiles > <profile> > Required Password Change Period, against Device > Setup > Management > Minimum Password Complexity.
controls.remediation: Either raise the global expiration period to match, or shorten the profile's Required Password Change Period so it is no longer than the global one. Setting the profile to 0 does not fix it - 0 means the password never expires, which is the weakest value available.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: Default baseline query.

controls.name: Certificate Key Strength Minimums
controls.description:
Every certificate on the device must meet RSA 2048 or ECDSA P-256 as a floor. Remediation is REISSUANCE, not a configuration write - a weak key cannot be strengthened in place.

Neither the key size nor the algorithm exists in any PAN-OS configuration field. The `algorithm` field reports RSA or EC - the key algorithm, not its size - and no operational command carries the bit length either. Both are decoded from the X.509 blob PAN-OS stores under the misleadingly named `public-key`, which holds the entire certificate.

The threshold is per ALGORITHM and cannot be a single number. 256-bit EC is strong and 256-bit RSA is broken, so `key_size_bits < 2048` would flag the vendor's own TLSv1.3_Default - which is EC secp256r1 - while passing a hypothetical RSA 512. So the verdict is computed per certificate into one column, `key_strength_band`, and the query rests on that column.

THE PAIRED FORM THIS REPLACES WAS MEASURED WRONG. It was an OR of three algorithm-and-size groups plus a parse-error group, and a certificate whose algorithm matches none of the three literals has NO size recorded: the integer comparison drops a null from both sides of an inequality, the parse error is empty, and the certificate passed every threshold in silence. An Ed25519 certificate is that case today, and so is any key family the vendor adds next. The band has a member for it - `algorithm_has_no_floor` - and that member is on the FIRING side, so an algorithm this assessment carries no floor for is reported rather than passed.

A certificate that could not be decoded is reported, not passed. An unreadable certificate is not a compliant one.

A key below HALF the floor for its own algorithm is reported at critical rather than high. RSA 512 against a 2048-bit floor is not the same finding as RSA 1024, and the two are told apart by the band rather than by a threshold.
controls.rationale: A weak key undermines every certificate that chains to it, and unlike most findings this one cannot be fixed by editing configuration - the certificate has to be reissued and redistributed, which makes early detection worth more than usual.
controls.audit: Device > Certificate Management > Certificates shows each certificate; the key size is visible in the certificate detail. Confirm RSA is 2048 or above and EC is P-256 or above. A certificate reported here whose detail shows NO key size at all is the unreadable case and is reported deliberately - it has not been shown to meet any floor.
controls.remediation: Reissue the certificate with a compliant key and replace it wherever it is referenced. For CAs and long-lived certificates the corpus prefers RSA 3072 or ECDSA P-384.

queries.name: The key is below the strength floor carried for its own algorithm
queries.short_description: Any band other than at-or-above-floor: below, far below, undecodable, or an algorithm this assessment carries no floor for.

queries.name: The key is far below the floor for its algorithm
queries.short_description: Below HALF the floor - RSA 512 against a 2048-bit floor. Reported critical.

controls.name: No Weak Signature Algorithms (SHA-1/MD5)
controls.description:
A certificate signed with MD5 or SHA-1 inherits the weakness of that hash: both have practical collision attacks, and a collision is a forged certificate.

Like the key size, the signature algorithm exists in NO PAN-OS field - `algorithm` reports the key algorithm - and is decoded from the certificate itself.

MD5 is the floor and SHA-1 is reported alongside it, because the control is named for both. The corpus allows SHA-1 "only for internal legacy with a documented expiry", which is an organisational exception this cannot see: a SHA-1 finding may legitimately be closed as accepted, an MD5 finding should not be. The preferred state is SHA-256 or stronger exclusively. MD5 is reported at this control's own severity and SHA-1 one band below it, which is the distinction those two sentences describe.

THE HASH IS RESOLVED RATHER THAN MATCHED, and the query rests on the resolved name. Reading the signature algorithm's identifier for the substrings `md5` and `sha1` was measured wrong: an RSASSA-PSS certificate stores the identifier `rsassaPss`, which names NO hash at all - for PSS the hash lives in the signature parameters - so a PSS certificate signed with SHA-1 matched neither substring, carried no parse error, and passed. Every SHA-3 variant has the same shape. The hash is therefore decoded to a bare name in its own column, and a hash that could not be resolved is reported rather than passed.
controls.rationale: A signature is the only thing binding a certificate's identity to its key. A hash with practical collisions makes that binding forgeable, so the certificate proves nothing about who holds the key.
controls.audit: Read the signature algorithm on each certificate. Anything whose signing hash resolves to md5 or sha1 reports; sha256WithRSAEncryption and ecdsa-with-SHA256 or stronger pass. A certificate reported here whose algorithm cell reads `rsassaPss` or an unfamiliar identifier is the unresolved case: the identifier does not name the hash, so the hash has to be read out of the certificate itself before the finding can be accepted or dismissed.
controls.remediation: Reissue with a SHA-256 or stronger signature. Where a SHA-1 certificate is a documented legacy exception, record the expiry it was accepted until and close the finding against that, rather than leaving it open indefinitely.

queries.name: The signing hash has a practical collision attack, or could not be resolved
queries.short_description: md5, sha1, or a signature identifier that names no hash at all.

queries.name: The signing hash is SHA-1
queries.short_description: SHA-1 rather than MD5 or an unresolved hash. Reported medium.

controls.name: Certificate Profiles Enforce Revocation Checking
controls.description:
Certificate profiles govern how the firewall validates peer certificates - admin certificate authentication, GlobalProtect client certificates, SAML, syslog TLS. CRL or OCSP checking must be enabled, or a revoked credential keeps working until it expires.

Either leaf satisfies the floor. Measured 2026-09-02 from the blank Add Certificate Profile form: use-crl and use-ocsp both default to DISABLED, as do all four block-* options, so a profile that sets nothing performs no revocation checking at all. That uniformity is worth knowing rather than assuming - on the management plane, server-verification absent means ENABLED while its neighbour means disabled.

THE CONTROL HAS A SECOND HALF AND IT ONLY APPLIES WHERE THE FIRST PASSES: where revocation IS checked, a check that cannot reach an answer must stop the session rather than let it through. The two blocking settings decide that, and a profile is reported where EITHER inconclusive outcome is still allowed - an unknown status or a timed-out one - not only where both are. A profile that blocks on an unknown status and not on a timeout is the reachable attack: an adversary who can delay or drop the path to the responder gets the same result as a revoked certificate being accepted, and needs no access to the firewall to do it.

The fail-closed half is deliberately SILENT on a profile that checks no revocation at all. Those blocking settings have no check to fail closed on, so a finding there would name a consequence that cannot arise - and nothing is hidden by the silence, because the profile is already reported by this control's first half at the same severity.

FAILING CLOSED CAN LOCK ADMINISTRATORS OUT OF THE DEVICE, which is the vendor's own warning. Before enforcing it on an administrative path, establish which access paths the customer accepts being blocked when the responder cannot be reached.

NO INTERVAL IS ASSERTED. Three timeout leaves sit on this screen - CRL receive, OCSP receive and certificate status - with no stated precedence between them and no vendor default for any of them, so which one governs the blocking decision is not establishable and a number asserted here would be one nothing states.
controls.rationale: Revocation is the only mechanism that withdraws trust from a credential before it expires. Without it, a compromised administrator certificate remains valid for its full lifetime no matter how quickly the compromise is detected.
controls.audit: At Device > Certificate Management > Certificate Profile, confirm each profile has Use CRL or Use OCSP ticked. Note that OCSP takes precedence over CRL where both are on, as the dialog states. On every profile that has one ticked, also read the two blocking checkboxes below: both must be ticked, and either one left clear is reported. A profile with NEITHER revocation method ticked is reported for that instead, and its blocking settings are not assessed.
controls.remediation: Enable Use OCSP with Use CRL as fallback, and set Block session if certificate status is unknown and Block session if certificate status cannot be retrieved within timeout - without those, a failed check is indistinguishable from a passed one.

queries.name: Neither revocation method is in use
queries.short_description: Default baseline query: no CRL and no OCSP, so nothing withdraws trust from a credential before it expires.

queries.name: Revocation is checked and an inconclusive answer is let through
queries.short_description: The profile checks revocation and still allows an unknown status, a timed-out one, or both. Reported at this control's own severity.

controls.name: SSL/TLS Service Profiles Enforce TLS 1.2 Minimum
controls.description:
SSL/TLS service profiles set the protocol floor for every service terminating TLS on the device: management UI, GlobalProtect portal and gateway, Captive Portal, syslog. TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are formally deprecated by RFC 8996.

This control asserts the FLOOR and nothing else, which is what the corpus specifies. It is worth being explicit about what that leaves out: measured 2026-09-02, an absent algorithm key means ENABLED, so a profile carrying only a version range permits SHA-1 authentication and CBC encryption. Every profile in the lab does. Those settings are collected and shown beside the floor so an engineer can see them; PAN-CRT-009 asserts the SHA-1 authentication setting and nothing fires on the CBC or key-exchange ones.

THE FLOOR IS ASSERTED AS A PROPERTY AND NOT AS A LIST OF FORBIDDEN VALUES, which is a correction to how this control used to be queried. The old form enumerated tls1-0, tls1-1 and an empty floor; both halves of it were measured wrong. A stored token that is none of the four the device offers read as COMPLIANT under an enumeration, because it matched no forbidden literal - so a value nobody recognises passed. And an EMPTY floor is not a real state on a profile that exists: measured 2026-10-25 on pan-fw-201, a profile that omits min-version enforces a TLS 1.2 floor and therefore MEETS this control, so firing on the empty string reported every profile in the estate that simply does not write the key. The floor is now ranked against the device's own order and the assertion is 'below the rank of TLS 1.2', with an unrecognised token ranked BELOW tls1-0 so that it fires.

Assessed per profile per appliance per SCOPE. A name is not unique on a device - TLSv1.3_Default exists as both a predefined and a shared entry - and the predefined definition is the one in force.
controls.rationale: A profile is reusable by design, so a weak floor set once is inherited by every service that binds it. Auditing the bound profile alone misses the profile that is about to be bound.
controls.audit: At Device > Certificate Management > SSL/TLS Service Profile, confirm Min Version is TLSv1.2 or higher on every profile, not only the one bound to the management interface.
controls.remediation: Set Min Version to TLSv1.2 on each profile, or TLSv1.3 where every client supports it. A profile reported here whose Min Version cell is EMPTY in the dialog has not failed this control for being empty - read the running configuration, because an unrecognised stored token renders the same way and is what fires. Consider also unticking SHA1, which PAN-CRT-009 asserts, and the CBC encryption algorithms, which are enabled by default and are not covered by either control.

queries.name: The protocol floor is below TLS 1.2, or is a version this assessment does not recognise
queries.short_description: Default baseline query: the floor's rank in the device's own version order is below TLS 1.2's, which an unrecognised token also is.

controls.name: Management Certificate Issued by Trusted CA
controls.description:
The management UI certificate should chain to an organisation-trusted CA rather than the factory self-signed certificate, so administrators can detect man-in-the-middle interception of management sessions.

Split from PAN-MGT-010 because the protocol floor and the certificate are independent and have different remediations. Measured 2026-09-02: the shipped TLSv1.3_Default profile - the obvious fix for PAN-MGT-010 - carries /config/predefined/certificate's TLSv1.3_Default, which is the device's OWN factory certificate, common-name equal to the chassis serial and self-signed. Remediating PAN-MGT-010 the easy way therefore leaves this control failing, which is exactly why it is its own control.

What is decidable here is CA-ISSUED versus SELF-SIGNED, from PAN-OS's own subject and issuer hashes. Whether the issuing CA is the ORGANISATION'S is not a configuration fact and this control does not claim to decide it - the issuer is reported so a human can. A CA-issued certificate from an unexpected authority will pass and still deserve attention, and the corpus's preferred state goes further still: an internal-CA certificate whose SAN matches the management FQDN and which admin browsers already trust.

WHAT THIS CAN AND CANNOT DECIDE. Trust is not readable from configuration - there is no trust store here - so this classifies the ISSUER CHAIN as far as the device shows it. A chain terminating at a self-signed CA that is itself on the device is a PRIVATE root: nothing trusts it by default, and a browser rejects it exactly as it rejects a self-signed leaf. A chain that leaves the device may reach a public root, which cannot be confirmed here and is not claimed.

That distinction was previously collapsed, and the collapse hid a real case: a certificate signed by a lab CA created minutes earlier classified as CA-issued and PASSED, while Chrome refused the same chain with NET::ERR_CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID. The control was named for trust and asserted only 'not self-signed'.

The private-CA case is graded DOWN from the self-signed one rather than treated as equal. An organisation's own internal CA is also private, and a certificate it issued is a different conversation from one the device signed for itself - the remediation is to distribute the root or move to a public CA, not to stop using self-signed certificates. Jason, 2026-09-07.

THIS SEVERITY SCALE IS LOCAL, not from the corpus. controls.json carries no scale for this control; the bands below were added with the classification they grade.
controls.rationale: A self-signed management certificate trains administrators to click through browser warnings, which is precisely the reflex a man-in-the-middle on the management network depends on. The warning is the only thing distinguishing the real device from an impostor, and it stops being a signal once it is always present.
controls.audit: Confirm the SSL/TLS service profile bound at Device > Setup > Management > General Settings names a certificate whose Issuer differs from its Subject, and that the issuer is an authority the organisation recognises. Device > Certificate Management > Certificates shows both.
controls.remediation: Issue a certificate for the management interface from the organisation's CA, import it under Device > Certificate Management > Certificates, and reference it from the bound SSL/TLS service profile. Where no profile is bound yet, PAN-MGT-010 must be remediated first - the certificate is carried by the profile.

queries.name: The management certificate's issuer chain is not CA-issued
queries.short_description: Default baseline query: self-signed, a private CA on this device, undetermined, or nothing bound at all.

queries.name: The management certificate was issued by a private CA on this device
queries.short_description: A chain terminating at a self-signed CA held on the appliance. Reported low: the remediation is to distribute the root or move to a public CA, not to stop using self-signed certificates.

controls.name: Master Key Changed from Default
controls.description:
The master key encrypts every private key and stored secret on the device. The factory default is a PUBLICLY KNOWN value, so a firewall that never set one is protecting its key material with a shared secret anybody can look up - including the private keys behind its certificates.

Detected from `show system masterkey-properties`. An `expire-at` of 0 - which the CLI renders as 'unspecified' - means no key was ever set. The inference is that a lifetime is MANDATORY when setting one, in both the CLI and the GUI, so a key that has been set always carries a concrete expiry.

The corpus names this control '...and Rotated'. One test covers both halves: a concrete expiry means a key was set AND that a lifetime exists for it, so there is a rotation schedule. What cannot be established is WHEN it was changed - expire-at minus lifetime breaks when auto-renew is non-zero, since the expiry moves without the key changing - nor by whom, since no attribution field exists anywhere.
controls.rationale: Every other cryptographic control on the device rests on this one. A hardened SSL/TLS profile with a CA-issued certificate protects nothing if the private key behind it is encrypted with a value published in vendor documentation.
controls.audit: Run `show system masterkey-properties`. Expiry and reminder reading 'unspecified' means the default key is still in use. Concrete dates mean a key has been set.
controls.remediation: Set a master key at Device > Master Key and Diagnostics, or with `request master-key new-master-key <value> lifetime <hours>`, and store the value in the organisation's secret manager - it is unrecoverable and required to restore a configuration. Note this re-encrypts all key material through an auto-commit, and on an HA pair both members must carry the same key. From PAN-OS 12.2.2 this stops being optional: the device starts a 60-day grace period on detecting the default key, after which commits FAIL and HA sync is suspended.

queries.name: No master key has been set, or it could not be established that one has
queries.short_description: Default baseline query: the factory default is still in use, or the reading that would have said otherwise was never taken.

controls.name: Weak Algorithms Excluded from SSL/TLS Service Profiles
controls.description:
An SSL/TLS service profile controls far more than its protocol floor. It also selects the key exchange, encryption and authentication algorithms every service that binds it will negotiate, and ABSENT MEANS ENABLED - measured 2026-09-02 from a profile writing only a version range, whose every algorithm box renders ticked.

So a profile can satisfy PAN-CRT-005 with a TLS 1.2 floor and still permit SHA-1 authentication, CBC-mode encryption and static RSA key exchange. Every profile in the lab does.

This control asserts the MINIMUM, matching how the corpus draws that line on every other cryptographic surface: PAN-IKE-004 and PAN-IPS-003 exclude MD5 and SHA-1, PAN-MCR-003 requires SHA-2, PAN-DCP-002 removes 3DES, RC4 and MD5. SHA-1 is the only primitive of that class an SSL/TLS service profile can select, so it is the floor here. The preferred state goes further - AEAD ciphers only and ECDHE only, which is exactly PAN-DCP-002's preferred wording - and is remediation guidance rather than a second assertion.

A PROFILE PINNED TO TLS 1.3 IS NOT EXCLUDED, BUT ONLY AN EXPLICIT SELECTION FIRES THERE. Setting Min Version to TLSv1.3 greys SHA1 out and unticks it in the web interface, so a profile built there cannot carry both and does not fire. The XML API performs no such validation, so the combination CAN be written, and where it has been this control reports it. The vendor implemented the rule in one interface and not the other; that is their defect, and the configuration it allows should be rare. We report it because nobody can say how the device behaves in a state its own interface forbids, and an operational problem is a worse thing to leave unreported than an inert checkbox is to raise. This is a general principle for this corpus: where the UI validates a combination and the API does not, the assessment reports what is configured and says that its effect is not established.
controls.rationale: A profile is reusable by design, so weak algorithms selected once are inherited by every service that binds it - management UI, GlobalProtect, Captive Portal, syslog. And because absent means enabled, this is the state a profile arrives in by default: an administrator who sets only a version floor has not narrowed the algorithms at all, and the configuration gives no sign of it.
controls.audit: At Device > Certificate Management > SSL/TLS Service Profile, open each profile and read the Authentication Algorithms group. SHA1 must be unticked. Note that an unconfigured profile shows every box ticked, so nothing having been changed is the failing state rather than a neutral one. AND IF THIS FIRES ON A PROFILE WHOSE MIN VERSION IS TLSv1.3, THE BOX WILL LOOK UNTICKED AND GREYED OUT - that is not a false positive. The web interface greys it once the floor is TLSv1.3 and will not show you what is stored underneath; read the running configuration for `auth-algo-sha1` instead. A profile in that state was written over the XML API, which does not enforce the rule the UI does.
controls.remediation: Untick SHA1 under Authentication Algorithms. For the preferred state also untick the CBC encryption algorithms, leaving AES-GCM and CHACHA20-POLY1305, and untick RSA under Key Exchange Algorithms so that only DHE and ECDHE remain, which gives forward secrecy. Verify client compatibility first: removing CBC and static RSA breaks very old clients, which is why they are the preferred state rather than the floor.

queries.name: The profile selects SHA-1 among its authentication algorithms
queries.short_description: Default baseline query: SHA-1 is selected, either written on or left absent at a version range that renders it.

controls.name: SSH Management Ciphers Restricted to Strong Algorithms
controls.description:
Restricts the management SSH server to the corpus PREFERRED cipher - aes256-gcm, with aes256-ctr allowed beside it. The control fires on either fault: a cipher outside that pair is offered, or aes256-gcm is not offered at all.

ASSERTS THE PREFERRED VALUE, NOT THE MINIMUM, from 2026-09-14. The minimum (AES-128-CTR or stronger) could only fail through a profile that adds one of the three CBC modes, because nothing weaker is selectable and the default offer contains none - so almost every device passed a cipher control while offering chacha20-poly1305, aes128-ctr, aes192-ctr and aes128-gcm. The preferred value is reachable everywhere, and an unrestricted device now reports at this control's own severity. Jason, 2026-09-14: "the preferred should replace the minimum. I'll let the consultant reduce severity based on risk." The corpus parenthetical "(add aes256-ctr for older clients)" is an ALLOWANCE beside the preferred cipher, not an alternative to it, which is why a list of aes256-ctr alone still fires.

The subject is what the management SSH server OFFERS: the bound profile's list where it sets one, and the device's built-in default where it does not - measured 2026-09-11 on 11.1 (PA-5220) and 11.2 (PA-VM), identical. A profile that sets only some lists leaves the others at the default. A bound profile is not in force until the SSH service restarts (`set ssh service-restart mgmt`), which the configuration does not record, so a finding describes the configured offer.

NOTHING EXPLICIT IS A FINDING IN ITSELF. Where no profile sets this list the device offers its own default, and that default is weak on CURRENT releases - measured on 11.1.13-h3 and 11.2.3, both of which offer hmac-sha1 and diffie-hellman-group14-sha1. So an estate can be fully patched, misconfigured nowhere, and still presenting SHA-1 to administrators. Upgrading does not change it; setting the list explicitly does. `ciphers_default`/`kex_default`/`macs_default` record which case a device is in, and the finding says so, because the remediation differs: bind a profile, or edit the one already bound. Measured 2026-09-11: an empty list node behaves exactly as an absent one, so "not configured" is one state however it is written.
controls.rationale: AES-256-GCM is an AEAD cipher at the largest key size PAN-OS offers; everything else in the default offer is smaller, unauthenticated, or both, and the CBC modes a profile can add are exposed to plaintext-recovery attacks.
controls.audit: Device > Certificate Management > SSH Service Profile - the profile bound under Device > Setup > Management > SSH Management Profiles: Ciphers. No profile, or no cipher list in it, means the device's whole default offer.
controls.remediation: Set the bound profile's cipher list to aes256-gcm, adding aes256-ctr only for clients that cannot do GCM, commit, then run `set ssh service-restart mgmt`.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: A cipher outside aes256-gcm/aes256-ctr is offered, or aes256-gcm is not.

controls.name: SSH Key Exchange Algorithms Restricted
controls.description:
Restricts the management SSH server's key exchange to the corpus PREFERRED family - ECDH over a NIST curve, with curve25519 accepted as the alternative the corpus names. The control fires on either fault: a KEX outside that set is offered, or no ECDH is.

With no SSH management profile bound - or a bound profile whose KEX list is absent OR EMPTY - the device advertises its entire built-in set: curve25519, the NIST ECDH curves, group-exchange-sha256, group16-sha512, group14-sha256 and diffie-hellman-group14-sha1. Measured 2026-09-11 on 11.1 (PA-5220) and 11.2 (PA-VM), identical; an explicitly empty `<kex/>` commits and offers exactly what an absent list does. Jason, 2026-09-11: "we fire if KEX is missing." The finite-field groups in that set are what makes it fire, so an unrestricted device still reports.

ASSERTS THE PREFERRED VALUE, NOT THE MINIMUM, from 2026-09-14. The corpus minimum excludes group1 and group-exchange-sha1, which no release advertises: the Compatibility Matrix lists nine KEX algorithms for administrative sessions on 10.2, 11.2 and 12.2, and neither is among them. A list that keeps diffie-hellman-group14-sha1 - SHA-1 key exchange, which RFC 9142 calls deprecated and a last resort - used to report at low as a preferred-state gap; it now reports at this control's own severity, and the graded band is gone. Jason, 2026-09-14: "the preferred should replace the minimum. I'll let the consultant reduce severity based on risk."

A bound profile is not in force until the SSH service restarts (`set ssh service-restart mgmt`), which the configuration does not record, so a finding describes the configured offer.

NOTHING EXPLICIT IS A FINDING IN ITSELF. Where no profile sets this list the device offers its own default, and that default is weak on CURRENT releases - measured on 11.1.13-h3 and 11.2.3, both of which offer hmac-sha1 and diffie-hellman-group14-sha1. So an estate can be fully patched, misconfigured nowhere, and still presenting SHA-1 to administrators. Upgrading does not change it; setting the list explicitly does. `ciphers_default`/`kex_default`/`macs_default` record which case a device is in, and the finding says so, because the remediation differs: bind a profile, or edit the one already bound. Measured 2026-09-11: an empty list node behaves exactly as an absent one, so "not configured" is one state however it is written.
controls.rationale: An unrestricted SSH server negotiates whatever the client asks for, SHA-1 key exchange included; the ECDH curves are the only KEX algorithms PAN-OS marks recommended.
controls.audit: Device > Setup > Management > SSH Management Profiles - the bound server profile's KEX list (Device > Certificate Management > SSH Service Profile). No profile, or no KEX list in it, means every KEX the device supports.
controls.remediation: Bind an SSH management profile whose KEX list is ecdh-sha2-nistp256/384/521, commit, then run `set ssh service-restart mgmt`.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: A key exchange outside the ECDH curves is offered, or none of them is.

controls.name: SSH MAC Algorithms Restricted
controls.description:
Restricts session integrity to the corpus PREFERRED MAC - hmac-sha2-512, with hmac-sha2-256 kept beside it for compatibility. The control fires on either fault: a MAC outside that pair is offered, or hmac-sha2-512 is not offered at all. The device default offers hmac-sha1, hmac-sha1-etm and umac-64/128 alongside SHA-2, so an appliance with no profile - or one whose profile leaves MACs unset - fires, as does a profile that selects hmac-sha1.

ASSERTS THE PREFERRED VALUE, NOT THE MINIMUM, from 2026-09-14. Jason, 2026-09-14: "the preferred should replace the minimum. I'll let the consultant reduce severity based on risk." In practice this control moves least of the five: the corpus parenthetical "(keep 256 for compatibility)" is an explicit ALLOWANCE, so a list of hmac-sha2-512 and hmac-sha2-256 is the preferred state and does not report - what changed is that a SHA-2-only list MISSING hmac-sha2-512 now fires at the control's own severity, and the low band that used to grade hmac-sha2-256 as a preferred-state gap is gone. A graded band between the minimum and the preferred is no longer built on any control.

The subject is what the management SSH server OFFERS: the bound profile's list where it sets one, and the device's built-in default where it does not - measured 2026-09-11 on 11.1 (PA-5220) and 11.2 (PA-VM), identical. A profile that sets only some lists leaves the others at the default. A bound profile is not in force until the SSH service restarts (`set ssh service-restart mgmt`), which the configuration does not record, so a finding describes the configured offer.

NOTHING EXPLICIT IS A FINDING IN ITSELF. Where no profile sets this list the device offers its own default, and that default is weak on CURRENT releases - measured on 11.1.13-h3 and 11.2.3, both of which offer hmac-sha1 and diffie-hellman-group14-sha1. So an estate can be fully patched, misconfigured nowhere, and still presenting SHA-1 to administrators. Upgrading does not change it; setting the list explicitly does. `ciphers_default`/`kex_default`/`macs_default` record which case a device is in, and the finding says so, because the remediation differs: bind a profile, or edit the one already bound. Measured 2026-09-11: an empty list node behaves exactly as an absent one, so "not configured" is one state however it is written.
controls.rationale: SHA-1 and 64-bit UMAC tags are below the SHA-2 floor for session integrity, and hmac-sha2-512 is the strongest tag PAN-OS offers.
controls.audit: The bound SSH management profile's MAC list, or the device default when none is bound or the list is unset.
controls.remediation: Bind an SSH management profile whose MAC list is hmac-sha2-512, keeping hmac-sha2-256 only where a client needs it, commit, then run `set ssh service-restart mgmt`.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: A MAC outside hmac-sha2-512/hmac-sha2-256 is offered, or hmac-sha2-512 is not.

controls.name: Strong SSH Host Key
controls.description:
