The management SSH server authenticates itself to administrators with ONE host key - the default type only, measured 2026-09-11: tpa-b, whose profile sets ECDSA 256, offers ecdsa-sha2-nistp256 and nothing else, while the untouched devices offer RSA (2048, read off the wire with ssh-keyscan).

ASSERTS THE CORPUS PREFERRED VALUE - ECDSA with a 256-bit key - from 2026-09-14. The minimum says the default RSA 2048 "meets the floor ... no change required", which leaves the control no reachable failure at all, since every selectable value is at least 112-bit. Jason, 2026-09-14: "the preferred should replace the minimum. I'll let the consultant reduce severity based on risk." So an RSA host key now reports at ANY size, including the 3072 and 4096 that passed under this control's earlier 128-bit-floor reading; the relaxation for an estate standardised on large RSA keys is the consultant's to make.

A STRONGER ECDSA CURVE IS NOT A FINDING. ECDSA 384 and 521 are above the preferred value, and replacing the minimum with the preferred does not turn being better than preferred into a failure. On a FIPS-CC device, ECC key-pair generation is listed for P-256 and P-384 only, so an ECDSA 521 host key may not be a validated operation there - a reason to prefer 256 or 384, not to report 521 here.

HOSTKEY = ALL REPORTS, measured 2026-09-14 on tpa-a: `all` takes no key size and serves an RSA key alongside ecdsa-sha2-nistp256/384/521 at once, so an administrator can still be presented with the RSA 2048 key this control is about. The same measurement found the ECDSA keys persist after the setting is deleted, so on a device that has ever been set to `all`, an absent hostkey no longer means RSA alone.

Key ROTATION is not assessed: the configuration records the key's type and size, never its age. The subject is the management SSH server's effective configuration: the bound profile's value where it sets one, the device default where it does not - measured 2026-09-11 on 11.1 and 11.2. A bound profile is not in force until `set ssh service-restart mgmt`, which the configuration does not record.

AN UNSET HOST KEY IS REPORTED AS UNSET, from 2026-10-06, rather than as the RSA 2048 the guide gives. The same 2026-09-14 measurement that put `all` in scope found the ECDSA keys it generates are still served after the setting is deleted, so an absent hostkey means RSA 2048 on most devices and something else on an unknown subset - and no configuration read can tell which. Normalization therefore stores nothing and records `not_configured`, and the finding says what the configuration shows: no key type is set, so what the server presents is unestablished and likely below the preferred value. WHEN IT FIRES IS UNCHANGED - the baseline is "not ECDSA", and an unset key was never ECDSA.
controls.rationale: An RSA 2048 host key is 112-bit strength, deprecated for signatures after 2030; ECDSA 256 is 128-bit and is the one host key type PAN-OS marks recommended.
controls.audit: Device > Certificate Management > SSH Service Profile > Hostkey, on the profile bound under Device > Setup > Management. Unset stores NO value and is reported as unestablished - the guide gives RSA 2048, and 2026-09-14 measured that unreliable on a device ever set to All, whose generated ECDSA keys survive the setting being deleted. Only the live SSH offer can say what is presented; All means RSA and every ECDSA curve together.
controls.remediation: Set the bound profile's host key to ECDSA 256, commit, then run `set ssh service-restart mgmt`. Regenerating a host key keeps the existing type, so the type has to be set here. Administrators' known_hosts entries change.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: The host key type in force is not ECDSA - a type somebody chose that is not ECDSA, or no type chosen at all.

controls.name: SSH Session Rekeying Configured
controls.description:
Rekeying bounds how much traffic one session key protects. PAN-OS offers three triggers - data volume, time interval and packet count - and whichever is reached first rekeys. Only the TIME INTERVAL is assessed, and its default is no time-based rekeying at all (Help p.905): this fires when no interval is set.

THE PREFERRED VALUE IS ALREADY THE ASSERTION. The corpus preferred is 3600 seconds - "rekeys at least hourly" - and the interval's configurable range is 10 to 3600, so every settable value satisfies it and a shorter interval is stronger rather than weaker. Applying the preferred-value rule of 2026-09-14 to this control therefore changes nothing: 'configured' remains the whole assertion, with no threshold comparison to make.

RFC 4253 section 9 recommends rekeying after one gigabyte or one hour, whichever comes sooner. The data trigger is not assessed: its default is the cipher's own limit of 1-4 GB, and an interactive management session rarely moves a gigabyte, so the interval is the trigger that acts.

NOT A FIPS-CC CHECK. The guide's rekeying REQUIREMENT (p.1308, p.1310) is about the HA1 control link in FIPS-CC mode, not the management SSH server, and HA profiles are not modelled here. A firewall in FIPS-CC mode with an unconfigured HA1 rekey is a different finding this control does not make.

The subject is the management SSH server's effective configuration: the bound profile's value where it sets one, the device default where it does not - measured 2026-09-11 on 11.1 and 11.2. A bound profile is not in force until `set ssh service-restart mgmt`, which the configuration does not record.
controls.rationale: With no time-based rekey, one session key protects a management session for its whole life.
controls.audit: Device > Certificate Management > SSH Service Profile > Interval, on the bound profile. Unset means no time-based rekeying.
controls.remediation: Set the bound profile's rekey Interval (10-3600 seconds; 3600 matches RFC 4253), commit, then run `set ssh service-restart mgmt`.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: No time-based rekey interval is set.

controls.name: Disable Telnet on Management Surfaces
controls.description: Telnet transmits credentials and session content in cleartext. It must remain disabled; SSH is the only acceptable CLI transport. Every management surface - MGT, Aux-1, Aux-2, and any layer-3 interface carrying an interface-management-profile - is assessed, because the risk is the same wherever the service is exposed.
controls.rationale: Telnet exposes administrator credentials and session content to anyone able to observe the path, and a management surface is by definition reachable by administrators.
controls.audit: Review each management surface and verify Telnet is not enabled. Telnet is disabled by default on current releases, so a finding means it was deliberately re-enabled.
controls.remediation: Disable Telnet on the surface reporting it and use SSH instead.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: Default baseline query.

controls.name: Disable HTTP on Management Surfaces
controls.description: Unencrypted HTTP management exposes credentials and session tokens. HTTPS must be used instead. Every management surface - MGT, Aux-1, Aux-2, and any layer-3 interface carrying an interface-management-profile - is assessed, because the risk is the same wherever the service is exposed.
controls.rationale: HTTP management carries administrator credentials and session cookies in cleartext, and offers no assurance that the device being managed is the intended one.
controls.audit: Review each management surface and verify HTTP is not enabled. HTTP is disabled by default, so a finding means it was deliberately re-enabled.
controls.remediation: Disable HTTP on the surface reporting it and use HTTPS instead.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: Default baseline query.

controls.name: Restrict Management Access to Permitted IP Addresses
controls.description: Limits which source addresses may reach a management surface. A surface with no permitted-source list accepts any host that can route to it. Every management surface - MGT, Aux-1, Aux-2, and any layer-3 interface carrying an interface-management-profile - is assessed, because the risk is the same wherever the service is exposed.
controls.rationale: Restricting permitted IP addresses reduces exposure of the management plane and limits administrative access attempts to trusted networks or jump hosts.
controls.audit: Review each surface's permitted-source list and verify only approved administrative networks or hosts appear. An absent or empty list means unrestricted.
controls.remediation: Configure permitted IP addresses using approved management subnets or jump-host addresses. Avoid broad ranges unless explicitly justified.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: Default baseline query.

controls.name: Administrative Services on Data-Plane Interfaces
controls.description:
Every data-plane interface with an administrative service enabled is reported, so that those facing untrusted networks can be identified. Management on a data-plane interface bypasses the management-plane isolation model.

This control enumerates rather than judges. Whether an interface faces an untrusted network cannot be determined from configuration - a zone name carries no trust semantics the device enforces - so the finding states a fact and the assessor decides. Only the five administrative services raise a finding; ping, response pages, HTTP-OCSP and the User-ID listeners are reachability and service functions and are reported as context.
controls.rationale: An administrative service on a data-plane interface is reachable from whatever that interface faces, which may include untrusted or Internet-facing networks. The management-plane isolation model assumes administration arrives on the management plane.
controls.audit: Review each reported interface. Confirm the interface does not face an untrusted network, or that the exposure is operationally required and restricted by a permitted-source list.
controls.remediation: Remove the interface management profile, or reduce it to the services actually required and bind a permitted-source list.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: Default baseline query.

controls.name: Login Banner Configured
controls.description:
A login banner presented before authentication states who may use the device and that use is monitored. Absent, an administrator sees nothing before the prompt.

The wording is site-specific and legal rather than technical, so this control asserts only that a banner exists. Whether it carries approved language is an interview question, not a configuration one.
controls.rationale: A banner is the notice that makes unauthorised use provable in many jurisdictions, and several frameworks require one before any authentication prompt.
controls.audit: Confirm a login banner is present and carries organisation-approved wording.
controls.remediation: Set Device > Setup > Management > Login Banner.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: Default baseline query.

controls.name: Force Admins to Acknowledge Login Banner
controls.description:
Requires an administrator to positively acknowledge the login banner rather than read past it.

Reported wherever acknowledgement is off, including on a device with no banner. PAN-OS greys the setting out until a banner exists, so remediating this one may mean setting a banner first - which is PAN-MGT-007, and the two are reported independently rather than one standing in for the other.
controls.rationale: Acknowledgement converts a passive notice into a recorded action by the administrator, which is what gives the banner evidentiary weight.
controls.audit: Confirm administrators must acknowledge the banner before proceeding.
controls.remediation: Enable Force Admins to Acknowledge Login Banner. The setting is unavailable until a login banner is configured, so set the banner first where there is none.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: Default baseline query.

controls.name: Verify Update Server Identity
controls.description:
Validates the update server's TLS certificate before content is downloaded, so a man-in-the-middle cannot deliver tampered content updates.

Enabled by default: absent from configuration means ON, measured 2026-09-01. A finding here therefore means it was deliberately turned off.
controls.rationale: Content updates are executable inputs to inspection. Accepting them from an unauthenticated server undermines every signature-based control on the device.
controls.audit: Confirm Verify Update Server Identity is enabled.
controls.remediation: Enable Device > Setup > Services > Verify Update Server Identity.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: Default baseline query.

controls.name: Harden Management Interface TLS Protocol
controls.description:
Binds an SSL/TLS service profile to the management web interface so administrative sessions negotiate TLS 1.2 or better.

Scope is the PROTOCOL FLOOR only. The certificate that profile presents is PAN-CRT-006, and the two are genuinely independent: the shipped TLSv1.3_Default profile satisfies this control and still serves the device's own self-signed factory certificate, so passing here says nothing about trust.

Absence is a finding, not a default pass. Measured 2026-09-02 by negotiation: with no profile bound, a PA-5220 management interface accepts TLS 1.1 and refuses only TLS 1.0. Binding a profile is what raises the floor.

The profile name resolves over two scopes, and PREDEFINED BEATS SHARED. A custom profile written under the shipped name TLSv1.3_Default is ignored entirely, settings and certificate alike, so the name alone does not tell you what is in force.
controls.rationale: The management interface carries full administrative authority, and TLS 1.1 has no acceptable modern cipher suites. An unbound interface is not merely unhardened: it is measurably weaker than the hardened profile PAN-OS already ships and could have bound for free.
controls.audit: Confirm an SSL/TLS service profile is bound at Device > Setup > Management > General Settings, and that the profile it resolves to sets Min Version to TLS 1.2 or higher. Where the bound name matches a predefined profile, read the PREDEFINED definition - a same-named custom profile is not in force.
controls.remediation: Bind an SSL/TLS service profile with Min Version TLS 1.2 at Device > Setup > Management > General Settings > SSL/TLS Service Profile. The shipped TLSv1.3_Default profile satisfies this control on its own. It does NOT satisfy PAN-CRT-006, because the certificate it carries is the device's own self-signed one.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: Default baseline query.

controls.name: Enable Log on High DP Load
controls.description:
Logs a system event when dataplane CPU is sustained at a high level - an early signal of flooding, decryption overload, or a device outgrowing its sizing.

Disabled by default: absent from configuration means OFF, measured 2026-09-01, so an untouched device reports this finding.
controls.rationale: Sustained high dataplane load degrades inspection before it degrades throughput, and without this event the first symptom is usually a user complaint.
controls.audit: Confirm Enable Log on High DP Load is set.
controls.remediation: Enable Device > Setup > Management > Logging and Reporting Settings > Log Export and Reporting > Enable Log on High DP Load.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: Default baseline query.

controls.name: Unused Interface Management Profiles
controls.description:
An interface management profile that no interface references is configuration debt. It grants no access while it stays unbound, but it is a definition nobody is maintaining, and binding it later applies whatever it was left enabling.

Reported per appliance. A profile pushed from a Panorama template exists separately in each firewall's configuration, and bound on one device but unbound on another is two different facts about two devices.
controls.rationale: Unused definitions accumulate, are not reviewed with the configuration that is in use, and are the most likely thing to be bound by mistake or in haste. Removing them reduces what has to be read to understand how a device is administered.
controls.audit: Review each reported profile and confirm no interface references it. A profile kept deliberately for a planned change is an accepted finding rather than a defect.
controls.remediation: Delete the profile, or bind it to the interface it was created for.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: Profiles bound to no interface.

controls.name: Application-Default Service Preferred
controls.description:
Every allow rule binds its applications to their default ports.

THE CHECK IS "not application-default", NOT "service any". `any` allows every permitted application on every port and is the obvious failure; a rule pinned to explicit ports is the other one, and it is reported rather than excused. The corpus names application-default as both the minimum and the preferred value, and the vendor agrees - Help p.131: application-default "is recommended for allow policies because it prevents applications from running on unusual ports and protocols". An assessor holding the documentation for a nonstandard port can clear such a finding; the configuration records only the port, never that it was intended.

MEASURED 2026-09-16 on fw-core-tpa-a, and the query rests on both:
- `service` is REQUIRED. A rule without it is accepted at the write and refused at the commit - "svc-probe-absent is missing 'service'" - so every committed rule carries a service list. A rule with no service is therefore a predefined default rule or a collection gap, never a rule whose author left the field alone.
- `application-default` is EXCLUSIVE. Writing it beside another member is refused outright: code=12, "'application-default' should not be used with another service". So "has an application-default member" and "is application-default" are the same question, and one clause answers it.

SCOPE. Allow rules only: the vendor's recommendation is for allow policies, and a deny restricted to a port is a narrower deny rather than a weaker one. The two predefined rules are excluded - `intrazone-default` allows, exists in no rulebase, carries no service, and has none to set.
controls.rationale: A permitted application allowed on any port can be run over an unusual one - SSH over 443 - and the traffic is indistinguishable from what the rule was written to allow. application-default is what turns that evasion back into a policy violation.
controls.audit: Policies > Security > <rule> > Service/URL Category. The Service column should read application-default on every allow rule.
controls.remediation: Set the rule's service to application-default: `set rulebase security rules <name> service application-default`, or `set device-group <dg> pre-rulebase security rules <name> service application-default` on Panorama. A `set` MERGES into a member list and application-default may not share one, so remove the existing members rather than adding to them. Where a nonstandard port is deliberate, keep the explicit service object and record why.

controls.name: No Port-Only Rules (App-ID Required)
controls.description:
Every allow rule names the applications it permits.

A rule with `application any` forgoes App-ID entirely: whatever is tunnelled over the ports it opens passes, and the rule's own name is the only record of what it was for.

THE UNTRUST QUALIFIER IS DROPPED, DELIBERATELY. controls.json sets the minimum at "no allow rule CROSSING AN UNTRUST BOUNDARY has application any", and no configuration says which zone is untrusted - the same wall PAN-MGT-006 hit over "untrusted interfaces". The preferred value has no such qualifier ("all allow rules application-based"), it is the stricter reading, and it is decidable, so it is what this asserts.

OVERLAPS PAN-POL-002 ON PURPOSE. A rule with `application any` AND an unbounded address fires both, because they are two different statements about it: this one says the rule identifies nothing, and PAN-POL-002 says how much address space it exposes. Fixing the application clears this one and leaves that one standing. This previously named PAN-POL-001, which was dropped on 2026-10-06 into PAN-POL-002's critical band.
controls.rationale: Port-only rules are how an allowed port becomes an allowed tunnel. App-ID is the control the platform exists to provide, and a rule that declines to use it is trusting a number.
controls.audit: Policies > Security > Application. Any allow rule whose Application column reads `any` is the finding; Policy Optimizer lists the applications each one actually carried.
controls.remediation: Replace `any` with the applications the rule is for - Policy Optimizer proposes them from observed traffic. Where a custom or unidentified application is involved, name it with a custom App-ID rather than leaving the rule open.

controls.name: Security Profiles on All Allow Rules
controls.description:
An allow rule that permits traffic without inspecting it.

Every allow rule should carry antivirus, anti-spyware and vulnerability protection. A rule with none of the three passes whatever it permits uninspected, which is why that case is CRITICAL and a rule missing some of them is high.

THE PROFILE GROUP IS RESOLVED, NOT COUNTED. A rule names either individual profiles or one profile group, and the group is the common case. The group is looked up by name, by scope, and read for the profile types it actually contains - because a group that names nothing protects nothing. On the lab 113 rules name a group called `default` which names NO PROFILES AT ALL: they look configured in any view that stops at "does this rule carry a profile group", and they inspect nothing. Resolution is done in normalization and lands in three columns, for the same reason the address-breadth counts are columns - the search layer compares a field to a literal and cannot follow a reference and read what it points at.

WHAT IT DOES NOT ASSERT. Nothing about the CONTENT of the profiles it finds. A rule carrying a `default` antivirus profile satisfies this control; whether that profile blocks anything is PAN-SPY-001's and PAN-VLN-001's question for the two types they cover, and no control covers antivirus profile content yet. URL filtering, file blocking and WildFire analysis are deliberately out of scope: the corpus minimum names these three.

SCOPE. Enabled allow rules, excluding the two predefined default rules, whose profile setting cannot be edited. A deny rule needs no inspection profile.
controls.rationale: Threat prevention is the reason the firewall is in the path. An allow rule without profiles is a hole in that regardless of how tightly its addresses and applications are scoped, and it is invisible in a rulebase review because the rule looks complete - all of its match columns are filled in.
controls.audit: Policies > Security, the Profile column. Where a rule names a group, open the group: the finding is about what the group CONTAINS, and an empty group reads the same as a full one in the rule list.
controls.remediation: Attach a profile group carrying all three types, and check the group is not empty. Where a group is shared across rules, fixing the group fixes every rule naming it.

controls.name: Anti-Spyware Profile Blocks Critical/High/Medium Severity
controls.description:
Anti-spyware signatures detect command-and-control, credential theft and post-exploitation beaconing. Critical and high severities must be blocked; leaving them at alert turns C2 detection into a log entry while the channel stays open.

WHAT IS ASSESSED. Every custom Anti-Spyware profile - local vsys, local shared, and Panorama-pushed - and the predefined `default` and `strict` profiles WHEN a rule or profile group uses them (Jason, 2026-09-11). An unused predefined profile protects nothing; the shipped `default` protecting a rule is the commonest weak configuration there is.

THE VERDICT IS ORDER-INDEPENDENT. A severity is blocked only when a catch-all rule covers it - any threat name, any category - and every rule that can match it takes a blocking action. No document says whether profile rules are first-match, and this reading does not need to know: it cannot pass a weak profile. Its cost is that a non-blocking rule BELOW a broad blocking one still fails the severity.

BLOCKING is drop, reset-client, reset-server, reset-both or block-ip. The corpus minimum names reset-both alone; any blocking action passes here (Jason, 2026-09-11). `default` is NOT blocking - a signature's default action is typically alert or reset-both (Web Interface Help p.272), so it cannot be relied on, and the predefined `default` profile is exactly that case.

Fires when critical OR high is not blocked, which is the corpus minimum. Medium is the corpus PREFERRED value: it is on the row and queryable, and fires nothing.

REPORTED PER RULE, not per profile (2026-10-12). A profile nothing uses endangers nothing, and a rule is what carries traffic, so the subject is the rule and the finding names the profile in force on it. One profile behind forty rules therefore produces forty findings - which is the point: each is a distinct piece of traffic.

SCOPE. Allow rules that are not the predefined default rules - the same exclusions as PAN-AVW-003 and PAN-POL-008. A rule that denies, drops or resets passes no traffic for a profile to inspect, so a profile on it, or the lack of one, protects nothing either way. Unlike those two controls, a DISABLED allow rule is reported: it is in the configuration and one click from carrying traffic, and its finding says it is disabled (Jason, 2026-10-14).

A rule with NO anti-spyware profile in force IS reported here - the absence is this control's own finding, not only PAN-POL-008's (Jason, 2026-10-12). So the two overlap on an allow rule carrying none: PAN-POL-008 says the rule is uninspected, this control says which inspection it is missing.

WHY MEDIUM CANNOT BE REPORTED HERE, measured 2026-10-31. The graded column reads `medium` only when critical and high are BOTH stopped - and that makes this control's own assertion true, so every query on it excludes the row. A profile stopping critical and high but not medium is therefore below the vendor's recommendation and is reported by nothing. Reporting it needs an assertion this control does not make, which is stage 3's decision and not this entry's.
controls.rationale: Critical and high severity signatures that only alert turn detection into a log entry while the attack proceeds.
controls.audit: Objects > Security Profiles > Anti-Spyware > <profile> > Rules, and which Security policy rules and Security Profile Groups reference it.
controls.remediation: Give the profile a catch-all rule for critical and high severity with a reset or drop action, and remove or tighten any rule that alerts on those severities. For a predefined profile, point the rules and groups using it at `strict` or at a custom profile instead - predefined profiles cannot be edited.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: Rules whose anti-spyware profile does not block critical and high severity threats.

queries.name: Critical severity left un-stopped
queries.short_description: Rules whose anti-spyware profile leaves critical severity signatures un-stopped.

queries.name: High severity left un-stopped
queries.short_description: Rules whose anti-spyware profile stops critical but leaves high severity signatures un-stopped.

controls.name: Redundant NTP Servers Configured
controls.description:
Two NTP servers must be configured. PAN-OS has exactly two slots - `ntp-servers/primary-ntp-server` and `secondary-ntp-server`, measured 2026-09-14 on 11.1 (PA-5220) and 11.2 (PA-VM) - so this fires when fewer than two are set.

TWO THINGS THE CORPUS ASKS FOR ARE NOT DECIDABLE HERE, and the control says so rather than implying it checked them. The preferred value is "primary plus secondary from independent trusted internal sources": the device records two addresses and nothing about who operates them, so TRUSTED and INDEPENDENT are the assessor's judgement. And SYNCHRONIZATION is operational - `show ntp` reports `reachable` and `status: synched` per server, which is why the corpus marks this control live-device-state - while this reads configuration. A server that is configured and answering nothing satisfies this control, and every finding carries that caveat.

The lab holds both states without any change being made for it: pan-fw-111 configures one server and fires, both PA-5220s configure two and pass.
controls.rationale: A single time source is a single point of failure for log timestamps, certificate validity and scheduled jobs - and the corpus notes STIG requires two authoritative sources.
controls.audit: Device > Setup > Services > NTP. Confirm both NTP Server Address fields are populated, and confirm with the operator that the two are independent trusted sources.
controls.remediation: Configure a second NTP server from a different trusted internal source: `set deviceconfig system ntp-servers secondary-ntp-server ntp-server-address <ntp2>`.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: Fewer than two NTP servers are configured.

controls.name: NTP Authentication Enabled
controls.description:
Every configured NTP server must authenticate its time updates with a symmetric key. `authentication-type` is a choice node completing to exactly `none`, `symmetric-key` and `autokey` on 11.1 and 11.2, and Help p.751 states None is the default - which is the state of all three lab devices.

ASSERTS THE PREFERRED VALUE. The corpus minimum is explicitly no requirement at all ("unauthenticated NTP from trusted internal sources meets the floor"), so asserting it would give a control that can never fire; the preferred value is the literal `symmetric-key`.

AUTOKEY DOES NOT SATISFY IT. It is a different mechanism rather than a stronger grade of the same one, and the corpus names the symmetric-key literal. A device using autokey reports, and the finding names it as autokey rather than as unauthenticated, because the remediation differs.

A DEVICE WITH NO NTP SERVER ALSO FIRES: it has no authenticated time source. PAN-SVC-001 is what reports the absence itself, so the two are separate findings about one cause.

The ALGORITHM is recorded and not asserted. PAN-OS offers `sha1` and `md5` and nothing else, so there is no stronger choice to require.
controls.rationale: Unauthenticated NTP lets an attacker on the path skew device time, which defeats log correlation and certificate expiry checks.
controls.audit: Device > Setup > Services > NTP > Authentication Type, on BOTH servers. None is the default.
controls.remediation: Set Authentication Type to Symmetric Key on each configured server, with a Key ID, an algorithm and a shared key: `set deviceconfig system ntp-servers primary-ntp-server authentication-type symmetric-key key-id <id> algorithm sha1 authentication-key <key>`.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: A configured NTP server does not authenticate with a symmetric key.

controls.name: SNMP v3 Only (v1/v2c Disabled)
controls.description:
SNMP monitoring access must use v3. `snmp-setting/access-setting/version` is a choice node completing to exactly `v2c` and `v3` on 11.1 and 11.2, so the control fires on a device configured for v2c.

THE TITLE NAMES A STATE PAN-OS CANNOT BE IN. There is no v1 in the schema on either measured release, so "v1/v2c disabled" is v2c in practice; the title is the corpus's and is left alone.

AN UNCONFIGURED DEVICE DOES NOT FIRE. controls.json says it outright - "If SNMP is unused, leave snmp-setting unconfigured entirely" - so the baseline requires `is_configured` as well as `uses_v2c`, and a device with no SNMP at all is compliant rather than unassessed. That is the state of all three lab devices, which is why this control needed a subject built for it.

AN ACCESS-SETTING WITH NO VERSION CHILD IS READ AS v2c, from Help p.740 ("Version: V2c (default) or V3"), and the row records that the version was inferred rather than read - a finding resting on a vendor sentence should say so.

The preferred value is the same literal, `v3`, with the description adding SHA-256/AES-256, scoped MIB views and dedicated monitoring accounts. That is remediation guidance rather than a second assertion - the same reading PAN-CRT-005 takes of its own preferred state.
controls.rationale: SNMP v2c authenticates with a cleartext community string and offers no encryption, so anyone on the path can read the community and then the device's statistics.
controls.audit: Device > Setup > Operations > SNMP Setup > Version. Also confirm whether any management surface actually enables the SNMP service - the two are configured apart.
controls.remediation: Select V3 and define views and users: `set deviceconfig system snmp-setting access-setting version v3 views {NAME} view {NAME} oid 1.3.6.1 option include`. If SNMP is not used, delete `snmp-setting` entirely instead.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: SNMP is configured and answers v2c.

controls.name: No Default or Weak SNMP Community Strings (Hygiene)
controls.description:
Where v2c is still in use, the community string must not be one of the published defaults. Fires when a configured device's community string is `public` or `private`, compared case-insensitively.

"GUESSABLE" IS NOT DECIDABLE and is not asserted. The corpus minimum is "no default community strings ('public'/'private') and any remaining v2c exposure documented with an expiry date": the first half is a string comparison, the second is a document. Help p.740 names the same two strings ("Don't use the default community string public").

THE COMMUNITY STRING IS NOT STORED by this project. It is a live credential that grants read access to the device's statistics, and the control answers without its value - the row carries only whether it is set and whether it is a default. It appears in the configuration backup either way, which is the reason the control exists.

EVERY FINDING SAYS WHETHER SNMP IS REACHABLE. `snmp-setting` and the per-surface `disable-snmp` are configured apart, and `disable-snmp` is implicit YES - so a device can hold a default community string that no surface exposes. That is latent rather than live, and it becomes live the moment SNMP is enabled on a surface.
controls.rationale: A default community string is a published password, and v2c sends it in cleartext on every poll.
controls.audit: Device > Setup > Operations > SNMP Setup > SNMP Community String, on a device using V2c.
controls.remediation: Move to v3 (PAN-SVC-004). Where v2c must remain, replace the community string with an unguessable value and restrict which sources may poll it: `delete deviceconfig system snmp-setting access-setting version v2c`.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: A configured device uses a default community string.

controls.name: Static IP on Management Interface
controls.description:
The management interface must not take its address from DHCP. `deviceconfig/system/type` is a choice node completing to exactly `static` and `dhcp-client`, and the corpus sets minimum and preferred to the same value: "DHCP on a management interface has no acceptable production use".

AN ABSENT `type` NODE IS STATIC, measured 2026-09-14 rather than assumed, and this is the unusual direction: absence is the SAFE state here. fw-core-tpa-b carries no `type` node at all and its compiled interface state reads `'ip-type': static` with `'disable-dhcp': True`, while `show system info` reports `is-dhcp: no`. A reader treating absence as undetermined would report a compliant device. The row records whether static was read or resolved, and the tab shows it.

THIS IS AN APPLIANCE FACT, NOT A PER-SURFACE ONE. `aux-1` accepts ip-address, netmask, default-gateway and permitted-ip but has NO `type` - completing it returns `code=6 Invalid sequence` - so addressing mode exists only for MGT and does not belong beside the aux and data-plane surfaces.

pan-fw-111 is a `dhcp-client` and fires; both PA-5220s pass, one explicitly and one by absence.
controls.rationale: A rogue DHCP server on the management segment can reassign the firewall's address, gateway and DNS, which moves management traffic to attacker-controlled infrastructure.
controls.audit: Device > Setup > Interfaces > Management > IP Type. Static is the required value; a device with nothing written is already static.
controls.remediation: Set a static management address: `set deviceconfig system type static`, with ip-address, netmask and default-gateway.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: The management interface is a DHCP client.

controls.name: Timezone Standardized on UTC
controls.description:
The device's time zone is UTC, so correlating its logs with another device's needs no offset arithmetic.

UTC IS THE CORPUS PREFERRED VALUE - "UTC timezone estate-wide so multi-device log correlation needs no offset math" - and `timezone` is a 566-value enum on both measured platforms. The corpus minimum asks instead for a time zone that is merely CONSISTENT estate-wide, which is not a property of any one device: a row cannot tell whether it agrees with an estate it cannot see. Asserting the preferred value makes the control decidable per device as well as stricter, which is the 2026-09-14 preferred-value ruling applied to a case where the minimum was unusable rather than merely weaker.

SPLIT FROM THE FACTORY-HOSTNAME HALF on 2026-09-15. The corpus bundles both assertions under this id, and firing on either produced ONE finding for two independent defects with different remediations - a device could not clear it by fixing one, and the finding count could not say how many devices had which. The hostname half is now PAN-SVC-010. This id keeps the time zone because the corpus entry's xpath, set command and `preferred_value` (UTC) all describe it.
controls.rationale: A device on a local time zone makes multi-device log correlation manual and error-prone, and a mis-ordered timeline during an incident is the cost.
controls.audit: Device > Setup > Management > General Settings > Time Zone.
controls.remediation: Set the time zone to UTC: `set deviceconfig system timezone UTC`.

controls.name: Hostname Not Left at Factory Default
controls.description:
The device is not still answering to the name PAN-OS gave it.

THE FACTORY HOSTNAME IS THE MODEL, which is what makes this decidable. Help p.700: "If you don't enter a value, PAN-OS uses the firewall model (for example, PA-5220_2) as the default." So the check compares the stored hostname with the appliance's model plus an optional NUMERIC suffix, rather than pattern-matching a name, and an absent hostname is the same state spelled differently.

THE SUFFIX IS MATCHED AS DIGITS. An earlier implementation accepted any suffix, which also matched deliberately chosen names leading with the model - `PA-5220_EDGE-01`, `PA-5220_DC1` - so on an estate using that convention every device reported as unnamed.

ORIGIN: split from PAN-SVC-009 on 2026-09-15, which the corpus bundles with the time-zone assertion. Two independent defects with different remediations produced one finding that could not be cleared by fixing either half. See scratch/control-changes.json.
controls.rationale: A device named for its model cannot be told apart from its siblings in a log line, and misattribution during incident response is the cost.
controls.audit: Device > Setup > Management > General Settings > Hostname.
controls.remediation: Give the device a meaningful unique hostname: `set deviceconfig system hostname <name>`.

controls.name: Vulnerability Protection Blocks Critical/High/Medium Severity
controls.description:
Vulnerability signatures stop exploit attempts against client and server CVEs in transit. Critical and high must be blocked - the shipped `default` profile only takes each signature's default action, which documents intrusions instead of preventing them.

WHAT IS ASSESSED. Every custom Vulnerability Protection profile - local vsys, local shared, and Panorama-pushed - and the predefined `default` and `strict` profiles WHEN a rule or profile group uses them (Jason, 2026-09-11). An unused predefined profile protects nothing; the shipped `default` protecting a rule is the commonest weak configuration there is.

THE VERDICT IS ORDER-INDEPENDENT. A severity is blocked only when a catch-all rule covers it - any threat name, any category, any CVE and vendor ID, for the client AND the server side - and every rule that can match it takes a blocking action. No document says whether profile rules are first-match, and this reading does not need to know: it cannot pass a weak profile. Its cost is that a non-blocking rule BELOW a broad blocking one still fails the severity.

BLOCKING is drop, reset-client, reset-server, reset-both or block-ip. The corpus minimum names reset-both alone; any blocking action passes here (Jason, 2026-09-11). `default` is NOT blocking - a signature's default action is typically alert or reset-both (Web Interface Help p.272), so it cannot be relied on, and the predefined `default` profile is exactly that case.

Fires when critical OR high is not blocked, which is the corpus minimum. Medium is the corpus PREFERRED value: it is on the row and queryable, and fires nothing.

REPORTED PER RULE, not per profile (2026-10-12). A profile nothing uses endangers nothing, and a rule is what carries traffic, so the subject is the rule and the finding names the profile in force on it. One profile behind forty rules therefore produces forty findings - which is the point: each is a distinct piece of traffic.

SCOPE. Allow rules that are not the predefined default rules - the same exclusions as PAN-AVW-003 and PAN-POL-008. A rule that denies, drops or resets passes no traffic for a profile to inspect, so a profile on it, or the lack of one, protects nothing either way. Unlike those two controls, a DISABLED allow rule is reported: it is in the configuration and one click from carrying traffic, and its finding says it is disabled (Jason, 2026-10-14).

A rule with NO vulnerability protection profile in force IS reported here - the absence is this control's own finding, not only PAN-POL-008's (Jason, 2026-10-12). So the two overlap on an allow rule carrying none: PAN-POL-008 says the rule is uninspected, this control says which inspection it is missing.
controls.rationale: Critical and high severity signatures that only alert turn detection into a log entry while the attack proceeds.
controls.audit: Objects > Security Profiles > Vulnerability Protection > <profile> > Rules, and which Security policy rules and Security Profile Groups reference it.
controls.remediation: Give the profile a catch-all rule for critical and high severity with a reset or drop action, and remove or tighten any rule that alerts on those severities. For a predefined profile, point the rules and groups using it at `strict` or at a custom profile instead - predefined profiles cannot be edited.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: Rules whose vulnerability protection profile does not block critical and high severity threats.

queries.name: Rule never assessed for vulnerability inspection
queries.short_description: Allow rules the vulnerability assessment pass has never run over, so nothing established what inspects their traffic.

controls.name: External Dynamic List Content Not Collected
controls.description:
An address object a security rule relies on whose content this assessment never read, so the number of addresses that rule admits is unknown.

THIS IS A FINDING ABOUT THE ASSESSMENT, NOT THE DEVICE. Nothing here says the firewall is misconfigured. It says a question could not be answered, and it exists because the alternative is silence: an object with no size falls through a breadth score as the NARROWEST possible value, which is a false negative on the controls whose whole purpose is finding rules that permit too much.

TWO HALVES, AND EITHER ONE FIRES. An imported list - an external dynamic list - whose content the firewall has never fetched; and a name-based object - an FQDN - for which this collection never read the firewall's own resolution table. They are one control because they are one question asked of two kinds of object, and the answer a reader needs is the same: the rule's reach was not established. Which half fired is on the row, in the setting the finding marks.

WHY IT HAPPENS. EDL and FQDN content lives only in the device's runtime cache, never in its configuration, so it is collected by the separate "Refresh EDL/FQDN Cache" action rather than by a configuration sync. That action is deliberately not part of a regular refresh - FQDN is one cheap call per appliance, but EDL collection is one call per referenced list, each potentially paged - so a freshly synced estate legitimately has none of it.

ONLY REFERENCED OBJECTS REPORT. A list sitting unused in the address book is not a gap; collection follows normalized rule references, so an unreferenced list is expected to be unsized. A firewall does not resolve a name no policy uses either - measured: a committed FQDN object was absent from the resolution table fourteen minutes and several refresh windows after a successful commit - so reporting unreferenced objects would report the whole address book.

WHAT "NEVER READ" IS, MEASURED RATHER THAN INFERRED. A list the firewall has never fetched does not answer empty: it answers one valid member, the literal 0.0.0.0/32. That is a syntactically valid address, so every count derived from it reads as a successful collection - the recorded total becomes 1, the size becomes 1 host, and a rule naming that list scores its side as the narrowest thing on the device. The member literal is the discriminator and no count is. A fetch the firewall ATTEMPTED AND FAILED answers nothing valid with the reason in its own words, and a fourth reply carries every counter zero with no members at all; both of those are also "not read", because nothing in the reply separates a list fetched and found empty from one never fetched.

A DEVICE THAT TRIED AND FAILED NOW REPORTS HERE, which is a change from this control's first implementation. That state is a defect in the customer's configuration - a live rule behind a list the firewall cannot reach - and it is PAN-POL-023's subject, which today has no generator and therefore reports nowhere. Reporting the worst case and letting the engineer reduce it is the standing decision; a silence that reads as "collected and fine" is not available. The remediation below says which case a reader is looking at: if the object is still unread after a refresh, the device could not supply it and the fault moves to the customer.
controls.rationale: A breadth score computed over an object of unknown size is not a conservative estimate, it is a wrong one in the dangerous direction - the rule reads as tight and nobody has reason to doubt it. Medium because the assessment, not the estate, is what is incomplete; it should be visible and actioned, not compete with real findings.
controls.audit: Objects > Addresses. An external dynamic list showing no resolved content, or a name-based (FQDN) object with no resolved addresses. The remedy is to run the EDL/FQDN cache refresh, which contacts the device; a configuration sync will not fill it.
controls.remediation: Run "Refresh EDL/FQDN Cache" for the management station, then regenerate findings. A row that clears was a gap in this assessment and nothing more. A row that remains is the device's own: the firewall cannot fetch the list, or cannot resolve the name, which is the customer's to fix and is PAN-POL-023's ground rather than this control's. For a name-based object, confirm with the engineer whether the name is expected to resolve from the firewall's own resolution path - the record cannot tell a name nobody looked up from a name that was looked up and answered with nothing, and the two need different remedies.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: A referenced external dynamic list whose content the firewall has never fetched.

queries.name: Name-based object resolution never read
queries.short_description: A referenced FQDN object for which the firewall's resolution table was not read.

controls.name: External Dynamic List Content Truncated at the Collection Ceiling
controls.description:
An external dynamic list a security rule relies on whose content was collected only in part, so the number of addresses recorded for it is a known under-count.

THE CEILING IS OURS, NOT THE DEVICE'S. The firewall reports the full total and will serve it; collection stops at 50,000 members per list to bound how much of one response has to be held and stored. So this is a limit of the assessment rather than a fault on the device.

WHAT IT MEANS FOR ANYTHING SCORED FROM IT. A breadth figure derived from a partly collected list is a floor rather than a figure: the object is at least this broad and may be far broader. The device's own reported total is kept beside the collected count, so the shortfall is readable rather than inferred, and the severity on the row is set by how large it is - within about one step of the truth is low, a sample large enough to mislead is medium, several bands below the truth is high.

THE FLAG IS WIDER THAN THIS CONTROL'S NAME. Any shortfall between what the device reported and what was kept sets it, including a paging walk that ended early; the 50,000 ceiling is never consulted when it is written. So a row here says "we kept less than the device said it holds", which is the fact a reader can act on, and not specifically "this list exceeds fifty thousand entries".

A LIST NOBODY FETCHED IS NOT PART-KEPT, and is excluded here rather than left to arithmetic. A list the firewall has never fetched answers one valid member - the literal 0.0.0.0/32 - so a ratio computed over it is exactly 1.0 and would land in the gentlest band, reporting the most incomplete object on the device as the most compliant. Those rows report under PAN-COV-001 instead, at its own severity. The two controls partition: PAN-COV-001 fires where the content was never fetched, this one only where it was, so no unread list is silent and none is reported twice.

It is also worth knowing on its own terms. A list of tens of thousands of entries is a large thing for a rule to depend on, and whether anyone has looked at what is in it is a fair question for an assessor to ask.
controls.rationale: An under-count reads as a smaller object, and a smaller object reads as a tighter rule. Recording the truncation is what stops a partial collection being mistaken for a complete one. Medium for the same reason as PAN-COV-001: the gap is in what was measured, not in the estate.
controls.audit: Objects > Addresses. The object reports both the number of members collected and the total the device reported; they disagree, and the band on the finding says by how much.
controls.remediation: Nothing on the device. Either accept the floor, or raise the collection ceiling and re-run the EDL/FQDN cache refresh if the exact size matters to a finding that rests on it. Where the shortfall is large, treat every breadth figure taken from this object as a lower bound until it is collected whole.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: A referenced external dynamic list whose fetched content was kept only in part.

queries.name: Shortfall up to two times
queries.short_description: The kept part already fixes the order of magnitude: worth recording, not worth alarming.

queries.name: Shortfall more than ten times
queries.short_description: A reach computed from the kept part can sit several bands below the truth.

controls.name: Source/Destination Address Breadth Bounded
controls.description:
How much address space an allow rule exposes, on its broader side.

SEVERITY COMES FROM THE SIZE, not from a boolean. The host count on each side is converted to the smallest subnet that would contain it - network_bits = 32 - ceil(log2(n)) - and the bands run: /0-/7 critical (over 16,777,216 addresses, including `any`), /8-/11 high, /12-/14 medium, /15-/16 low, /17-/18 informational, and /19 or narrower reports nothing. Rounding UP is deliberate: the RFC1918 aggregate is 17,891,328 addresses and lands at /7, critical, where rounding to nearest would call it /8. Jason, 2026-09-30: "RFC1918 rules may be poorly considered."

A SIDE'S COUNT IS THE UNION OF ITS OBJECTS, DE-DUPLICATED - two members covering the same /8 are one /8, not two - and it is read AFTER NEGATION. A negated side keeps its member refs and gains a synthetic complement beside them; the complement is what the rule actually permits. Scoring the members instead would read a negated rule as its own inverse, so negating one host would score /32 rather than the whole space but one.

AN INDETERMINATE SIDE REPORTS AT MEDIUM rather than nothing. A side is unknowable when it names a dynamic address group or a region, when an EDL or FQDN on it has no resolved content, or when that content was truncated at the collection ceiling and is a known under-count. The count is NULL in those cases, never 0 - zero is the narrowest value there is, and a rule nobody could measure must not read as the tightest rule on the device. Why a particular object could not be sized is reported separately by the PAN-COV coverage controls.

SCOPE. Allow rules only, excluding the two predefined default rules, whose match tuple cannot be edited, and excluding disabled rules, which permit nothing.

v1 IS ADDRESSES ONLY, which is what this control's name asserts. The wider permissiveness methodology also scores service and application and combines the per-field tiers into an aggregate; service is PAN-POL-003 and needs a ServiceObject model that does not exist, application needs application-group resolution that does not exist, and the aggregate needs all four. See rule-permissiveness-scoring.md.

PAN-POL-001 WAS DROPPED INTO THIS CONTROL on 2026-10-06, and this control now carries its STIG reference alone. It asserted that no allow rule leaves BOTH its source and its destination covering the whole address space - read semantically, so a 0.0.0.0/0 object counted as `any` - which is a subset of this control's critical band. Measured before the drop: 45 of its 46 lab findings also reported here, all at critical. The 46th was a DISABLED any/any rule, which 001 reported because its baseline had no `disabled` clause and this one does. That was a false positive by the reasoning here - a disabled rule permits nothing - and disabled rules are PAN-POL-014's subject, which is not yet built. Until it is, a disabled rule of any breadth is reported by nothing.
controls.rationale: A rule's reach is the product of what it permits on each side, and the side nobody narrowed is the one that decides it. Breadth is also the property an assessor can act on without knowing the business: naming one end of a rule is usually a short change, where deciding what traffic a rule was ever for is not.
controls.audit: Policies > Security. Read Source Address and Destination Address as address SPACE rather than as member counts - one object can be a /8. The rule's own row carries the resolved host count for each side, and `Unknown` where it could not be established.
controls.remediation: Narrow the broader side to the hosts or subnets the flow actually needs. Where a side is reported Unknown, the breadth is not known to be acceptable - run the EDL/FQDN cache refresh and re-check, or replace a dynamic group or region member with something resolvable.

queries.name: Broader than /8 on a side, or any
A side's breadth could not be established

controls.name: Disabled Rules Removed (Hygiene)
controls.description:
A disabled allow rule left in the policy, and how much it would permit if switched on.

THE TRIGGER IS PRESENCE, NOT AGE. controls.json states this control as "no rule has been disabled longer than 90 days", with 30 days preferred. Nothing in a configuration says when a rule was disabled - it needs config-history correlation this assessment does not have - so asserting a grace period would be asserting something unmeasured. Every disabled allow rule reports, and the finding says nothing about how long it has been that way.

SEVERITY COMES FROM THE BREADTH, using PAN-POL-002's thresholds and its severities unchanged: over 131,072 addresses on a side is medium, over 1,048,576 high, over 16,777,216 critical. The floor is low, which is the corpus severity and what a disabled rule of any size reports.

WHY A DISABLED RULE IS GRADED AT ALL. Jason, 2026-10-07: "A highly permissive but disabled rule could be worse then an operational-permissive rule. The disabled rule could be intentionally dangerous, previously used for testing purposes... Disabled rules could be more poorly designed, outside of governance type risks." A rule built broad for a test and left behind was never reviewed as production policy, and it is one click from being exactly the finding PAN-POL-002 reports. PAN-POL-002 excludes disabled rules because breadth scoring of an INACTIVE rule measures nothing about current exposure - not because such rules are less serious - so the two controls divide the rulebase rather than disagreeing about it.

SCOPE. Disabled allow rules, excluding the two predefined default rules, whose match tuple cannot be edited. A disabled DENY rule is a different defect - protection that was turned off - and is not covered here or anywhere else yet.

An indeterminate side reports at the baseline only. PAN-POL-002 raises an unmeasurable side to medium because it might permit anything; on a disabled rule it permits nothing either way, so that argument does not carry over.
controls.rationale: Disabled rules preserve intent nobody has revisited. They escape review as production policy, survive audits because they match no traffic, and get re-enabled "temporarily" during an incident by whoever is on call. Grading by breadth puts the ones that would open the most at the top of the list, which is the order an engineer can act in.
controls.audit: Policies > Security, with Disabled rules shown. The rule's own row carries the resolved host count for each side, and `Unknown` where it could not be established. Read the count as what the rule WOULD permit: it permits nothing while disabled.
controls.remediation: Delete the rule - configuration history preserves it for archaeology - or, if it is being kept deliberately, narrow it to what the flow it was written for actually needs and record the owner. A rule kept broad because it is disabled is a rule nobody has decided about.

controls.name: Security Rule Zones Explicit
controls.description:
An allow rule names the zones it applies to, on both sides.

A rule with `from any` or `to any` applies to every zone pair the firewall has, including pairs nobody considered when it was written - and adding a zone later silently widens it without anyone editing the rule.

SEVERITY COUNTS THE UNNAMED SIDES. One side `any` is medium; both sides `any` is high. Jason, 2026-10-07. A rule with one zone named still says which direction it applies in; a rule with neither says only "somewhere to somewhere".

NOT CRITICAL. The address and application axes are where unbounded reach is scored - PAN-POL-002 and PAN-POL-005 - and a rule whose addresses and application are all named but whose zone is `any` is a narrower problem than either. Of the lab's rules with an `any` zone, all but one are broad elsewhere too and already report PAN-POL-002.

WHERE THIS CAME FROM. controls.json states it only inside PAN-POL-001's preferred value - "zones always explicit" - and PAN-POL-001 never asserted it. When 001 was dropped into PAN-POL-002 on 2026-10-06 nothing was left pointing at this ground, so it became its own control. 20 corpus controls mention a zone and none of them asserts this: PAN-ZON-001 through 008 are zone PROTECTION profiles, PAN-POL-010 is about interzone deny rules, and PAN-UID-001 and PAN-IOT-002 scope features to zones.

SCOPE. Allow rules only, excluding the two predefined default rules - which carry no zone elements at all and cannot be edited - and excluding disabled rules, whose zones are PAN-POL-014's business.

INTRAZONE RULES ARE IN SCOPE, measured rather than assumed. PAN-OS refuses an intrazone rule whose source and destination zones differ, at the WRITE: code=12, "Intrazone rule has different set of source and destination zones" (pan-fw-111, 2026-10-07). So such a rule can satisfy this control - by naming the same zone on both sides - and an intrazone rule with `from any` necessarily has `to any`, which puts it in the high band rather than the medium one.
controls.rationale: A zone pair is the coarsest statement a rule makes about where it applies, and it is the one an engineer reads first. `any` there defers the decision to whatever the network becomes: every zone added after the rule was written inherits it. Naming the zones is also usually a short change, because the author knew the answer at the time and did not have to write it down.
controls.audit: Policies > Security. Read the Source Zone and Destination Zone columns. `any` on one side is medium, on both sides high. The predefined intrazone-default and interzone-default rules carry no zone elements and are out of scope.
controls.remediation: Name the zones the flow actually crosses. Where a rule genuinely applies to every zone - a deny-all at the bottom of the rulebase, for instance - that is a deliberate `any` and the assessor can clear it; nothing in the configuration distinguishes it from an unconsidered one.

controls.name: Antivirus Profile Blocks Malware on All Decoders and Application Exceptions
controls.description:
An antivirus profile that detects malware on a protocol without stopping it.

THE CONFIGURATION DOES NOT ANSWER THIS. Every decoder of every unedited antivirus profile stores the literal `default`, the shipped one included - measured 2026-10-07, `/config/predefined/profiles/virus/entry[@name='default']` returns `action=default` on all seven. What `default` MEANS is per protocol and PAN-OS states it only in the UI:

    http, http2, ftp, smb   ->  reset-both
    smtp, imap, pop3        ->  alert

So the shipped `default` profile detects mail-borne malware and lets it through, on three of its seven decoders. controls.json says the same thing in words - "the shipped 'default' profile only alerts on several decoders - detection without prevention" - and the two agree, which is the evidence this rests on. Neither is the device's own words. The resolution is a named table in OptivEdgeIntegrations rather than a scattered assumption, so a PAN-OS release that changes it changes one place.

WHAT IT ASSERTS. Every inspection point on the profile carries an EXPLICITLY SET, drop-like action. Three things must hold of each one: it is set, it is recognised, and it stops the transfer.

THE INSPECTION POINTS ARE: each of the seven protocol decoders in each of its THREE action columns - 21 cells - and each application exception.

A POINT PASSES only when it resolves to drop, reset-client, reset-server or reset-both. Everything else is a finding, and the failures fall into two kinds worth keeping apart because the remediation differs:

NOT DROP-LIKE - `alert` and `allow`. A decision was made and it does not stop the transfer. The fix is to change a value.

NOT DETERMINATELY DROP-LIKE - no element at all, a value this implementation does not recognise, and on an application exception the literal `default`, which resolves per signature and so has no single action to test. The fix is to set the value explicitly. A DECODER's `default` is NOT in this group: it resolves per protocol and that resolution is measured - reset-both on http/http2/ftp/smb, alert on smtp/imap/pop3 - so a decoder at `default` is judged on what it resolves to. The one exception is a protocol PAN-OS adds in a later release, which has no measured resolution and therefore fails.

BOTH KINDS PRODUCE A FINDING, and that is deliberate. A control that passed the second kind would be reporting "we checked and it was fine" where the truth is "no single action is determined here" - which is the one direction an inspection control must never fail in.

The corpus names `reset-both` for both its minimum and its preferred value, differing only in scope - minimum is the HTTP decoder, preferred is all of them - and this asserts the preferred, per the checklist's rule of asserting the stricter and letting an assessor relax it.

BLOCKING IS A SET, not the single literal `reset-both`: drop, reset-client, reset-server and reset-both. A profile that drops malware has not failed to block it. Same deviation PAN-SPY-001 makes, recorded in control-changes.json.

NOT ASSERTED HERE. The WildFire inline ML models, which are PAN-AVW-002, and the wildfire-action column, which resolves the same way and is carried on each decoder row for an assessor's own query.

A DECODER ACTION IS NOT THE LAST WORD, which is why this control asks two questions rather than one. An antivirus profile's `application` node is a PER-APPLICATION ACTION OVERRIDE - entry-keyed, each entry naming an application and carrying the same seven actions as a decoder. A profile can read `reset-both` on all seven decoders and still allow malware over a named application, and until 2026-10-08 this control reported such a profile as hardened. The node was in the config the whole time; it surfaced only when the profile's key set was enumerated from the device with `action=complete` instead of read off a sample.

WHAT THE OVERRIDE ACCEPTS, measured 2026-10-08 by writing each shape. The application key is a REFERENCE and eligibility is ENFORCED AT THE WRITE: the device offers 1454 of its 5552 predefined applications and refuses an entry naming one outside that set - `ping 'ping' is not a valid reference`, code=12. An entry with NO action is accepted and stores an absent action, which reads as `allow` by the same rule as an absent decoder action; an entry with an EMPTY action element is refused. So the permissive case is reachable and the ambiguous one is not.

THE LITERAL `default` ON AN EXCEPTION RESOLVES PER SIGNATURE, measured 2026-10-09. Two profiles carrying the same eleven `default` exceptions and differing only in their decoders - one left at `default`, one set explicitly and INVERTED - render the bare word on all 22 rows and agree with each other. That rules out inheriting the application's decoder, the per-protocol table, and any single fixed value; the same export brackets the decoder column in the same row, so the missing bracket is real. It is also what the vendor says: Help p.272, the page p.277 points to for this field, describes a signature's default as the action that signature ships with.

SO SUCH AN EXCEPTION IS REPORTED. A signature's own default is typically alert or reset-both, so an exception left at `default` lets whatever the alerting signatures catch through. It is a real gap rather than an unknown, and the finding names it as "each signature's own action" rather than claiming a resolved value that does not exist.

NOTE THE TWO MECHANISMS ON ONE SCREEN. A DECODER's `default` resolves to one action per protocol and the UI brackets it. An EXCEPTION's does not. Carrying the decoder's resolution across to the exception would have been wrong.

SEQUENCE. The override rows are written by normalization, so this control reports on them only after a re-normalize: migrate, RENORMALIZE, reseed, regenerate. A profile row collected before the override model existed has no override rows and reads as clean, which is indistinguishable from a profile that has no overrides.

A DECODER HAS THREE ACTION COLUMNS AND THIS ASSERTS ALL THREE. The UI's decoder table carries SIGNATURE ACTION, WILDFIRE SIGNATURE ACTION and WILDFIRE INLINE ML ACTION per protocol, and `default` resolves by the same per-protocol table in every one of them - measured 2026-10-07 from the create form, where all three columns render identically row for row. They are three VERDICT SOURCES on one protocol: a signature hit, a WildFire-derived signature hit, and an inline ML verdict.

Until 2026-10-08 only the first was collected and only the first was asserted, so a profile that was `reset-both` on signature action and `allow` on both WildFire columns passed this control while delivering anything WildFire caught. The corpus wording is "reset/drop malware across every protocol decoder", and a decoder that allows a WildFire verdict is not resetting malware on that decoder.

DISTINCT FROM PAN-AVW-002. This control asks what happens to a verdict; PAN-AVW-002 asks whether the inline ML MODELS run at all. Both are needed - a profile can enable every model and allow every verdict it produces, and neither control alone sees that.

A DECODER ROW WITH NO INLINE ML VERDICT RECORDED IS REPORTED, not passed. `mlav-action` was never collected before 2026-10-08, so rows written earlier carry no value and there is nothing to backfill them from - a value invented at migration time would be a guess this control then scores. Such a row reports as "not yet computed", which names itself rather than reading as a hardened estate. Re-normalizing clears it.

REPORTED PER RULE, not per profile (2026-10-12). A profile nothing uses endangers nothing, and a rule is what carries traffic, so the subject is the rule and the finding names the antivirus profile in force on it. One profile behind forty rules therefore produces forty findings - each is a distinct piece of traffic.

SCOPE. Allow rules that are not the predefined default rules - the same exclusions as PAN-AVW-003 and PAN-POL-008. A rule that denies, drops or resets passes no traffic for a profile to inspect, so a profile on it, or the lack of one, protects nothing either way. Unlike those two controls, a DISABLED allow rule is reported: it is in the configuration and one click from carrying traffic, and its finding says it is disabled (Jason, 2026-10-14).

A rule with NO antivirus profile in force IS reported here - the absence is this control's own finding, not only PAN-POL-008's (Jason, 2026-10-12). So the two overlap on an allow rule carrying none: PAN-POL-008 says the rule is uninspected, this control says which inspection it is missing.
controls.rationale: Antivirus is the cheapest inspection the firewall does and the shipped profile is what a rule gets when nobody chose one. Three of its seven decoders alert rather than block, so mail-borne malware is logged on its way past. The gap is invisible in the configuration, which says `default` everywhere, and invisible in the UI unless someone reads the resolved action beside each protocol.
controls.audit:
Objects > Security Profiles > Antivirus. Read the decoder table's THREE action columns - SIGNATURE ACTION, WILDFIRE SIGNATURE ACTION, WILDFIRE INLINE ML ACTION - for all seven protocols, and then the APPLICATION EXCEPTIONS tab of the same screen.

In the DECODER table a `default` renders with its resolution in brackets - `default (alert)` or `default (reset-both)` - and the bracketed word is the one that matters; the configuration itself says only `default`. All three columns must read a blocking action on every protocol: a profile hardened in the first column alone still delivers what WildFire and inline ML catch.

In the APPLICATION EXCEPTIONS table there is NO bracket, because an exception's `default` resolves per signature rather than to one action. An exception set to `default`, or left with no action, is not a determinable block - and any exception overrides the decoder for that application, so a profile hardened on every decoder can still allow malware over whatever is listed there.
controls.remediation:
Set every action explicitly and to a blocking value. The predefined `default` profile cannot be edited, so this means creating a profile and attaching it wherever `default` is referenced - a profile group reaches more rules at once than the rules do.

Set all THREE decoder columns, not just Signature Action: WildFire Signature and WildFire Inline ML are separate verdict sources and share the same per-protocol default, which alerts rather than blocks on smtp, imap and pop3.

For each application exception, either remove it or give it an explicit blocking action. Leaving one at `default` is not equivalent to the decoder's `default`: it defers to each signature's own action, and signatures that ship defaulting to alert will let their detections through.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: Rules whose antivirus profile lets malware through on a decoder or an application exception.

controls.name: WildFire Inline ML Enabled
controls.description:
An antivirus profile with WildFire Inline ML models switched off.

Inline ML blocks never-before-seen malware - PE files, ELF, MSOffice, PowerShell, shell scripts - in real time, rather than waiting for a cloud verdict that arrives after the file has landed. A model that is off is a file type nothing inspects in line.

THE SHIPPED PROFILE IS STRONGER THAN A HAND-MADE ONE HERE, which is the reverse of the usual direction and the reason this control earns its place. Measured 2026-10-07: the predefined `default` profile enables every model, and a profile created through the Panorama UI without touching a single setting writes `disable` for every one. An administrator who builds their own profile to be careful ends up with LESS inline ML than if they had left the shipped one alone.

`mlav-policy-action` HAS THREE VALUES, not two - `enable`, `enable(alert-only)` and `disable`, enumerated from the device with action=complete on 2026-10-08. A model on alert-only RUNS and does not STOP the file, so this control asks whether each model BLOCKS, which is the literal the corpus names for its minimum and its preferred alike. Treating alert-only as simply "enabled" would pass a profile that logs malware and delivers it.

A MODEL THE CONFIG NEVER MENTIONS IS OFF. A profile with no `mlav-engine-filebased-enabled` node renders every model as disabled in the UI - the same rule as an absent decoder action, which means `allow`. So the absence of a setting is never read here as the absence of a problem.

THE MODEL NAMES COME FROM THE CONTENT RELEASE, not from PAN-OS, and controls.json says to enumerate them on the target version rather than assume them. Nothing here hardcodes a list: the catalogue is read from the predefined profile, which carries every model the device knows about - eight on the lab. A content update that adds a ninth is assessed with no change to this control.

WHAT IT ASSERTS. Every available model enabled. The corpus minimum is Windows Executables alone and its preferred is every model; this asserts the preferred, per the checklist's rule of asserting the stricter and letting an assessor relax it.

A rule protected by the predefined `default` antivirus profile passes this control on every estate.

REPORTED PER RULE, not per profile (2026-10-12). A profile nothing uses endangers nothing, and a rule is what carries traffic, so the subject is the rule and the finding names the antivirus profile in force on it. One profile behind forty rules therefore produces forty findings - each is a distinct piece of traffic.

SCOPE. Allow rules that are not the predefined default rules - the same exclusions as PAN-AVW-003 and PAN-POL-008. A rule that denies, drops or resets passes no traffic for a profile to inspect, so a profile on it, or the lack of one, protects nothing either way. Unlike those two controls, a DISABLED allow rule is reported: it is in the configuration and one click from carrying traffic, and its finding says it is disabled (Jason, 2026-10-14).

A rule with NO antivirus profile in force IS reported here - the absence is this control's own finding, not only PAN-POL-008's (Jason, 2026-10-12). So the two overlap on an allow rule carrying none: PAN-POL-008 says the rule is uninspected, this control says which inspection it is missing.
controls.rationale: Signature-based antivirus cannot catch what has no signature yet, which is precisely the malware that reaches a target first. Inline ML is the part of the profile that does, and it is off by default on every profile an administrator creates - so the gap appears exactly where someone has taken the trouble to build their own profile.
controls.audit: Objects > Security Profiles > Antivirus, the WildFire Inline ML tab, ACTION SETTING column. The predefined `default` reads `enable (inherit per-protocol actions)` on every model; a profile created and left alone reads `disable (for all protocols)`.
controls.remediation: Set every model to enable. `enable (inherit per-protocol actions)` ties the ML verdict to the per-protocol decoder action, so hardening the decoders - PAN-AVW-001 - carries through to inline ML rather than needing a second decision.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: Rules whose antivirus profile has a WildFire inline ML model that does not block.

controls.name: Unused AV / WildFire Profiles (Hygiene)
controls.description:
An antivirus or WildFire analysis profile that no security rule and no profile group names.

BOTH KINDS, AS TWO ONE-KIND QUERIES (2026-10-31). V1 was antivirus only, where the corpus names antivirus AND WildFire analysis profiles. That was never a judgement about WildFire analysis - it was a structural limit: the configuration explorer has one page per profile KIND, mirroring PAN-OS's own tabs, a control query is linked to the page whose scope its clauses contain, and a query SPANNING two kinds matches neither page, so the resolver refuses to guess rather than send an assessor somewhere plausible and wrong.

The limit is about one query, not about one control. A control fires when either half holds (standing ruling 6), and every active query is OR'd when the control is evaluated - so two queries, each naming ONE kind, cover both subjects while each stays answerable against its own page. Nothing new was needed in the store: every column both queries name already shipped on the profile row.

An unreferenced profile is drift: it was built for something, that something changed, and the profile stayed. The risk is not the profile sitting there - it is the next administrator attaching it believing it current, which is how a rule ends up protected by settings nobody has looked at in two years.

WHAT COUNTS AS A REFERENCE. A rule naming the profile directly in its profile-setting, or a profile group naming it. Both are already resolved - `is_used` and `referrer_count` are written by the referrer walk, which reads rules and groups across every scope a reference can resolve through.

THE PREDEFINED PROFILES ARE OUT OF SCOPE. `default` ships with the device and exists whether anyone uses it or not; an unused one says nothing about the estate. A rule protected by it is PAN-AVW-001's and PAN-AVW-002's business, not this control's. Same scope decision as PAN-SPY-001 reaches from the other side.

IT SAYS NOTHING ABOUT THE PROFILE'S CONTENTS. An unused profile that blocks everything reports here exactly like an unused one that blocks nothing - the finding is that it is unattached. Whether it would protect anything is PAN-AVW-001, 002 and 003.

LOW, and deliberately. Nothing is exposed by a profile nobody uses. The corpus marks it hygiene and so does this - it belongs in the same sweep as the other unused-object controls, not in a remediation queue.
