controls.rationale: A rulebase accumulates profiles the way it accumulates rules, and nothing in the UI distinguishes a profile in service from one abandoned three migrations ago. An assessor can clear the list quickly once it exists; nobody produces it by hand.
controls.audit: Objects > Security Profiles > Antivirus and > WildFire Analysis. The finding names the profile and its scope; the referrer count on its row is zero, which is the whole assertion.
controls.remediation: Delete it, or attach it where it was meant to go. If it is kept deliberately - a pre-staged profile for an incident, say - record that, because nothing in the configuration distinguishes it from one that was forgotten.

queries.short_description: Antivirus profiles that no security rule and no profile group names.

controls.name: WildFire Analysis Profile Submits All File Types
controls.description:
A security rule whose traffic is not fully sent for WildFire sandbox analysis.

PER RULE, NOT PER PROFILE. A WildFire analysis profile nothing uses endangers nothing; a rule carries traffic. The same profile can be correct for one rule and absent from another, and the remediation - attach a profile, or widen one - belongs to the rule. PAN-AVW-006 is the control that asks about unused profiles.

THREE WAYS A RULE FAILS, and they have different fixes, so the finding says which:

  - NO PROFILE REACHES IT. The rule names none, or names a profile group that names no WildFire analysis profile, or names one that resolves to nothing in scope. Nothing is sent. On the lab this is the common case: 113 rules point at a group called `default` that names no profiles at all.
  - THE PROFILE SENDS NOTHING. A profile with no `rules` node, an empty one, or a rule carrying only a name are all valid configuration - measured 2026-10-09 by writing each - and all three submit nothing while looking configured.
  - THE PROFILE IS TOO NARROW. Its rules name specific file types rather than `any`, or specific applications, or a single direction.

WHAT IT ASSERTS. Some rule in the profile in force covers `any` file type, `any` application and both directions. The corpus names `any` for both its minimum and its preferred value, differing only in that the preferred adds direction `both` and all application traffic; this asserts the preferred, per the checklist's rule of asserting the stricter and letting an assessor relax it.

BOTH DIRECTIONS MATTER and the corpus says why: inbound is delivery, outbound is exfiltration and beacon staging. A profile set to `upload` only leaves every delivered file unanalysed.

A RULE WITH NO DIRECTION SET IS REPORTED, not passed. The device accepts a profile rule carrying no `direction` and stores none; the UI writes `both` when a rule is added through the form, so no instance of the absent case exists to read and nothing establishes what the device then does. Unestablished must not render as fine.

THE SHIPPED PROFILE PASSES, which is the reverse of PAN-AVW-001 and 002. The predefined `default` carries one rule: file-type `any`, application `any`, direction `both`, analysis `public-cloud` - read off the device 2026-10-09. So a rule that uses the shipped profile is fine here, and the finding is about rules that reach no profile or a hand-narrowed one.

PRIVATE CLOUD IS NOT THE SAME COVERAGE, and this control does not report it. Help p.308: "A WildFire private cloud (hosted by a WildFire appliance) does not support analysis of APK, Mac OS X, archive, and linux files." So a rule whose profile asks for `file-type any` at `analysis private-cloud` still leaves four types unanalysed. The corpus explicitly permits private-cloud where data residency requires it, so firing on it would contradict the corpus - and the claim is documentation, not measurement: no WildFire appliance exists on the lab to confirm it. Recorded here so an assessor reading a passing private-cloud rule knows what the pass means.

WHAT THIS CONTROL DOES NOT COVER. Device-wide WildFire settings gate what is actually forwarded regardless of the profile - a file type listed here is still never analysed if it exceeds `deviceconfig/setting/wildfire/file-size-limit` for its type. That is PAN-AVW-004 and it is a separate subject; this control asserts what the profile asks for, not what the platform ultimately sends.

SCOPE. Allow rules that are not the implicit defaults - the same scope as PAN-POL-008 and as the eleven threat-profile controls, because the question is the same shape: what inspection is in force on traffic this rule permits.

A DISABLED ALLOW RULE IS REPORTED (2026-10-31). V1 also carried `disabled eq false`, which made this the one av-wildfire control that excluded switched-off rules. That clause is the one Jason ruled out on 2026-10-14 - "keep disabled rules in scope", because a disabled allow rule is one click from carrying traffic and its finding already says DISABLED - and 3e2cc5a left it out of the eleven threat-profile baselines for exactly that reason. This control was passed over by that commit on the ground that it "already led with three scope clauses", which was true and left the ruled-out clause standing. Removed here, so all twelve per-rule threat-profile controls now scope alike.
controls.rationale: WildFire is the only thing that catches malware with no signature yet, and the profile decides what it ever sees. A file type the profile filters out is an unanalysed delivery channel, and a rule that reaches no profile at all is every file type filtered out. The gap is invisible from the rule itself: it shows a profile group and looks configured.
controls.audit: For each enabled allow rule, resolve what it actually reaches: Policies > Security, the rule's Profile column, then Objects > Security Profile Groups for the group it names and whether that group lists a WildFire Analysis profile. Then Objects > Security Profiles > WildFire Analysis for that profile's Rules tab - FILE TYPES must read `any`, APPLICATIONS `any`, and DIRECTION `both`. A profile with an empty Rules tab sends nothing. Note the ANALYSIS column too: `private-cloud` does not analyse APK, Mac OS X, archive or linux files at all, so a private-cloud profile asking for every file type still leaves four unanalysed.
controls.remediation: Attach a WildFire analysis profile to every rule that permits traffic, through the profile group the rules already name rather than rule by rule. The predefined `default` profile already submits everything, so referencing it is sufficient where no local policy requires otherwise; where a custom profile exists, give it a rule with file type `any`, application `any` and direction `both`. Check the device-wide file size limits too - PAN-AVW-004 - since a type above its limit is never analysed whatever the profile says.

controls.name: WildFire File Size Limits Tuned
controls.description:
An appliance whose WildFire file size limits are all still at the PAN-OS default.

EVERY TYPE, NOT ANY TYPE (2026-10-31). V1 asserted `size_limits_untuned`, which fires when ANY asserted type is still at its default. The sentence above - and the whole of this description - is about a platform nobody has sized AT ALL, which is the ALL quantifier, and the store carries both columns for exactly this reason. An estate that sized one type and left the other nine is making a decision this control has no business reporting, and the lab separates the two readings: fw-core-tpa-a has moved `pe` off its default and nothing else, so V1 reported it and this does not.

A TUNING CHECK, not a maximisation check (Jason, 2026-10-09). The corpus asks for the platform maximum; Help p.774 advises the opposite in the paragraph that describes the field - "if the limit is too large and prevents the firewall from forwarding multiple large zero-day files at the same time, lower and tune the maximum limit based on the amount of available firewall buffer space." Both cannot be asserted, and asserting the maximum would call the vendor's own advice a finding. So this asks the question that IS answerable from configuration - has anybody sized these at all - and is neutral on direction: a value moved off its default, up or down, is evidence of a decision.

THE DEFAULTS ARE PAN-OS'S OWN, from two agreeing vendor sources - Help pages 774-776 and Panorama's Size Limit tooltip: pe 16 MB (1-50), apk 10 MB (1-50), pdf 3072 KB (100-51200), ms-office 16384 KB (200-51200), jar 5 MB (1-20), flash 5 MB (1-10), MacOSX 10 MB (1-50), archive 50 MB (1-50), linux 50 MB (1-50), script 20 KB (10-4096).

WHAT THIS FINDING MEANS, AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. The default IS the vendor's best-practice recommendation for nine of the ten - the Help restates each default as its own recommendation. So an estate at defaults is AT the recommended starting point, not below it, and this control is NOT saying the limits are too low. It says nobody has evaluated whether this platform can afford more. Help p.775: the recommendations are "a good starting place for setting effective limits that don't overtax firewall resources", and "if more buffer space is available, you can increase the file size limit above the best practice recommendation." That evaluation needs the platform's buffer headroom, which is not in the configuration - hence a low severity and a remediation that asks for a decision rather than a number.

MacOSX IS THE ONE PLACE THE VENDOR DISAGREES WITH ITSELF: default 10 MB, recommendation "Set the size for MacOSX files to 1MB". Every other bullet restates its own default and 1 MB is the range minimum, so it reads like a documentation error. Recorded, not acted on - the control compares against the DEFAULT, as it does for every other type.

THE VENDOR SAYS THESE VALUES MOVE. p.776: they "might differ based on the current version of PAN-OS or the content release", and the Size Limit tooltip is the live authority. A CONTENT release can change them, not only a PAN-OS upgrade, so this table is a snapshot and should be re-read against the tooltip when either changes.

TWO EARLIER TABLES WERE WRONG and both inferred the defaults from a DEVICE - one took a template STACK's configuration for the platform's defaults, the other read one device and could cover only one release. Both were avoidable: the Help states the defaults outright, one page further on than the page the search returned.

RELEASE-INVARIANT, for what this asserts. 11.2 adds `eml` to the key set - ten types on 11.1, eleven on 11.2 - and `eml` is excluded, so the ten asserted here are the same on both.

TWO TYPES DEFAULT TO THEIR MAXIMUM, archive and linux - fatal to the reading this control does NOT take, since a check asserting limits 'raised to the platform maximum' could never fire on those two however an estate was configured.

WHAT COUNTS AS UNTUNED. Every file type the release has a default for, not only the ones the configuration names. An absent entry is the clearest case of untouched there is, and walking only what is present would report a device that configures nothing as fully tuned - which is exactly the PA-5220s' shape.

`eml` IS NEVER ASSERTED. A TEMPLATE cannot set it - the write is refused with `eml 'eml' is not a valid reference`, and a template's key set is ten where an 11.2 device's is eleven. On a Panorama-managed estate its only remediation would be a device-local override, and a control whose sole remedy is to create an override is asking for the thing treated as a defect everywhere else here.

THE UNITS ARE NOT UNIFORM - the UI renders pe as 16 MB and pdf as 3072 KB - so a value is compared only against its own default and never against another type's.
controls.rationale: A file above its forwarding limit is never analysed, and attackers pad payloads past default limits precisely because the defaults are predictable and widely unchanged. The limits that suit an estate depend on its hardware and traffic, so the finding is not that a number is wrong - it is that nobody has chosen one.
controls.audit:
Device > Setup > WildFire > General Settings > File Size Limits. Compare each per-type value against the PAN-OS default for that type; a type missing from the list is at its default by definition. Click in a Size Limit field to see the live range and default - the vendor states they can change with a PAN-OS or content release, so the tooltip beats any written table including this one.

Note the units differ per type - pe is MB, pdf is KB - so read each row against its own default rather than against its neighbours. On a Panorama-managed estate check the template STACK as well as the templates: the stack overrides its members, so a value set in a template may not be the one in force.
controls.remediation:
Size each limit against the platform's available buffer space and the file types the estate actually carries, and record the reasoning - the point is a deliberate choice, not a particular number. The permitted ranges are pe 1-50 MB, apk 1-50 MB, pdf 100-51200 KB, ms-office 200-51200 KB, jar 1-20 MB, flash 1-10 MB, MacOSX 1-50 MB, archive 1-50 MB, linux 1-50 MB, script 10-4096 KB.

Raising every limit to the maximum is NOT the vendor's advice: Help p.774 warns that a limit too large prevents the firewall forwarding multiple large zero-day files at once. Note also that archive and linux already default to their maximum.

On a Panorama-managed estate set these in the TEMPLATE or the template STACK, not on the firewall, or the next push reverts them - and remember the stack overrides its member templates, so a value set in a template will not take effect if the stack also sets it.

controls.name: WildFire Session Information Sharing Enabled
controls.description:
An appliance that withholds session context from WildFire, or does not report benign and grayware verdicts.

BOTH HALVES, EITHER ONE FIRES (Jason, 2026-10-09). The corpus entry names two different things - its title and description are about session information sharing, its xpath is `report-grayware-file` - and they are two different nodes in opposite states on the lab. The control asserts both.

THE CONFIG STORES EXCLUSIONS, SO THE UI IS INVERTED, and reading it the other way round gets this control exactly backwards. `session-info-select` holds twelve `exclude-*` members - exclude-url, exclude-username, exclude-filename and nine more - so a ticked checkbox on Device > Setup > WildFire means the exclusion is ABSENT. An empty list is FULL sharing and the state this control wants. That is the opposite of the usual rule that an absent key is the weaker end, which is why it is stated here rather than left to be rediscovered.

THE TWO REPORT FLAGS ARE PLAIN. `report-benign-file` and `report-grayware-file` are yes/no and both are implicitly NO - absent on pan-fw-111 and both boxes render unticked, measured 2026-10-09. So an untouched device fails this half, and the finding says so rather than reading like somebody turned them off.

WHAT IT DOES NOT ASSERT. The Inline Session Information Settings block (`cloud-inline-wf-session-info-select`) carries the same twelve exclusions for the inline-cloud engine. It is collected and shown, and not asserted - no corpus control names it, and inventing one here would be widening the corpus rather than implementing it.

THE REPORTING HALF IS GRADED, AS FOUR QUERIES ON ONE TOKEN (2026-10-31). V1 put all three columns in one OR'd baseline, which fires correctly and cannot carry a severity: the two reporting gaps rank differently - unwanted-file verdicts low, harmless-file verdicts informational - and a disjunction has one severity. So the baseline now carries the session-information half alone, and the reporting half is three calibration queries over `verdict_reporting_gap`, a token the normalizer derives from the same two booleans and which therefore can never disagree with them. Its four members are mutually exclusive on a single-valued column, so no appliance matches two of them.

WHEN BOTH HALVES FAIL AT ONCE, the reported severity is the worst matched calibration and not the baseline tier - which is how the severity machinery works for every graded control. An appliance withholding session context AND missing only harmless-file reporting therefore reports at informational rather than low. That is a real under-report and it is recorded in the stage 8 av-wildfire artifact rather than worked around here, because the fix is a decision about whether these two halves should be one control at all.
controls.rationale: A WildFire verdict is more useful with the session that produced it - the URL, the filename, the user - and the analysis report is richer for it. Benign and grayware reporting is what makes near-miss deliveries visible at all: without it the only samples an analyst ever sees are the ones already judged malicious, which is the wrong end of the funnel for hunting.
controls.audit: Device > Setup > WildFire. In Session Information Settings every box should be ticked - a ticked box means that attribute is NOT excluded. In General Settings, Report Benign File and Report Grayware File should both be ticked; both are unticked by default.
controls.remediation: Tick every Session Information Settings box and both report boxes. On a Panorama-managed estate set them in the TEMPLATE, not on the firewall. Note the privacy direction: these forward session context including usernames and URLs to the WildFire cloud, so an estate with a data-residency or privacy constraint should take the exclusions deliberately rather than by default - this control reports the default, which is to share everything and report nothing.

controls.name: DNS Sinkhole Enabled
controls.description:
Reports an anti-spyware profile whose Palo Alto Networks Content DNS signatures are not sinkholed. Sinkholing forges the answer to a malicious DNS query so the infected client tries to reach the sinkhole address instead, which both breaks command-and-control resolution and identifies the real client behind an internal DNS resolver.

Scoped to the Palo Alto Networks Content source. DNS Security categories are a licensed service with a different action set and are PAN-SPY-003's subject; an External Dynamic List with an allow or alert action is the documented way to express a DNS exception and is not reported.

REPORTED PER RULE, not per profile (2026-10-12). A profile nothing uses endangers nothing, and a rule is what carries traffic, so the subject is the rule and the finding names the profile in force on it. One profile behind forty rules therefore produces forty findings - which is the point: each is a distinct piece of traffic.

SCOPE. Allow rules that are not the predefined default rules - the same exclusions as PAN-AVW-003 and PAN-POL-008. A rule that denies, drops or resets passes no traffic for a profile to inspect, so a profile on it, or the lack of one, protects nothing either way. Unlike those two controls, a DISABLED allow rule is reported: it is in the configuration and one click from carrying traffic, and its finding says it is disabled (Jason, 2026-10-14).

A rule with NO anti-spyware profile in force IS reported here - the absence is this control's own finding, not only PAN-POL-008's (Jason, 2026-10-12). So the two overlap on an allow rule carrying none: PAN-POL-008 says the rule is uninspected, this control says which inspection it is missing.
controls.rationale:
Where the firewall sits north of a local DNS resolver, every malicious lookup appears to come from the resolver, so a blocked or alerted query names the wrong host and the infected client stays hidden. `block` stops the resolution and still loses the client, which is why it does not satisfy this control - the Help offers it only as the fallback when sinkholing is impossible (p.285).

The shipped profiles disagree with each other, so inheriting one is not a safe default: `strict` sinkholes and `default` only ALERTS, measured on 11.2.3-h3.
controls.audit: Objects > Security Profiles > Anti-Spyware > <profile> > DNS Policies. Read the Policy Action on the Palo Alto Networks Content row, and the DNS Sinkhole Settings beneath it for the address. A profile that has never been configured here shows the vendor default.
controls.remediation:
Set the Policy Action for Palo Alto Networks Content to `sinkhole`.

The sinkhole address is a PREREQUISITE and must be set first: the action is refused with "sinkhole IPv4 information is missing" until botnet-domains/sinkhole/ipv4-address exists, and an IPv6 address alone does not satisfy it. `pan-sinkhole-default-ip` is the vendor's own token and what the predefined `strict` profile carries; an internal address in a monitored zone is better, because sinkhole hits are then visible in traffic logs as incidents to triage.

A predefined profile cannot be edited - point the Security policy rules and Security Profile Groups using it at a custom profile instead.

controls.name: DNS Security Categories Enforced
controls.description:
Reports an anti-spyware profile that does not block or sinkhole the malicious DNS Security categories - command-and-control, malware and phishing. Leaving a category at `default` does not enforce it: PAN-OS Web Interface Help 11.2 p.284 says the cloud-based DNS Security is set to allow by default and that sinkholing must be configured explicitly. BOTH PREDEFINED PROFILES leave all ten categories at `default`, so a profile that inherits one reports.

Three of ten categories are asserted. Newly-registered, parked and DGA are a risk-tolerance judgement in the corpus and are not asserted; benign, ad-tracking, grayware, proxy-avoidance and dynamic-DNS are not named by it. `block` satisfies this control, which PAN-SPY-002 does not accept for the signature list - the two corpus entries differ on that point.

Assessed on every firewall regardless of DNS Security licensing. The configuration is accepted without the licence, so the setting is readable everywhere; a profile that passes on an unlicensed device is configured correctly and enforces nothing, because the licence gates the service rather than the config.

REPORTED PER RULE, not per profile (2026-10-12). A profile nothing uses endangers nothing, and a rule is what carries traffic, so the subject is the rule and the finding names the profile in force on it. One profile behind forty rules therefore produces forty findings - which is the point: each is a distinct piece of traffic.

SCOPE. Allow rules that are not the predefined default rules - the same exclusions as PAN-AVW-003 and PAN-POL-008. A rule that denies, drops or resets passes no traffic for a profile to inspect, so a profile on it, or the lack of one, protects nothing either way. Unlike those two controls, a DISABLED allow rule is reported: it is in the configuration and one click from carrying traffic, and its finding says it is disabled (Jason, 2026-10-14).

A rule with NO anti-spyware profile in force IS reported here - the absence is this control's own finding, not only PAN-POL-008's (Jason, 2026-10-12). So the two overlap on an allow rule carrying none: PAN-POL-008 says the rule is uninspected, this control says which inspection it is missing.
controls.rationale: DNS Security classifies domains in the cloud in real time, which is what catches infrastructure too new or too short-lived for a downloadable signature list. A category left at `default` lets those lookups resolve, so the firewall holds a subscription whose verdicts change nothing.
controls.audit: Objects > Security Profiles > Anti-Spyware > <profile> > DNS Policies, the DNS Security rows. Read the Policy Action on the command-and-control, malware and phishing categories. `default` is a pointer to the per-signature action, not an action - treat it as unconfigured.
controls.remediation:
Set the Policy Action on the command-and-control, malware and phishing DNS Security categories to `sinkhole`, or to `block` where sinkholing is not wanted. Sinkhole is the better choice for the same reason as PAN-SPY-002: it identifies the infected client behind an internal resolver, and it needs the profile's sinkhole IPv4 address set first.

A predefined profile cannot be edited - point the Security policy rules and Security Profile Groups using it at a custom profile instead.

Leave newly-registered, parked and the grayware-style categories to local risk tolerance; this control does not assert them.

controls.name: Inline Cloud Analysis (Advanced Threat Prevention) Enabled
controls.description:
An anti-spyware profile whose inline cloud-analysis detectors do not stop the traffic they catch.

Advanced Threat Prevention's deep-learning engines judge live traffic rather than waiting for a signature to be published, which is what catches unknown command and control - Cobalt Strike and Empire-style beacons among them. FIVE detectors on 11.2: HTTP, HTTP2, SSL, Unknown-TCP and Unknown-UDP Command and Control.

THE CORPUS POINTS THIS CONTROL AT A NODE THAT DOES NOT EXIST. controls.json names `cloud-inline-analysis/enabled`; writing it is refused with `cloud-inline-analysis is invalid` (code=12) on 11.2.3-h3 WITH an Advanced Threat Prevention licence active - measured 2026-10-10. The engine lives at `mica-engine-{kind}-enabled`, entry-keyed by detector, each carrying `inline-policy-action`. That is what the corpus DESCRIBES, just not where it points, so this is built against the real node and the deviation is recorded in control-changes.json. Jason approved, 2026-10-10.

`alert` RUNS THE DETECTOR AND LETS THE TRAFFIC THROUGH, which is why this asks whether each detector BLOCKS rather than whether it is on. It is the same distinction `enable(alert-only)` forced on PAN-AVW-002: a detector that only watches is not protection, and treating it as enabled would pass a profile that logs the attack and delivers it.

A DETECTOR THE PROFILE NEVER MENTIONS DOES NOT RUN, and has a row saying so. The detector names come from the content release, so nothing is hardcoded in the query - but unlike the antivirus ML models, the catalogue cannot be read from the predefined profiles: all four of them carry ZERO entries for this engine, measured 2026-10-10. A build-derived catalogue would be empty, no rows would be written, and a profile running no inline analysis at all would read as having nothing wrong. The catalogue therefore falls back to the measured key space.

WHAT IT ASSERTS. Every detector set to an action that stops the transfer - drop, reset-client, reset-server or reset-both. The corpus's preferred value is "yes ... with reset actions on verdicts", and this asserts that; its minimum is "not required without an Advanced Threat Prevention subscription", which is a licensing condition rather than a configuration one.

REPORTED PER RULE, not per profile (2026-10-12). A profile nothing uses endangers nothing, and a rule is what carries traffic, so the subject is the rule and the finding names the profile in force on it. One profile behind forty rules therefore produces forty findings - which is the point: each is a distinct piece of traffic.

SCOPE. Allow rules that are not the predefined default rules - the same exclusions as PAN-AVW-003 and PAN-POL-008. A rule that denies, drops or resets passes no traffic for a profile to inspect, so a profile on it, or the lack of one, protects nothing either way. Unlike those two controls, a DISABLED allow rule is reported: it is in the configuration and one click from carrying traffic, and its finding says it is disabled (Jason, 2026-10-14).

A rule with NO anti-spyware profile in force IS reported here - the absence is this control's own finding, not only PAN-POL-008's (Jason, 2026-10-12). So the two overlap on an allow rule carrying none: PAN-POL-008 says the rule is uninspected, this control says which inspection it is missing.
controls.rationale: Signature-based detection cannot catch a beacon whose signature does not exist yet, and that is precisely the traffic a live intrusion generates. The inline engine is the part of the profile that looks at behaviour instead - and a detector left on alert turns it into a logging feature.
controls.audit: Objects > Security Profiles > Anti-Spyware, the Inline Cloud Analysis tab. Every detector's Action should read a blocking value; `alert` means the detector runs and the traffic passes. A detector absent from the list is not running at all.
controls.remediation: Set every inline cloud-analysis detector to reset-both, or another blocking action. The feature requires an active Advanced Threat Prevention licence - without one the configuration is still writable but nothing enforces it.

controls.name: Brute-Force Signatures Blocked
controls.description:
Brute-force signatures detect authentication guessing - RDP, SSH, SMB and web logins. This reports a vulnerability profile that does not block the SOURCE of those attempts with `block-ip`, across critical, high and medium severity and on both the client and server sides.

REPORTED PER RULE, not per profile (2026-10-12). A profile nothing uses endangers nothing, and a rule is what carries traffic, so the subject is the rule and the finding names the profile in force on it. One profile behind forty rules therefore produces forty findings - which is the point: each is a distinct piece of traffic.

SCOPE. Allow rules that are not the predefined default rules - the same exclusions as PAN-AVW-003 and PAN-POL-008. A rule that denies, drops or resets passes no traffic for a profile to inspect, so a profile on it, or the lack of one, protects nothing either way. Unlike those two controls, a DISABLED allow rule is reported: it is in the configuration and one click from carrying traffic, and its finding says it is disabled (Jason, 2026-10-14).

A rule with NO vulnerability protection profile in force IS reported here - the absence is this control's own finding, not only PAN-POL-008's (Jason, 2026-10-12). So the two overlap on an allow rule carrying none: PAN-POL-008 says the rule is uninspected, this control says which inspection it is missing.
controls.rationale:
Password spraying is one host making thousands of attempts. A reset or drop action ends each attempt and leaves the source free to make the next, so the attack continues at full speed while every attempt is logged. Only `block-ip` takes the source out, and only with a `track-by` - which PAN-OS requires at commit time.

This is a different question from PAN-VLN-001, not a stricter version of it: a profile with `reset-both` on critical, high and medium satisfies that control and reports here. The vendor recommends reset-both for severity rules (Web Interface Help 11.2 p.291), so a profile following that advice exactly is the normal subject of this finding.
controls.audit: Objects > Security Profiles > Vulnerability Protection > <profile> > Rules. Read the Category and Action columns together: a rule covers brute force when its Category is `brute-force` or `any` and it does not narrow to particular signatures by Threat Name, CVE or Vendor ID. Action must be Block IP, which opens Track By and Duration beneath it.
controls.remediation:
Add a rule with Category `brute-force`, Severity any, Host any and Action Block IP, with Track By set to `source` (or `source-and-destination`) and a Duration between 1 and 3600 seconds. Leave the existing severity rules in place - they answer PAN-VLN-001 and this rule answers a different question.

A predefined profile cannot be edited: point the Security policy rules and Security Profile Groups using it at a custom profile instead.

Duration's implicit value has not been measured, so set it explicitly rather than relying on the default.

controls.name: Inline Cloud Analysis for Exploits Enabled
controls.description:
A vulnerability protection profile that does not run real-time exploit analysis, or whose inline cloud-analysis detectors do not stop the traffic they catch.

TWO HALVES AND EITHER ONE FIRES, per standing ruling 6. The profile-wide switch at `cloud-inline-analysis` decides whether the engine runs AT ALL, and each detector's `inline-policy-action` decides what happens to what it catches. Until 2026-10-31 only the second half was built, and a profile with both detectors on reset-both and the profile-wide switch off satisfied this control while running no analysis whatever. The two halves are one control with an OR - one `target_model`, no new control id - and the finding's matched queries say which half fired.

TWO detectors on 11.2 - SQL Injection and Command Injection - detecting exploit patterns in real time, ahead of signature coverage.

THE CORPUS POINTS THIS CONTROL AT A NODE THAT DOES NOT EXIST. controls.json names `cloud-inline-analysis/enabled`; writing it is refused with `cloud-inline-analysis is invalid` (code=12) on 11.2.3-h3 WITH an Advanced Threat Prevention licence active - measured 2026-10-10. The engine lives at `mica-engine-{kind}-enabled`, entry-keyed by detector, each carrying `inline-policy-action`. That is what the corpus DESCRIBES, just not where it points, so this is built against the real node and the deviation is recorded in control-changes.json. Jason approved, 2026-10-10.

`alert` RUNS THE DETECTOR AND LETS THE TRAFFIC THROUGH, which is why this asks whether each detector BLOCKS rather than whether it is on. It is the same distinction `enable(alert-only)` forced on PAN-AVW-002: a detector that only watches is not protection, and treating it as enabled would pass a profile that logs the attack and delivers it.

A DETECTOR THE PROFILE NEVER MENTIONS DOES NOT RUN, and has a row saying so. The detector names come from the content release, so nothing is hardcoded in the query - but unlike the antivirus ML models, the catalogue cannot be read from the predefined profiles: all four of them carry ZERO entries for this engine, measured 2026-10-10. A build-derived catalogue would be empty, no rows would be written, and a profile running no inline analysis at all would read as having nothing wrong. The catalogue therefore falls back to the measured key space.

THE TWO ENGINES ARE NOT ONE SHAPE. The anti-spyware equivalent has five detectors and its action accepts `drop`; this one has two and does not. A shared enum would offer a value the device rejects here, which is why they are measured and held separately.

REPORTED PER RULE, not per profile (2026-10-12). A profile nothing uses endangers nothing, and a rule is what carries traffic, so the subject is the rule and the finding names the profile in force on it. One profile behind forty rules therefore produces forty findings - which is the point: each is a distinct piece of traffic.

SCOPE. Allow rules that are not the predefined default rules - the same exclusions as PAN-AVW-003 and PAN-POL-008. A rule that denies, drops or resets passes no traffic for a profile to inspect, so a profile on it, or the lack of one, protects nothing either way. Unlike those two controls, a DISABLED allow rule is reported: it is in the configuration and one click from carrying traffic, and its finding says it is disabled (Jason, 2026-10-14).

A rule with NO vulnerability protection profile in force IS reported here - the absence is this control's own finding, not only PAN-POL-008's (Jason, 2026-10-12). So the two overlap on an allow rule carrying none: PAN-POL-008 says the rule is uninspected, this control says which inspection it is missing.
controls.rationale: An exploit attempt against an unpatched flaw arrives before the signature for it does. Inline analysis is what sees the pattern rather than the signature - and a detector on alert watches the exploit succeed.
controls.audit: Objects > Security Profiles > Vulnerability Protection, the Inline Cloud Analysis tab. Both detectors should read a blocking action; `alert` runs the detector and lets the traffic through.
controls.remediation: Set both detectors to reset-both or another blocking action. Note this profile's inline action does NOT offer `drop`, unlike the anti-spyware one. Requires an active Advanced Threat Prevention licence.

controls.name: Threat Exceptions Minimal and Documented (Hygiene)
controls.description:
An anti-spyware profile carrying signature exceptions.

Each exception disables a specific protection. They accumulate silently - added during an incident to stop a false positive, and routinely outliving the justification that produced them.

THE TRIGGER IS PRESENCE, not age. The corpus asks that every exception have an owner, a justification and a review date - none of which is in the configuration, and the corpus marks this control `config_settable: false` and `evidence_source: interview-data` for that reason. So this reports that exceptions EXIST and leaves the recertification judgement to an assessor who can ask. The same resolution PAN-POL-014 took when its corpus wording depended on a grace period nothing records.

EXCEPTIONS HIDE IN MORE THAN ONE PLACE and this counts all of them. An anti-spyware profile has FOUR surfaces - `threat-exception`, `botnet-domains/threat-exception`, `botnet-domains/whitelist`, and the `inline-exception-ip-address` / `inline-exception-edl-url` member lists - and controls.json names only the first. Measured 2026-10-10; before that the count read the first alone, so a profile exempting half an estate from inline analysis counted zero exceptions. The finding names the surface, because the remediation differs: a signature exception is removed in one place, an address exemption in another.

SEVERITY IS NOT SCALED BY COUNT. One exception with no justification is the finding; twenty well-documented ones are not worse in a way the configuration can show. An assessor reading the detail can see the number and where they live.

REPORTED PER RULE, not per profile (2026-10-12). A profile nothing uses endangers nothing, and a rule is what carries traffic, so the subject is the rule and the finding names the profile in force on it. One profile behind forty rules therefore produces forty findings - which is the point: each is a distinct piece of traffic.

SCOPE. Allow rules that are not the predefined default rules - the same exclusions as PAN-AVW-003 and PAN-POL-008. A rule that denies, drops or resets passes no traffic for a profile to inspect, so a profile on it, or the lack of one, protects nothing either way. Unlike those two controls, a DISABLED allow rule is reported: it is in the configuration and one click from carrying traffic, and its finding says it is disabled (Jason, 2026-10-14).

A rule with NO anti-spyware profile in force IS reported here - the absence is this control's own finding, not only PAN-POL-008's (Jason, 2026-10-12). So the two overlap on an allow rule carrying none: PAN-POL-008 says the rule is uninspected, this control says which inspection it is missing.
controls.rationale: An exception is a hole with a reason, and the reason expires faster than the hole does. The risk is not that exceptions exist - they are a legitimate tool - but that nobody revisits them, and the configuration cannot tell you which of those two situations an estate is in. Reporting their presence is what puts the question in front of someone who can answer it.
controls.audit: Objects > Security Profiles > Anti-Spyware, the Exceptions tab, and also the DNS Policies tab's exceptions and allow-list, and the Inline Cloud Analysis tab's exempt IP addresses and EDLs. For each, ask who added it, why, and when it was last reviewed. An exception scoped to specific source addresses (exempt-ip) is narrower than one that is not.
controls.remediation: Remove exceptions whose justification has expired. Where one is still needed, scope it as narrowly as the node allows - `exempt-ip` restricts a signature exception to named sources - and record an owner and a review date outside the configuration, since PAN-OS has nowhere to keep them.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: Rules whose anti-spyware profile carries threat exceptions.

controls.name: Vulnerability Exceptions Minimal and Documented (Hygiene)
controls.description:
A vulnerability protection profile carrying signature exceptions.

Each one disables exploit blocking for a specific threat ID. Unreviewed exceptions from a past false-positive incident leave a permanent hole against those CVEs.

THE TRIGGER IS PRESENCE, not age. The corpus asks that every exception have an owner, a justification and a review date - none of which is in the configuration, and the corpus marks this control `config_settable: false` and `evidence_source: interview-data` for that reason. So this reports that exceptions EXIST and leaves the recertification judgement to an assessor who can ask. The same resolution PAN-POL-014 took when its corpus wording depended on a grace period nothing records.

EXCEPTIONS HIDE IN MORE THAN ONE PLACE and this counts all of them. An anti-spyware profile has FOUR surfaces - `threat-exception`, `botnet-domains/threat-exception`, `botnet-domains/whitelist`, and the `inline-exception-ip-address` / `inline-exception-edl-url` member lists - and controls.json names only the first. Measured 2026-10-10; before that the count read the first alone, so a profile exempting half an estate from inline analysis counted zero exceptions. The finding names the surface, because the remediation differs: a signature exception is removed in one place, an address exemption in another.

SEVERITY IS NOT SCALED BY COUNT, IT IS SCALED BY WIDTH. One exception with no justification is the finding; twenty well-documented ones are not worse in a way the configuration can show. What does change the severity is how far the widest exemption reaches, which is a property of the surface it sits on: a per-signature exception narrowed to named addresses reports LOW, one with no address scope reports MEDIUM, and an entry on either inline-analysis exclusion list reports HIGH - one such entry takes a reference to an address group or an external dynamic list and so lifts every real-time detector for a population the configuration does not size. An assessor reading the detail can see the number and where they live.

FEWER SURFACES THAN THE ANTI-SPYWARE EQUIVALENT. This kind has no botnet tree, so two of the four cannot exist here - `threat-exception` and the two inline-exception lists are all there is. Its exception entry also carries a key the anti-spyware one lacks, `time-attribute`, so PAN-SPY-005's note that it 'applies equally' to this control is true of the intent and not of the node.

REPORTED PER RULE, not per profile (2026-10-12). A profile nothing uses endangers nothing, and a rule is what carries traffic, so the subject is the rule and the finding names the profile in force on it. One profile behind forty rules therefore produces forty findings - which is the point: each is a distinct piece of traffic.

SCOPE. Allow rules that are not the predefined default rules - the same exclusions as PAN-AVW-003 and PAN-POL-008. A rule that denies, drops or resets passes no traffic for a profile to inspect, so a profile on it, or the lack of one, protects nothing either way. Unlike those two controls, a DISABLED allow rule is reported: it is in the configuration and one click from carrying traffic, and its finding says it is disabled (Jason, 2026-10-14).

A rule with NO vulnerability protection profile in force IS reported here - the absence is this control's own finding, not only PAN-POL-008's (Jason, 2026-10-12). So the two overlap on an allow rule carrying none: PAN-POL-008 says the rule is uninspected, this control says which inspection it is missing.

WHETHER THAT IS RIGHT FOR THIS ONE CONTROL IS AN OPEN QUESTION, RAISED 2026-10-31 AND NOT SETTLED HERE. Stage 3 of the pipeline scopes this control to rules where a profile IS in force, on the ground that a review of exemptions has no subject on a rule that reaches no profile - the review has no subject rather than an unsatisfactory one - and that reporting ‘this profile carries exemptions’ about a profile that does not exist is a false finding. Stage 5 restated that as an applicability clause `vulnerability_profile_resolved equals true` AND recorded in the same breath that it contradicts the 2026-10-12 ruling, that the ruling is Jason's rather than a reading, and that a person should settle it before the narrowing is implemented. It is therefore NOT implemented: this entry still reports a rule that reaches no profile.

WHAT THE DECISION COSTS EITHER WAY, measured 2026-10-31 so it can be taken cheaply. Wide (what ships): on a 31-rule reconstruction of the lab's own profile shapes this control reports 7 rules - 3 of them rules that reach no resolvable profile, which already carry three other PAN-VLN findings plus PAN-POL-008's. Narrow: it reports 4, and on the real lab - where not one rule or profile group binds a vulnerability profile at all - it would report NOTHING, while the other three controls report every rule. Taking the narrow reading is one edit with no code change: add `vulnerability_profile_resolved equals true` to the three exemption queries, which is already a registered search field. The coverage companion query must NOT take that clause either way, because a rule nobody assessed must not be excluded by the test for whether it was assessed.
controls.rationale: A vulnerability exception is a decision to stop blocking a known exploit. That is sometimes right and always worth revisiting, and nothing in the configuration records whether anyone has.
controls.audit: Objects > Security Profiles > Vulnerability Protection, the Exceptions tab, and the Inline Cloud Analysis tab's exempt IP addresses and EDLs. For each, ask who added it, why, and when it was last reviewed.
controls.remediation: Remove exceptions whose justification has expired; scope the rest with `exempt-ip` where the signature allows it, and keep the owner and review date outside the configuration.

controls.name: IKEv2 Required on IKE Gateways
controls.description:
Requires every IKE gateway to be configured for IKE version 2 only. IKEv2 binds the identity to the key exchange, offers a DoS-resistant cookie exchange and protects the identities; IKEv1 does neither, and its aggressive mode transmits an identity hash that can be cracked offline against a pre-shared key.

WRITTEN AS A NEGATED EQUALITY, NOT AS A LIST OF BAD VALUES, and that is load-bearing. The protocol/version key CAN BE ABSENT on a committed gateway - proved by deleting it and committing, job 6876 OK - and the normalized column holds the empty string in that state. A positive test (`version is ikev1 or ikev2-preferred`) would pass a gateway whose version nobody read; the negation reports it. What the device does with the key absent is UNMEASURED and the two available readings disagree: the schema default reads `ikev2` on one lab release, while an ikemgr phase-1 commit abort on a keyless gateway names the IKEv1 section. So a gateway with no version key is reported at this control's own severity, and the finding says the version is not established rather than naming one.

THE CONFIGURED VERSION IS NOT THE NEGOTIATED VERSION. On `ikev2-preferred` the gateway negotiates version 2 with any peer that supports it and completes a version 1 exchange with one that declines, so that state carries a lower band rather than none. The operational read that would say which a tunnel is actually running - `show vpn ike-sa` - is not available to this assessment, so nothing here claims it.

A DISABLED GATEWAY IS OUT OF SCOPE AND NOT COMPLIANT. Every query carries `gateway_is_active`, because a finding on a gateway the device has switched off is a finding about a negotiation that cannot happen. The clause is on the derived column and never on the device's own `disabled` key, which is nullable: an applicability clause over a null drops the row and would suppress the control on every gateway nobody read.
controls.rationale: IKEv1 lacks the cryptographic binding between identity and key exchange that IKEv2 provides, has no cookie mechanism against half-open-exchange flooding, and in aggressive mode leaks an offline-crackable identity hash.
controls.audit: Network > Network Profiles > IKE Gateways > (gateway) > General: IKE Version. A gateway with no version selection stored is the state this control reports as unestablished.
controls.remediation: Set each gateway's IKE version to IKEv2 only. Where a named legacy peer genuinely cannot do IKEv2, record the exception against that gateway and leave it at IKEv2-preferred knowingly; the control will continue to report it at the lower band.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: The gateway is not configured for IKE version 2 only, or its version was not read.

queries.name: IKEv2 preferred with IKEv1 fallback
queries.short_description: The gateway prefers IKEv2 and still completes an IKEv1 exchange with a peer that declines.

controls.name: IKE Diffie-Hellman Group Strength
controls.description:
Requires every key-agreement group an IKE crypto profile OFFERS to be a 2048-bit finite field or an elliptic curve. The profile offers the whole list and takes the first group a peer accepts, so the weakest member on the list is the group an exchange can be driven down to - a weak group left in place is a live option, not a lower preference.

THE ASSERTION IS OVER THE WHOLE SET, which is why it rests on a derived verdict column rather than on a list test: a clause has one field slot and this is a universal quantifier. The verdict's finding side is also its stored default, so a profile nobody has recomputed is reported rather than passing.

THE VALUE SET IS MUCH LARGER THAN THE CONTROL'S OWN LIST AND IT GREW BETWEEN RELEASES. Nine members on one lab build, twenty-eight on another: the eighteen additions are post-quantum key-encapsulation names, which no severity band here ranks. A profile whose weakest member is one of those is reported at this control's own severity and the finding says the group is unranked, because reporting it at a graded severity would attribute a judgement nobody made.

AND `none` IS NOT A WEAK GROUP. It is a member - present on the newer lab builds and absent from the older - that can take the key agreement OUT of the proposal entirely; the device's own help string for it is "Make this round optional". It ranks with the broken groups rather than below them.
controls.rationale: Finite-field groups at 768, 1024 and 1536 bits fall to precomputation attacks of the Logjam family; 2048 bits is the current floor and the elliptic-curve groups give equivalent strength at far lower cost. A member that removes the key agreement altogether removes the forward secrecy the exchange exists to provide.
controls.audit: Network > Network Profiles > IKE Crypto > (profile): DH Group. Read the whole list, not the first entry - the list is an offer set tried in order until one succeeds.
controls.remediation: Remove every finite-field group below 2048 bits and the `none` member from each profile's DH Group list, leaving group19, group20 or group21 where the peers support them and group14 or above otherwise.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: The profile offers a key-agreement group below the 2048-bit floor, a non-elliptic-curve member, or a group no ordering places.

queries.name: Weakest group is the 1536-bit finite field
queries.short_description: Group 5 is the weakest member still offered.

controls.name: IKE Encryption Algorithm Strength
controls.description:
Requires every cipher an IKE crypto profile OFFERS to be AES. As with the key-agreement list, the profile offers the whole set and a peer takes the first member that succeeds, so one weak cipher left in place is negotiable.

THE VENDOR'S ONLY ADVICE HERE IS ABOUT ORDER, AND FOLLOWING IT TO THE LETTER LEAVES THE WEAK CIPHER NEGOTIABLE. One page says to change the order of the list top to bottom; another says the list is tried top to bottom until an attempt succeeds. A profile ordered exactly as recommended still offers 3DES to a peer that offers nothing else, which is why this control is a floor over the whole set rather than a check on the first member.

`des` IS NOT A MEMBER AT THIS POSITION ON ANY MEASURED APPLIANCE, though the control it came from ranks it bottom. The real floor of this field is 3DES; `des` lives on a manual-key tunnel's ESP leaf, which runs no key exchange at all. Nothing is lost by the control not reaching it, and a reader expecting `des` in a finding here will not see it.
controls.rationale: 3DES has a 64-bit block and is attackable by collision at feasible data volumes; AES at 128 bits or more is the floor for key-management traffic, and AES-256 is the target.
controls.audit: Network > Network Profiles > IKE Crypto > (profile): Encryption. Read the whole list.
controls.remediation: Remove 3DES from each profile's encryption list and leave aes-256-cbc, or aes-256-gcm where every peer on that profile supports authenticated encryption and negotiates IKEv2.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: The profile offers 3DES, or its cipher list was not read.

controls.name: IKE Integrity (Hash) Algorithm Strength
controls.description:
Requires every integrity algorithm an IKE crypto profile OFFERS to be from the SHA-2 family, with one exception the vendor itself mandates.

THE EXCEPTION IS WHY THIS CANNOT BE A TEST ON ONE LIST. Where a profile offers an AES-GCM cipher, the vendor's own instruction is to select the no-integrity member alongside it, because the integrity comes from the cipher's own construction. A one-list test would therefore fire on exactly the configuration a customer was told to make, and would spend their remediation budget on it. So the assertion is a predicate over TWO member lists and rests on a derived verdict column.

THE SAME LITERAL MEANS OPPOSITE THINGS ON TWO PROFILES. On a profile offering no authenticated-encryption cipher, the no-integrity member is not a weak hash - it is no integrity algorithm at all, and an exchange can be driven down to it. THE DEVICE DOES NOT ENFORCE THE PAIRING IN THAT DIRECTION: a profile offering {sha256, non-auth} with a CBC cipher and no AEAD cipher anywhere was accepted at the write and committed without complaint, so nothing on the firewall reports it and the constraint is entirely this assessment's to compute.

AND THE MIXED CASE: a profile offering both an AEAD cipher and a non-AEAD one needs the no-integrity member for the first AND a SHA-2 member for the second. An AEAD-justified no-integrity member on its own is not enough there.
controls.rationale: MD5 is collision-broken and unfit for key-management traffic; SHA-1 is deprecated with practical collisions demonstrated. A profile with no integrity algorithm and no authenticated-encryption cipher protects the exchange's integrity with nothing.
controls.audit: Network > Network Profiles > IKE Crypto > (profile): Authentication. Read it together with the Encryption list - the no-integrity member is correct beside an AES-GCM cipher and is a defect without one.
controls.remediation: Leave sha384 or sha512 in each profile's authentication list, removing md5 and sha1. Keep the no-integrity member only on a profile whose encryption list is AES-GCM only; where the profile also offers a CBC cipher, a SHA-2 member must stay beside it.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: The profile offers an integrity algorithm outside SHA-2, or the no-integrity member with no authenticated-encryption cipher to justify it.

queries.name: Weakest integrity algorithm is SHA-1
queries.short_description: SHA-1 is the weakest integrity algorithm still offered.

controls.name: IKE SA Lifetime and Re-authentication Interval Bounded
controls.description:
Bounds two quantities on one profile: how long a single IKE SA key stays in service, and the IKEv2 re-authentication interval that key lifetime feeds.

THE LIFETIME IS A CHOICE NODE WHOSE FOUR CHILDREN ARE THE UNITS, and the element that EXISTS is what says the unit. A comparison on the hours leaf alone misses a lifetime written in days, minutes or seconds entirely - and a comparison on the raw number without the unit reads a 1800-second lifetime as the worst in the estate. The normalized column coalesces all four branches into hours and rounds UP, so a sub-hour lifetime stores one hour and never zero. WRITING ONE BRANCH SILENTLY DESTROYS ANOTHER, measured: with an hours value stored, a write of seconds at the same container was accepted, the read-back carried only seconds, and the commit returned OK. Nothing reports the discard.

A PROFILE WHOSE LIFETIME NOBODY COULD READ IS REPORTED, NOT PASSED. The lifetime container is this object's only optional choice container and a committed profile can carry none. A threshold over a null integer matches nothing, so such a profile would pass a bound it was never compared against; a separate query reports exactly those rows, and the finding says the lifetime was not established rather than that it is too long.

ZERO IS NOT A SMALL RE-AUTHENTICATION INTERVAL. The authentication multiple is a multiplier on the key lifetime, and the device's own words are that 0 means re-authentication disabled - the UNBOUNDED end of the axis while sorting as the smallest number, so every numeric comparison reads it as the strictest setting available. The device's stated range for the key EXCLUDES zero (writing 51 is refused with a 1-to-50 message) and zero is accepted and stored anyway. The verdict column special-cases it before comparing.
controls.rationale: An excessive IKE SA lifetime extends the value of any single compromised key, and an unbounded re-authentication interval lets a tunnel stay up indefinitely on an identity that has not been re-proved.
controls.audit: Network > Network Profiles > IKE Crypto > (profile): Key Lifetime, and IKEv2 Authentication Multiple. Read which unit the lifetime is written in, not only the number.
controls.remediation: Set each profile's key lifetime to 8 hours or less. Set the IKEv2 authentication multiple so that multiple times lifetime stays within 24 hours, and do not leave it at 0, which disables re-authentication rather than tightening it.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: The profile's key lifetime is more than 24 hours.

queries.name: Key lifetime between one day and one week
queries.short_description: More than 24 hours and up to 168 hours on one key.

queries.name: Key lifetime not established
queries.short_description: No key lifetime was read on this profile, so no bound was applied to it.

queries.name: IKEv2 re-authentication interval not bounded
queries.short_description: On a profile a version-2 gateway uses, the re-authentication interval exceeds 24 hours, is switched off by a zero multiplier, or could not be computed.

controls.name: Certificate Authentication Preferred over Pre-Shared Keys
controls.description:
Requires each IKE gateway to authenticate its peer with a certificate AND to name a certificate profile that constrains how that certificate is validated.

THERE IS NO METHOD FIELD AND NO ENUMERATION ON THE DEVICE. The choice is expressed by WHICH OF TWO SUBTREES EXISTS beneath the gateway's authentication node, and the profile pointer is a separate leaf from the branch - which is what makes a certificate gateway with no validation profile distinguishable from one with it. The normalized column resolves three states over those two presence tests.

THE TWO BRANCHES ARE EXCLUSIVE AND THE EXCLUSION IS ENFORCED BY SILENT REPLACEMENT AT THE WRITE. Staging a certificate profile over a committed pre-shared key DELETES the shared-secret branch from the candidate configuration without comment, while the running configuration still shows the key. So for the duration of a staging the two views disagree about how the gateway authenticates. This assessment reads the candidate, so a finding here reports the STAGED answer and says so.

A CERTIFICATE GATEWAY WITH NO VALIDATION PROFILE RANKS WITH THE SHARED-SECRET STATE RATHER THAN BELOW IT: the shared secret is gone and nothing is configured to constrain validation of the credential that replaced it, so the gateway has given up the secret without gaining the ability to stop trusting a credential. Whether the named profile actually CHECKS revocation is a separate control's claim, not this one's.

WHAT THIS CONTROL CANNOT SAY: anything about a pre-shared key's strength, length or reuse. A 31-character plaintext reads back as a 77-character ciphertext, so a length comparison on the stored value measures the encoding and would pass a four-character key. The presence of a shared secret is all the configuration holds.
controls.rationale: Certificate authentication removes the shared-secret distribution problem and makes revocation possible. A gateway on a shared secret has a credential that cannot be revoked and whose strength nothing on the device records.
controls.audit: Network > Network Profiles > IKE Gateways > (gateway) > Authentication: the Certificate / Pre-Shared Key choice, and the Certificate Profile beside it.
controls.remediation: Move each gateway to certificate authentication and name a certificate profile on it. Where a shared secret must remain for a named peer, record the exception and vault the secret - its strength is not assessable from the configuration.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: The gateway is not on certificate authentication with a validation profile named, or its authentication was not read.

controls.name: No IKEv1 Aggressive Mode
controls.description:
Requires any gateway that can still complete an IKE version 1 exchange to negotiate in main mode.

THE SHIPPED DEFAULT IS NEITHER OF THE TWO VALUES THE CONTROL NAMES, AND IT BEHAVES LIKE THE FORBIDDEN ONE. The exchange-mode key has three members - auto, main and aggressive - and `auto` is the schema default on every measured appliance. The vendor's own description of it: "In auto mode (default), the device can accept both main mode and aggressive mode negotiation requests." A gateway left at `auto` therefore completes the exposing exchange whenever the peer initiates it, so `auto` ranks with `aggressive` and not between it and `main`. A control written as a two-state main-versus-aggressive comparison passes every default gateway in an estate.

THE KEY LIVES UNDER THE VERSION 1 BRANCH, so the population is the gateways configured for version 1 or for version-2-preferred, written as a negated equality against version 2 - which also leaves a gateway whose version nobody read IN scope rather than silently excusing it. An absent exchange-mode key on such a gateway is reported, because both of the vendor's own statements read the absence as `auto`.
controls.rationale: IKEv1 aggressive mode transmits an identity hash in the clear, which can be cracked offline against the pre-shared key. Main mode protects the identities.
controls.audit: Network > Network Profiles > IKE Gateways > (gateway) > Advanced Options > IKEv1: Exchange Mode. A gateway with no selection stored is at `auto`, which accepts aggressive mode.
controls.remediation: Set Exchange Mode to Main on every gateway that can still complete an IKEv1 exchange. `Auto` is not an acceptable intermediate setting. Moving the gateway to IKEv2 only removes the node altogether.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: A gateway that can complete an IKEv1 exchange is not in main mode - aggressive, auto, or no mode stored.

controls.name: Dead Peer Detection and IKEv2 Liveness Probing Enabled
controls.description:
Requires the dead-peer-detection switch on a gateway's version 1 branch and the idle liveness probe on its version 2 branch.

THESE ARE TWO NODES AND NOT EQUIVALENTS, and a control written once against either answers for half an estate. The two branches differ STRUCTURALLY: the version 1 subtree has three children - enable, interval and retry - and the version 2 subtree has two, measured on every appliance, so a reading written once for both loses the retry count. A GATEWAY SET TO VERSION-2-PREFERRED IS IN BOTH POPULATIONS AND CAN HOLD BOTH SUBTREES.

THE CLAIM A FINDING MAY MAKE ON THE VERSION 2 BRANCH IS NARROWER, and the vendor says so in the same paragraph as the field: "The IKEv2 Liveness Check is always on; all IKEv2 packets serve the purpose of a liveness check." So a finding saying an IKEv2 gateway cannot detect a dead peer would be false. What is true is that it sends no probe while the tunnel is IDLE.

A SWITCH NOBODY COULD READ IS REPORTED AND NOT PASSED. Both switches are nullable, and `equals false` over a null matches nothing - so a gateway whose switch was never read would pass a test it was never subjected to. A separate query per branch reports exactly those rows, and the finding says the switch was not established.

THE INTERVAL AND THE ENABLE ARE TWO KEYS. A gateway can carry an interval with no enable, in which case the interval describes a probe that may not be being sent; a finding quoting the interval without the switch would describe a configuration that does nothing.
controls.rationale: Without dead-peer detection a stale security association is not torn down, so traffic to a peer that has gone away is black-holed and failover is delayed until the SA expires on its own.
controls.audit: Network > Network Profiles > IKE Gateways > (gateway) > Advanced Options: IKEv1 Dead Peer Detection, and IKEv2 Liveness Check beside it. Read the enable, not only the interval.
controls.remediation: Enable dead-peer detection on the IKEv1 branch of every gateway that has one, and set an IKEv2 liveness-check interval on every gateway with a version 2 branch. Tune the interval and retry count to the failover objective the tunnel is expected to meet.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: A gateway that can complete an IKEv1 exchange has dead-peer detection switched off.

queries.name: IKEv2 idle liveness probe switched off
queries.short_description: A gateway with a version 2 branch sends no liveness probe while the tunnel is idle.

queries.name: IKEv1 dead-peer-detection switch not established
queries.short_description: The version 1 dead-peer-detection switch could not be read on this gateway.

queries.name: IKEv2 liveness-check switch not established
queries.short_description: The version 2 liveness-check switch could not be read on this gateway.

controls.name: No Gateway Relies on a Factory-Shipped IKE Crypto Profile
controls.description:
Requires every gateway to name a crypto profile that was defined for this estate, rather than relying on one that arrived with the firewall.

BOTH POINTERS, NOT ONE. A gateway has a crypto-profile pointer under EACH protocol version's branch and the vendor states they can name different profiles. A control reading one pointer answers for half the references in an estate and reports the other half as absent.

ALL THREE FACTORY NAMES, NOT ONLY `default`. A firewall ships three such entries, and they are ORDINARY WRITABLE, DELETABLE CONFIGURATION at the same path as a custom entry - no template marker, no predefined counterpart, nothing that distinguishes them but the name. That is what makes removal possible at all, and it is also why the assertion is about PROVENANCE AND OWNERSHIP rather than about algorithms: a proposal nobody chose is a proposal nobody owns. One lab appliance's `default` profile does offer 3DES, SHA-1 and Group 2 - measured - but an estate may equally have hardened it in place, and the strength controls assert over every profile regardless of its name.

AND A GATEWAY WITH NEITHER POINTER SET IS REPORTED TOO. Such a gateway still CONSUMES a proposal set - an ikemgr phase-1 commit abort proves the version 1 section demands algorithms with no pointer present - and nothing stored says which one. A gateway whose proposal nothing records is a gateway secured by something nobody has identified, so it is reported rather than passed. The finding distinguishes the two cases, because their remediations differ.
controls.rationale: A proposal set nobody selected for this estate is a proposal set nobody owns or reviews, and its contents can change under a release upgrade with no local change to show for it.
controls.audit: Network > Network Profiles > IKE Gateways > (gateway) > Advanced Options: the IKE Crypto Profile under IKEv1 and the one under IKEv2. Check both, and check for a gateway with neither set.
controls.remediation: Point each gateway at a named, reviewed crypto profile under every protocol-version branch it uses, and then delete the factory-shipped entries no gateway names.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: The gateway names a factory-shipped crypto profile from either pointer, or names none at all.

controls.name: No Expired Certificates In Use (Hygiene)
controls.description:
A certificate whose validity period has already ended, where nothing establishes that nothing on the device depends on it. An expired certificate a live service presents causes silent authentication failures and trains administrators and users to click through warnings, which is the reflex every certificate warning afterwards depends on.

THE EXPIRY IS DECODED FROM THE CERTIFICATE AND NOT READ FROM A FIELD, which matters because the device offers three renderings of one expiry and they are not established to agree: the operational read returned the SAME WRONG DATE for three different certificates on one appliance. The decoded certificate is the authority on itself, and `not_valid_after` is reported beside the verdict as the evidence a reader checks.

THE VERDICT IS A SNAPSHOT AGAINST A CLOCK. It was computed when the configuration was normalised and it goes stale between passes - a certificate that expires tomorrow reads as current today and as expired after the next collection. That is a real property of any stored verdict about time rather than a defect, and it is the reason the date is kept beside it.

WHAT THE FINDING DOES AND DOES NOT CLAIM. It says the certificate has expired and that nothing establishes that nothing depends on it. It does NOT say the certificate is in use. The reference map behind that distinction is a FLOOR and not a census: of 69 known locations on this platform where a certificate can be referenced, 65 are covered by no collected model at all, so the walk can prove a certificate IS referenced and can never prove that it is not. A certificate whose reference map was never walked therefore REPORTS here rather than passing, which is the direction that errs toward telling a customer to look.

ONE HALF OF THIS CONTROL IS NOT REPORTED. The corpus also asks that the firewall raise its own warning as its certificates approach expiry, which is a single device-wide setting rather than a property of a certificate. A control reports against one subject, and this control's subject is the certificate; the device-wide setting is collected and is asserted by no control in this catalogue.
controls.rationale: An expired certificate does not fail safely. The service keeps running, the warning lands on whoever is using it, and the habit of dismissing it is what a man-in-the-middle later depends on. Remediation is also not instant - a certificate has to be reissued, redistributed and rebound - so the warning is worth having before the expiry rather than after.
controls.audit: Device > Certificate Management > Certificates: read the Expires column on every scope, including the predefined entries. Then check the Certificate Profile and SSL/TLS Service Profile grids, GlobalProtect portal and gateway, decryption settings and the syslog server profiles for a reference to each expired entry - and read its Issuer against the other certificates' Subjects, because an authority that nothing NAMES is still in use if it signed something the device holds.
controls.remediation: Reissue the certificate, import the replacement, and repoint every profile and service that names the old one before deleting it. A PREDEFINED entry reported here cannot be remediated on the device at all - it is the vendor's and is read-only - and the action is to stop referencing it. Where the certificate is an authority, reissue the authority and re-sign what it issued rather than deleting it: a delete refused for references answers with the referrer's name, which is itself the cheapest reference test.

queries.name: Expired, and nothing establishes that nothing depends on it
queries.short_description: Default baseline query: the decoded validity end is in the past, and the reference walk has not shown the certificate to be unused.

controls.name: Unused Certificates and Profiles Removed (Hygiene)
controls.description:
A certificate AUTHORITY certificate the device still holds where the reference walk ran and found nothing relying on it. An authority is not an ordinary unused object: while it sits in the store it extends trust to everything it ever signed, and a key nobody is watching is a key nobody notices the loss of.

RELIANCE IS NOT A NAME COUNT. Within one configuration surface a certificate's issuer hash equals its issuer's subject hash, which is how a chain is read without parsing anything - so an authority that NO object names is still in use when it signed a certificate the device holds. Both edges count here, and a control written on name references alone would propose deleting authorities that are still issuing. The chain is also SURFACE-LOCAL: it cannot be followed from the firewall's own store into the vendor's predefined namespace, and the subject and issuer STRINGS cannot be compared instead, because the device formats one name five different ways depending on where it is read.

THIS CONTROL IS DELIBERATELY SILENT WHERE THE REFERENCE WALK HAS NOT RUN, and that is the opposite of how the rest of this catalogue treats a missing reading. The reason is the remediation: the finding says to review an authority for removal, the action is a DELETE, and an authority whose private key is held nowhere else cannot be recreated. The map behind the walk is a FLOOR and not a census - of 69 known reference locations on this platform, 65 are covered by no collected model - so firing on an incomplete walk would advise deleting the most sensitive key in an estate on the strength of not having looked. The opposite direction is covered rather than ignored: PAN-CRT-001 reads the same column in the other sense, so an EXPIRED certificate whose reliance is unknown does fire, and no customer is told an expired certificate is safe.

A CERTIFICATE'S OWN FORWARD-TRUST FLAG IS ITSELF A FORM OF RELIANCE, so an authority carrying it is not orphaned however few objects name it.

ONE HALF OF THIS CONTROL IS NOT REPORTED, and it is not reportable. The corpus also asks that every certificate, validation profile and service profile be accounted for against something that uses it, with the unused ones reviewed. The assertion there is that somebody has LOOKED, and an item kept for a stated reason meets it - configuration cannot show intent, so that half is an engineer's question rather than a query, and it reaches three subjects where a control reports against one.
controls.rationale: Every certificate an authority signed remains verifiable while the authority is trusted, so an authority kept past its purpose is a standing grant of trust with no owner. Unlike an unused policy object, the cost of leaving it is not clutter.
controls.audit: Device > Certificate Management > Certificates: for each entry whose CA flag is set, look for its name in the Certificate Profile CA lists and in the SSL/TLS Service Profile, GlobalProtect portal and gateway, decryption and syslog configurations - then read every other certificate's Issuer against this one's Subject, because a signed certificate is reliance even where no object names the issuer. An entry reported here is a candidate for review, not a confirmed orphan.
controls.remediation: Establish what the authority was for before removing it. Where it is genuinely finished, delete it and record that the key is gone - the delete is irreversible and the key is not recoverable from a configuration backup. Attempting the delete is itself a reference test: a refusal answers with the name of the object that still points at it. Where the authority is still issuing, leave it and record the decision, because the next assessment will raise it again.

queries.name: An authority certificate the reference walk found nothing relying on
queries.short_description: Default baseline query: the entry is a CA, and the walk completed and found no name reference and no signed certificate.

controls.name: High Availability Deployed for Critical Paths
controls.description:
Requires every firewall whose failure would interrupt traffic the business cannot lose to have a LIVE redundant peer - one of a pair, or a member of a session-synchronising cluster - and requires that relationship to be formed and exchanging state rather than merely switched on.

THE SWITCH IS NOT THE ASSERTION, and that is the whole point of this control. An `enabled: yes` with no peer answering is worse than no redundancy at all, because the outage arrives at the moment the organisation believes it has already been engineered away. Measured on the lab pair this was built against: both members hold `configuration-synchronization/enabled: yes` while the device reports `state-sync: User-disabled` and `conn-ha2: down`, so no session state is being exchanged and a configuration review passes it.

SO THE VERDICT SPANS CONFIGURATION AND AN OPERATIONAL READ, which no clause can join: it is computed at normalization from the configuration switches plus `show high-availability all`, and the firing side is also the stored default. An appliance whose runtime state nobody collected is therefore REPORTED rather than passed, and the finding says the relationship was not established rather than that it failed. No collector issues that read today, so this control currently fires on every HA-enabled appliance and the finding names the read that would settle it.

WHICH FIREWALLS OUGHT TO BE REDUNDANT IS NOT READ FROM A FIREWALL. Nothing in a firewall's own configuration distinguishes a branch office from a data-centre perimeter, so every firewall without a live peer is reported for a person to decide rather than suppressed - and 'nobody told us which firewalls mattered' must not come back as a firewall that did not need redundancy. ABSENCE IS THE FINDING HERE AND NOT THE PASS: an appliance with no high-availability node at all has no peer, and the device's own operational reply answers `enabled: no` for that state.
controls.rationale: A firewall carrying critical traffic alone turns any single hardware or software fault into an outage of everything behind it. One configured for redundancy that never completed the relationship with its peer is worse: the configuration says the risk was engineered away and the failover does not happen.
controls.audit: Device > High Availability > General: Enable HA, and the Group's mode and peer. Then `show high-availability all` or `show high-availability state` on each member - the configuration cannot tell you whether the peer is answering, whether `running-sync` reads `synchronized`, or whether session state is being exchanged. Read both members: the two nodes genuinely differ and neither one is the pair.
controls.remediation: Pair every firewall the customer names as critical with a peer, and then verify on the device that the relationship is formed: `group/local-info/state` active or passive, `group/peer-info/conn-status` up, `running-sync` synchronized, and state synchronisation enabled rather than User-disabled. Where a firewall is deliberately standalone, record that decision - the configuration cannot carry it.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: The appliance has no formed, state-exchanging redundant peer by either mechanism - which includes an appliance whose runtime state nobody read.

controls.name: HA1 Control Link Encryption Enabled
