controls.description:
Requires the link carrying configuration and session-ownership state between two high-availability peers to be encrypted, so that nothing able to reach the path between them can read what the peers synchronise or forge what they tell each other.

THE SWITCH ALONE CANNOT SATISFY THIS AND THE DEVICE AGREES. HA1 encryption needs an imported high-availability key, and without one the firewall refuses to commit the switch at all - `validate full` answers "High-availability ha1 encryption requires an import of the high-availability-key", measured directly. So the verdict is computed from the configuration switch, the operational confirmation that encryption is in force, and the key's presence; an appliance missing the confirming read is reported rather than passed, because the switch can read `yes` on a link that is not encrypted.

THE SEVERITY VARIES WITH HOW FAR THE LINK TRAVELS, not with which key is absent. A control link on the management port shares the out-of-band management network, so every host that can route to management can reach the peer conversation; one on an in-band data interface travels wherever that segment travels, which on a virtual firewall is the ORDINARY case because the platform takes a free interface name here rather than a dedicated port. Both are high. A dedicated high-availability or auxiliary port sits at this control's own severity and is still a finding: the port value does not say the cable is direct, and the vendor's cross-site case runs over those ports too.

WHAT NO FINDING HERE CAN SAY: encryption is a property of the PAIR. The operational reply carries no identifier that would let the two members' rows be joined, so a pair with the key imported on one member only reports as two independent findings rather than as one broken link.

A STANDALONE FIREWALL IS EXCLUDED AND NOT PASSED. The control applies only where high availability is switched on, because there is no peer control link until the firewall is in a pair - so the absence of a finding on a standalone firewall says nothing about it. An appliance nobody collected is reported by this control's own coverage query instead, because the applicability clause cannot match an uncollected row.
controls.rationale: Anything on that path reads the whole ruleset as it is synchronised and can forge the state deciding which peer owns a session, so one foothold beside the link yields both firewalls and a failover nobody ordered - and the pair bought for resilience becomes the single thing an attacker has to stand next to.
controls.audit: Device > High Availability > General > Control Link (HA1): Encryption Enabled, and the Port the link is assigned to. Then `show high-availability all` for `group/local-info/ha1-encrypt-enable` and `ha1-encrypt-imported` - the switch is not the state, and the port key is frequently ABSENT from the configuration while the operational reply names one.
controls.remediation: Export the high-availability key from one peer and import it on the other, then enable encryption on the HA1 control link on both members and confirm `ha1-encrypt-enable: yes` on each. Where the peers are not directly cabled, do this before anything else: the vendor's own recommendation for encryption is conditioned on exactly that case.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: High availability is on and the HA1 control link is not encrypted - the switch is off or absent, the runtime confirmation is missing, or no HA key is imported.

queries.name: Unencrypted control link on the management port
queries.short_description: The peer conversation shares the out-of-band management network, so every host that can route to management can reach it.

queries.name: Unencrypted control link on an in-band data interface
queries.short_description: The peer conversation rides the dataplane and travels as far as that interface's segment.

queries.name: High-availability configuration not collected
queries.short_description: The high-availability subtree was not collected for this appliance, so the setting was not established.

controls.name: HA1 Backup and Heartbeat Backup Configured
controls.description:
Requires the peers to have a second way of telling each other they are alive that shares neither the first way's physical port nor its subnet - a backup control link, or keepalives over the management path where the primary link is not already on it - and requires that second way to be complete enough to carry traffic rather than half-configured.

THE NAIVE READING PASSES THE COMMONEST BROKEN STATE. `interface/ha1-backup` exists as a PRESENT AND EMPTY committed container on both members of the lab pair this was built against - no port, no address, no netmask - so a check for the container returns a node and reports a second path that has no far end. What settles it is a backup link with a port AND a backup address for the peer, on a different port and a different subnet from the primary; that is the vendor's own independence test, and it is a comparison between two fields rather than a value, so it is computed at normalization and not in a clause.

THE HEARTBEAT BRANCH REVERSES MEANING when the primary control link already rides the management port: a 'backup path over management' is then the same path, and a pair with it switched on has one keepalive route and not two. The verdict folds that in.

ONE COMPLETE MECHANISM MEETS THE MINIMUM AND NOT THE PREFERRED, which this control does NOT report. The catalogue prices that gap at low and this control's assertion is the single-path case, so an appliance with one complete mechanism satisfies the assertion and produces nothing - the gap between minimum and preferred is not reported here, and the absence of a finding does not mean both mechanisms are present.

A STANDALONE FIREWALL IS EXCLUDED AND NOT PASSED, for the same reason as the encryption control: there is no peer to send keepalives to. The vendor's rule that the control, data and packet-forwarding links are unsupported between cluster members that are not pairs is carried by the same exclusion, which holds on this estate's leaf semantics rather than as a general truth.
controls.rationale: With one keepalive path, losing that single link while both peers are alive leaves each believing the other is dead, and two firewalls both claiming the active role fight over the same addresses and sessions until a person intervenes - an outage produced by the redundancy mechanism itself, on an estate whose availability review it passed.
controls.audit: Device > High Availability > General > Control Link (HA1 Backup): Port, IPv4/IPv6 Address, Netmask, and Backup Peer HA1 IP Address; and Election Settings > Heartbeat Backup. Read the BACKUP PEER ADDRESS, not the container: a backup link with no far end is the state this control exists to find, and it looks configured. Then check the backup link is on a different physical port and a different subnet from the primary.
controls.remediation: Give the backup control link a dedicated port, its own address and netmask on a subnet that does not overlap the primary link's, and set the Backup Peer HA1 IP Address on each member. Where the primary control link is not on the management port, enable Heartbeat Backup as well - and where it IS on the management port, use a backup control link instead, because heartbeat backup would share the same path.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: High availability is on and the peers have no second, independent keepalive path - including a backup control link with no backup address for the peer.

queries.name: High-availability configuration not collected
queries.short_description: The high-availability subtree was not collected for this appliance, so the setting was not established.

controls.name: HA Link and Path Monitoring Enabled
controls.description:
Requires each firewall in a redundant relationship to hand over when the traffic it is actually forwarding stops being deliverable - a monitored interface going down, or a monitored next hop becoming unreachable - and not only when its peer stops answering, with at least one real group of interfaces or destinations under monitoring rather than an empty switch.

AN ABSENT MONITORING KEY ASSERTS THAT MONITORING IS ON, which is why this control does not read the switches. Measured directly: an appliance holding no `group/monitoring` node at all reports `link-monitoring: {enabled: yes, failure-condition: any, groups: null}` and the same for path monitoring. So the default state of an estate is MONITORING ENABLED AND MONITORING NOTHING - a query over the two enables would pass every unconfigured appliance in it, and a reader who assumed the absent key meant 'no' would raise a gap the device denies. What decides this control is the GROUPS.

AND A POPULATED COUNT DOES NOT SETTLE IT EITHER: a link group carrying no interface is valid configuration the device accepts, measured with `validate full`. The verdict therefore rests on whether any interface or any destination is actually under monitoring, computed at normalization because it needs a count over a child collection and an existence test inside each entry.

LINK MONITORING ALONE MEETS THE MINIMUM AND NOT THE PREFERRED, and this control does not report that gap: an appliance with a populated link group satisfies the assertion and produces nothing, so the absence of a finding here does not mean path monitoring is in place. The failure-condition setting is deliberately not graded - the vendor documents the all-groups choice as legitimate with a reason, and no severity was ever assigned to it.

A STANDALONE FIREWALL IS EXCLUDED AND NOT PASSED: monitoring that triggers a handover is inert without a peer to hand over to. A cluster member that is not in a pair is excluded with it, which narrows the control against what stage 3 intended and is recorded rather than hidden - the cluster participation key holds nothing on any appliance in any estate today, so admitting it would suppress the control everywhere instead of widening it.
controls.rationale: A firewall whose peer is alive and whose own forwarding path has died keeps the active role and keeps accepting traffic it can no longer deliver, so the pair bought to survive a failure sits through a total blackhole with both members reporting healthy and nothing in the estate raising a hand.
controls.audit: Device > High Availability > Link and Path Monitoring: read the LINK GROUPS and PATH GROUPS, not the Enabled switches - the switches report themselves as on when their keys are absent, and the vendor says twice on this screen that a switch does nothing without a group. Then open each group: a link group with no interface in it, and a path group with no destination, both commit cleanly and monitor nothing.
controls.remediation: Define at least one link group holding the interfaces whose loss should move the active role, and at least one path group holding destinations beyond the next hop, on both members. Then confirm `groups` is non-empty in `show high-availability all` rather than trusting the Enabled switch.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: High availability is on and no interface and no destination is actually under monitoring - the device reports monitoring enabled with no groups.

queries.name: High-availability configuration not collected
queries.short_description: The high-availability subtree was not collected for this appliance, so the setting was not established.

controls.name: Panorama Connectivity Redundant and Secured
controls.description:
Two assertions over one firewall's channel to its central management estate, at two severities.

FIRST, THE FIREWALL NAMES EVERY MANAGEMENT APPLIANCE IT IS MEANT TO REACH - both of them where the management estate is a redundant pair - so that losing one appliance does not leave it unmanaged. This is the medium half. An absent second address slot is a MEASURED reading and not an unread one: the firewall's own `show panorama-status` gains and loses a second server block with the leaf, paid in both directions on a real appliance.

SECOND, THE CHANNEL AUTHENTICATES WITH THE CUSTOMER'S OWN CERTIFICATE MATERIAL and the firewall satisfies itself that the appliance answering is the one it meant to reach, rather than trusting the certificate pair every appliance of this make ships with. This is the low half, and low because the channel is already encrypted with those predefined certificates: what is missing is certificate ownership and peer identity, not confidentiality. It needs all three of a bound local certificate, the Panorama surface switched to use it, and the server-identity check on - and the commonest state in an estate is a certificate bound with nothing switched on to use it, which configures nothing the device presents.

THE TWO HALVES SHARE ONE ROW, because a finding is one row per control. So the HARDENING half is this control's baseline tier and the REDUNDANCY half is a calibration above it: either can match alone, and where both match the worse severity wins and the row is reported at the redundancy half's medium. That is the severity mechanism working as built rather than a trick - the baseline tier is discarded the moment a calibration matches - and it means the absence of a medium here is not the absence of the redundancy gap on some other row. `matched_query_names` on the finding says which half fired, and a reader who needs the other half reads the row's columns.

WHETHER THE MANAGEMENT ESTATE IS A PAIR IS ASSUMED AND NOT READ. The answer lives on the management appliance's own high-availability configuration, which is out of assessment scope, so no firewall can supply it and the applicability predicate defaults to APPLYING - a default the other way would suppress this control on every firewall. The consequence is stated on every finding: on a single-appliance management estate the redundancy half fires everywhere and its remediation is wrong, and an engineer's answer should override it.

AND THE APPLIANCE'S OWN HALF OF THE HANDSHAKE IS UNANSWERED BY DESIGN. Custom Certificate Only and Check Authorization List are switches on the management station and exist on no firewall - verified on both firewall platforms - so a firewall presenting the customer's certificate is still talking to an appliance that would have accepted the shipped one. Every finding here says which part needs the station.
controls.rationale: A firewall holding one management address loses central policy, central logging and central visibility the moment that appliance goes down, and because it keeps passing traffic perfectly well nobody notices until a change has to be pushed or an investigation needs the logs that were never collected. And anything holding the certificates the vendor ships with every appliance can stand in the middle of that channel: an attacker who reaches the management network takes the firewall's registration, serves it policy and collects the logs it forwards - so every artefact the organisation would use to notice comes from the attacker.
controls.audit: Device > Setup > Management > Panorama Settings: both Panorama Servers fields, and Secure Communication Settings for the Certificate Type, the per-surface Secure Client Communication switches and Verify Panorama Server Identity. Read `certificate-type` as WHICH CHILD is present - the explicit `none` branch and an absent key are two different stored states with the same meaning. Then note what cannot be read here: the station's Custom Certificate Only and Check Authorization List, and whether the estate is a pair at all.
controls.remediation: Where the management estate is a redundant pair, set the second Panorama Servers field on every managed firewall to the secondary appliance. For the channel: issue a device certificate from the customer's own authority, bind it under Certificate Type > Local, enable Secure Client Communication for the Panorama surface, and enable Verify Panorama Server Identity. Then do the station's half - Custom Certificate Only and Check Authorization List on the management appliance - because the firewall's three switches do not authenticate the channel on their own.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: The management channel is not hardened to customer certificate material with peer-name validation. The baseline tier, so the redundancy calibration overrides it where both match.

queries.name: No secondary management appliance named
queries.short_description: No secondary management appliance is named, on an estate taken to be a redundant pair. Carries the higher tier, so a firewall failing both halves reports at this one.

controls.name: Out-Of-Service Interface Residue
controls.description:
Requires an interface that is not in service to hold nothing a cable could use: no configured address, no security zone membership, no interface management profile, and administratively shut down. The finding is graded by what the port is left HOLDING, read as what someone who patches a cable into it gains - a port holding more than one takes the highest rank it earns.

WHICH PORTS ARE OUT OF SERVICE IS NOT A CLAUSE AND CANNOT BE ONE. No column can hold it: the configuration cannot answer it, a port carrying an address and a zone may be a spare built in advance of a project, and a port carrying nothing may be a live uplink waiting on the far end. Written as an applicability clause on a customer-supplied column it would SUPPRESS this control wherever the answer had not arrived, which reads as careful and is how a control stops reporting. So the control is delivered as a reported inventory of every port whose stored configuration and administrative state disagree, with the qualification attached, and the customer's list narrows which rows are called findings.

THE ASSERTION RESTS ON ONE VERDICT COLUMN RATHER THAN ON FOUR READINGS, because it is a conjunction of four negatives and its failing condition is therefore a DISJUNCTION, which a clause list that is one conjunction cannot express. The verdict also carries the precedence the grading needs. Its default is the firing side, so a port nobody has recomputed is reported rather than passing.

AND THE ADMINISTRATIVE STATE IS UNKNOWN ON EVERY PORT MEASURED SO FAR. The only oracle for the CONFIGURED administrative state conflates it with the physical link, and no port in the lab estate stores the key at all, so `administrative_state_unknown` is the state every stripped port in that estate is in. Under this programme's own rule an unknown fires, and it fires at this control's own severity because an unknown has no rank of its own.

TWO RESIDUE STATES ARE DELIBERATELY NOT REPORTED. A port holding only a comment or link speed and duplex settings carries neither reachability nor a policy position, and a port holding a routing-instance membership with no address was left unranked on purpose. Both are real configurations and both are excluded by this control's own clauses rather than dropped silently.
controls.rationale: A forgotten port that still holds an address, a zone or a management profile is a way into the estate that no policy was written for. An absent permitted-source list on a bound management profile means ANY host, so the port answers that profile's services to anything that can reach it; a zone membership makes traffic entering on the port that zone's traffic for every rule written for the zone; an address alone makes it routable. A port that is administratively down holds none of that in effect, which is why shutting it down is half of the requirement and stripping it is the other half.
controls.audit: Network > Interfaces > (interface): IPv4/IPv6 addressing, the Security Zone on the Config tab, and the Interface Management Profile on Advanced > Other Info. The administrative state is the Link State on Advanced > Link Settings - read the CONFIGURED value there and not `show interface all`, which reports the physical link and conflates the two. Zone membership is only expressible from the zone end: Network > Zones lists its members and the interface does not name its zone.
controls.remediation: On each port confirmed out of service: remove the IP addressing, remove the port from its security zone's member list, clear the Interface Management Profile binding, and set Link State to Down. Where the port is a member of an aggregate or a virtual wire, removing the membership is what strips it - six of the seven interface roles cannot hold an address or a profile binding at all.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: The port is not stripped and shut down, and what it holds is a state this control ranks.

queries.name: Management binding with no source restriction
queries.short_description: The port names an interface management profile that restricts no source, so the services it permits answer any host that can reach the port.

queries.name: Address only
queries.short_description: The port holds a configured address and nothing else - routable and reachable, with no service or policy position granted.

controls.name: Policy Re-Evaluation Of Running Sessions
controls.description:
Requires the firewall to re-evaluate running sessions against policy when a policy change is committed. Enabled, withdrawing a rule withdraws the access it granted; disabled, every connection open at the time of the commit keeps that access until the session ends by itself - which on a long-lived flow can be indefinitely.

AN APPLIANCE WHOSE SETTING NOBODY HAS ESTABLISHED IS REPORTED, NOT PASSED, and that is the whole shape of this control. The vendor says the capability is enabled by default and says so twice and consistently, and no oracle on the appliance confirms it: `show session info` carries about sixty dataplane settings and no rematch field, `show system state filter *rematch*` answers NO_MATCHES on every appliance measured, and `show session rematch` reports whether a rematch has EXECUTED rather than what the setting is. So nothing is stored for an absent key and the finding says the setting was never established rather than that it is off. Reading the vendor's documented default as compliance would have passed every appliance that has never touched the setting, which in the estate this was measured on was most of them - and the Help has been wrong about a default on this estate before.

THE TWO FAILING GROUPS ARE ALTERNATIVES AND SO ARE TWO QUERIES: the setting stored as off, and nothing stored at all. A clause list is one conjunction with no OR, so they cannot be one query. They report at the same severity, because an appliance whose rematch setting nobody has established may be leaving revoked access in force on exactly the long-lived flows this control is about.
controls.rationale: Policy is only as current as the sessions it governs. Without re-evaluation on commit, revoking access is an instruction about future connections only, so an attacker or a departed user holding an open session keeps what the rule change was meant to take away - and the longer-lived the flow, the longer the gap. This is the one device-wide setting in this domain whose failure silently unmakes a policy change an operator believes they have made.
controls.audit: Device > Setup > Session > Session Settings: 'Rematch Sessions'. Read the configured value rather than inferring it - no operational command on the appliance reports this setting, so an appliance whose checkbox has never been touched is a reading nobody has taken.
controls.remediation: Enable 'Rematch Sessions' on Device > Setup > Session and commit. On an HA pair set it on both members: each appliance holds its own row and nothing here compares the peers.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: The appliance does not re-evaluate running sessions against policy on commit.

queries.name: Setting never established
queries.short_description: No rematch key is stored on this appliance, so whether revoked access is withdrawn from running sessions is unknown.

controls.name: Link-Layer Discovery Announcements
controls.description:
Requires that no interface facing a network whose adjacent devices the customer does not control announces the firewall to its neighbour. The finding is graded by what an announcement actually puts on the wire, and every rank ADDS to a floor rather than replacing it: the mandatory items - chassis identifier and port name - go out whenever the protocol transmits at all, whatever a bound profile suppresses.

WHICH PORTS FACE AN UNTRUSTED NETWORK IS NOT A CLAUSE. The configuration holds each port's zone, address and routing instance and nothing about where the cable goes, and the same setting is routine on an internal access port and serious on a transit port. So the control delivers every interface transmitting and what each one transmits, with the untrusted subset marked as requiring confirmation and NOT suppressed - an applicability clause here would switch the control off on every port until a person answered.

A PORT WITH NO LLDP NODE IS COMPLIANT AND A PORT WITH NO PROFILE IS NOT. The operational read lists an interface if and only if its LLDP container exists - measured by construction, the interface appeared in the reply the moment an EMPTY container was committed and nothing else changed - so a finding built on that read would report only the ports somebody has already thought about. The assertion rests on the stored enable instead. And where announcements are on with NO profile attached, the firewall uses its GLOBAL defaults, which no document in the vendor corpus describes; so what such a port leaks is UNKNOWN rather than nothing, it fires, and it fires at this control's own severity because an unknown has no rank of its own. That is the state every announcing port in the estate this was measured on is in, since no LLDP profile exists anywhere in it.

THIS CONTROL ALSO ASSERTS THAT THE PROTOCOL IS OFF FIRMWARE-WIDE, AND THAT HALF IS NOT BUILT. The device-wide enable lives on a different object from the interface, and one catalogue control can assert over one object. The per-interface half is this control; the firewall-wide half is recorded as owed and is not silently folded in.
controls.rationale: Link-layer discovery is a broadcast introduction to whatever is on the other end of the cable. On a port facing equipment the customer does not control, it hands the device's own management address, its software build and its place in the topology to whoever owns the next hop - the management address being the one thing the rest of a hardening programme is about keeping unreachable, and the software build being a free answer to the question a vulnerability scan would otherwise have to ask.
controls.audit: Network > Interfaces > (interface) > Advanced > LLDP: the Enable checkbox and the Profile. Then Network > Network Profiles > LLDP for what that profile transmits. Do not read membership of `show lldp config all` as the answer - that reply lists an interface if and only if it carries an LLDP container, so a port with no container is absent from it rather than compliant in it.
controls.remediation: Clear the LLDP Enable checkbox on every interface facing a network whose adjacent devices are not the customer's, or set the protocol to receive-only. Where it must transmit, bind an LLDP profile that suppresses the management address, the system description and the system name - and note that the chassis identifier and port name go out regardless, so a fully suppressed profile is still an announcement.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: The interface transmits link-layer discovery and what it announces is a state this control ranks, so the mandatory chassis identifier and port name go out on it.

queries.name: Announces the management address
queries.short_description: The announcement carries an address of the firewall's own management plane.

queries.name: Announces the system description
queries.short_description: The announcement carries the software build, which names the advisories that apply.

controls.name: DHCP Service On Untrusted-Facing Interfaces
controls.description:
Requires that no interface facing a network the customer does not control carries a DHCP server configuration, and that none relays address requests to the customer's own address servers. Two independent halves: `server` and `relay` are sibling branches in the configuration, so the absence of one asserts nothing about the other, and one interface can violate both.

THE SERVER BRANCH'S EXISTENCE IS THE FINDING, NOT ITS MODE. The vendor's own gloss makes `auto` an enabled server - 'Auto mode enables the server and disables it if another DHCP server is detected on the network' - so a reading that passed anything but `enabled` would pass a server that is serving right now on any segment where no competitor happens to be present. Resting on the branch rather than on the mode also catches a server branch whose `mode` key is absent, which is a real state nobody has established the meaning of, and which a value comparison would have matched not at all. A server switched off but configured is still a finding, at a lower severity: the pool, the gateway and the resolver are all written down and one commit from being handed out.

THE PASSING STATE IS THE ABSENCE OF A ROW, which is why no query reports it. A `network/dhcp/interface` entry exists only where somebody configured DHCP on that port, so a firewall with no DHCP produces nothing for this control to match - correct, and also the one place in this domain where a collection gap is silent: an appliance with no DHCP and a collector that skipped the subtree are indistinguishable, and no column can carry the difference because there is no row for it to live on.

THE RELAY HALF ANSWERS FOR ONE MEASURED ADDRESS FAMILY. The two families are independent switches, so a reading that tests one has answered for neither; the verdict this control rests on reads both and takes the worse, but only the IPv4 switch is stored, because the measured key set for this node carries no IPv6 sibling. A relay configured for IPv6 alone therefore produces no finding, and that gap is recorded rather than hidden.

WHICH INTERFACES FACE AN UNTRUSTED NETWORK IS NOT A CLAUSE, for the reason the other interface controls give: the firewall holds each port's zone, address and routing instance and nothing that says where the segment on the other side goes.
controls.rationale: A DHCP server on a segment the customer does not control hands every host that appears there a gateway, a resolver, a time source and a name suffix of the firewall's choosing - which is a position from which to intercept and redirect. A relay is the mirror image: anything able to broadcast on that wire gets a delivered path to internal address servers it could never have routed to, and the internal gateway, resolver and time-server addresses come back out to it. Both are services offered to an untrusted population by a device whose job is to separate it from the trusted one.
controls.audit: Network > DHCP > DHCP Server and Network > DHCP > DHCP Relay, one entry per interface. Read the presence of the entry first and its Mode second - `auto` is an enabled server with a back-off, not a middle setting. On the relay tab check BOTH the IPv4 and the IPv6 server lists: they are independent switches and only the IPv4 one is recorded here.
controls.remediation: Delete the DHCP server entry for each interface facing a network the customer does not control - disabling it leaves the pool and the option set in place. Delete the relay entry rather than clearing its switches, for the same reason, and remove the relayed server addresses on both address families.

queries.name: Baseline - a DHCP server branch exists on this interface
queries.short_description: The interface carries a DHCP server configuration, in any mode, including one whose mode key is absent.

queries.name: Server configured and switched off
queries.short_description: The server is off but fully configured - the pool, gateway and resolver are one commit from being handed out.

queries.name: A DHCP relay is relaying on this interface
queries.short_description: The interface relays address requests to the customer's own servers on at least one address family.

queries.name: Relay configured with every switch off
queries.short_description: The relayed server addresses are recorded on this interface and one commit from being used.

controls.name: IPv6 Session Inspection
controls.description:
Requires session-level inspection of IPv6 traffic to be on wherever the firewall routes IPv6. Switched off, the firewall ignores every IPv6 rule it holds - the rules are present and have no effect, which is worse than their absence because the policy reads as covering the traffic.

AN ABSENT KEY MEANS THE CAPABILITY IS ON, MEASURED, AND THE NAIVE READING OF THE SAME ABSENCE INVERTS THIS CONTROL. The field is called an Enable and the vendor states no default, so reading an absent key as 'not enabled' is the obvious move and it is wrong: the device's own dataplane was paid in both directions on a committed state - the key absent reports IPv6 firewalling ON, `no` committed reports it off, the leaf deleted and committed reports it on again - and the result was corroborated on four appliances across two platforms, two major versions and both vsys modes. On the estate this was measured on, every appliance holds no key, so the naive reading would have raised a finding on all four where the control is satisfied. A finding from this control therefore means the key is stored as `no`.

WHAT THIS CONTROL CANNOT CURRENTLY SEPARATE is an appliance nobody collected from one whose key is absent. Both read as the measured default of on, because the column is non-nullable, so 'we asked and it was fine' and 'we never asked' are one value here. That is a known limitation of this control rather than a property of the estate, and it is recorded as owed work rather than scored as compliance.
controls.rationale: A firewall that routes IPv6 without inspecting it is a router. Every security rule written for IPv6 destinations - and every profile attached to one - is read by an operator as being in force and is not, so the traffic crosses on the strength of routing alone while the policy that was supposed to govern it reads as present. The vendor is explicit that all IPv6-based configuration is ignored when the capability is off.
controls.audit: Device > Setup > Session > Session Settings: 'Enable IPv6 Firewalling'. An unticked box here is not the same as an absent key in the configuration - the absent key means ON, measured on the device's own dataplane, so read the stored value and not the inference.
controls.remediation: Enable 'IPv6 Firewalling' on Device > Setup > Session and commit, or - where the key is stored as `no` - delete the leaf, which returns the appliance to the measured default of on. Set it on both members of an HA pair.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: IPv6 session inspection is switched off on this appliance, so every IPv6 rule it holds is ignored.

controls.name: Tunnel Content Inspection Coverage
controls.description:
Requires every enforcement point through which cleartext tunnels transit to open those tunnels to inspection - for every transiting protocol, across every zone pair they traverse, to the depth of encapsulation in use. The finding is graded by how much of that traffic the policy actually opens, and every rank below the top names traffic crossing the firewall that policy never sees.

THE PRESENCE OF A RULE IS NOT COVERAGE, which is why this rests on a verdict over the whole rulebase rather than on a rule count. A rule that exists can be switched off; can cover some transiting protocols and not others; can be scoped to zone pairs that do not include every pair the tunnels traverse; and can open one level of encapsulation where the tunnels are nested two deep. The commonest failing state is also the one a per-rule reading cannot report: NO RULE EXISTS, so there is no row to carry the finding and no rule for an engineer to open.

A VSYS COVERED FROM PANORAMA IS NOT A VSYS WITH NO POLICY. The merged configuration view does not carry a device group's tunnel-inspect rulebase, so counting rules from that read alone reports this control's worst rank on exactly the estates whose coverage is centrally managed. Each row says which config subtree its rules came from, and that says which copy a reader is looking at rather than who owns it.

FOUR OF THIS CONTROL'S RANKS CANNOT BE COMPUTED FROM CONFIGURATION AT ALL, and saying so is part of the control. Whether a rule covers the protocols that actually transited, the zone pairs they actually crossed, the depth they were actually nested to, and the overlay identifiers actually in use are all questions about traffic. A configuration-only reading that finds rules present and enabled reaches 'coverage unverified without a traffic answer' - which fires, at this control's own severity, because an unknown fires and has no rank of its own. The counters that look like an answer are not one: the active-tunnel counters read zero on every lab appliance, which is a lab with no traffic rather than an estate with no tunnels.

AND HARDWARE TUNNEL ACCELERATION EXEMPTS ONE PROTOCOL, NOT THE CONTROL. Where the vendor supports acceleration for the mobile-network user-plane protocol on the chassis platform and card set, and it is switched on, no inspection rule is required FOR THAT PROTOCOL. Written as an applicability clause the exemption would suppress this control on every protocol on every appliance where acceleration is on - which, because an absent acceleration node asserts ENABLED, is every appliance that has never touched the setting. So the setting is reported and clauses on nothing, and the exemption is applied per protocol when the protocol list arrives.

THREE DROP CONDITIONS AND THE TUNNEL-ZONE SETTING ARE OUT OF SCOPE HERE. What the firewall does with a packet it cannot read, a packet nested deeper than the configured depth, and a tunnel header failing a strict standards check are a different assertion from whether the tunnel is opened at all - and the vendor warns that enabling one of them breaks interoperability with implementations predating the standard it checks against.
controls.rationale: A cleartext tunnel crossing a firewall with no inspection policy is reported as one permitted session, and everything inside it reaches its destination unexamined - applications, users, files and threats alike, none of them matched by any rule or profile. Partial coverage is the harder case, because the firewall and its logs look like they are working: the protocol, zone pair, encapsulation level or overlay identifier that no rule names is the one carrying whatever was not meant to be seen.
controls.audit: Policies > Tunnel Inspection, per vsys. Count the rules, then read each one's state, its Protocol list, its Source and Destination Zones against the zone pairs the tunnels actually traverse, its Maximum Tunnel Inspection Levels against the nesting in use, and any Overlay ID scoping. On a Panorama-managed estate read the device group's rulebase too - the firewall's merged view does not carry it. Device > Setup > Session reports whether tunnel acceleration is on, which exempts one protocol and not the rest.
controls.remediation: Add or enable a tunnel inspection rule per vsys covering every cleartext tunnel protocol that transits it, scoped to every zone pair those tunnels traverse, with the maximum inspection level set to the deepest nesting in use and no Overlay ID narrowing unless every transiting tunnel is on the named identifiers. Where coverage is pushed from Panorama, make the change in the device group rather than locally.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: This enforcement point's tunnel inspection does not open every transiting protocol and zone pair to the depth in use - including the case where that cannot be established.

queries.name: One level of encapsulation only
queries.short_description: A rule covers the protocols at one level where the tunnels are nested two deep, so the inner tunnel's contents are never matched.

queries.name: Scoped to named overlay identifiers
queries.short_description: A rule names the overlay network identifiers it inspects, where tunnels on other identifiers also transit.

controls.name: Dynamic Routing Adjacency Protection
controls.description:
Requires every dynamic routing adjacency the firewall forms to authenticate its peer with a keyed digest from the stronger family the device offers, or - on the one protocol that offers it - to authenticate and encrypt the routing payload; and requires every BGP peer to carry a prefix ceiling that actually refuses the routes beyond it.

A PROFILE BEING ATTACHED IS NOT AUTHENTICATION, which is why the assertion reads the profile's CONTENT rather than the binding. Four states rank at the top severity with something attached or nothing to attach: a profile whose authentication is explicitly set to the disabled member the device offers, a cleartext password, a weaker attachment inside an area that has a stronger one, and no authentication at all. A keyed digest using an algorithm the vendor's own guidance elsewhere calls not secure ranks below them - it raises the cost of the attack without removing it. And where a protocol attaches authentication at more than one level, the WEAKEST attachment in use sets the rank, because the vendor documents the narrower attachment as overriding the wider one.

A CEILING THAT PERMITS EVERYTHING IS NOT A CEILING. The prefix limit leaf takes the keyword `unlimited` - measured as the only member of its own completion on every appliance asked - so a peer storing it has a value and no limit, and a presence test would call that compliant while the firewall accepts the peer's whole table. The keyword also sorts as a string rather than a magnitude, so a threshold query written as 'more than N' skips it silently. Absence and the keyword mean the same thing to the firewall and are two different row states, which is why this rests on a verdict that collapses them. A ceiling set far above any plausible table size still enforces and is accepted here; whether the number is sensible is the engineer's question and not a rank.

THE CONTROL APPLIES WHERE THE FIREWALL FORMS AN ADJACENCY, AND THAT NEEDS NO CLAUSE. A firewall routing only on static entries forms none, so it produces no row and there is nothing for a finding to attach to - reporting one would be a finding against a device this control was never about. The shape that makes this safe was measured: an absent peer-group means no adjacency exists, while an absent authentication-profile collection means no authentication material exists, which is the FAILING state - so a reading that tested only for the profile would have reported seven routers unauthenticated on an estate where the control does not apply.

TWO THINGS THIS CONTROL CANNOT SEE. The key itself: the authentication secret and the OSPF password are encrypted-text and cannot be read back from the firewall at all, so whether a key is unique to an adjacency or shared across every site is an engineer's question and nothing here pretends to it. And whether a configured ceiling WARNS rather than stops: the peer's measured key set carries no key that says which, so a peer whose limit only raises an alarm is indistinguishable from one that enforces and produces no finding. Both are recorded as owed work.
controls.rationale: An unauthenticated adjacency accepts routes from anything that can reach the interface. One host on that segment can advertise a better path to any destination and pull the traffic for it through itself - a redirection that needs no access to the firewall and leaves the policy intact and irrelevant. Authentication that exists on paper and not in effect is worse than none, because the configuration reads as solved. An unbounded peer is the other failure of the same relationship: a peer that leaks its whole table fills the routing table until there is no room for the routes the business depends on, and the firewall accepts it because nothing told it not to.
controls.audit: Network > Virtual Routers > (router) > BGP / OSPF / OSPFv3 / RIP. For each peer or interface attachment read the Authentication profile and then OPEN the profile: a name in the field says nothing about what is inside it. For OSPF check the attachment level - on the legacy routing engine authentication attaches at an area's children and there is no per-area node. For BGP read Max Prefixes per peer and treat `unlimited` as no limit.
controls.remediation: On each adjacency, attach an authentication profile carrying a SHA-2 family keyed digest - or, on OSPFv3, authentication with encryption - and remove any profile whose authentication is set to the disabled member or to a cleartext password. Where an area-wide profile exists, make sure no interface or virtual link inside it attaches something weaker. On each BGP peer set Max Prefixes to a number agreed with the peer's owner rather than to `unlimited`, and confirm the limit refuses routes beyond it rather than only warning.

queries.name: Baseline - the adjacency is not authenticated with a strong digest
queries.short_description: The adjacency's authentication amounts to less than a keyed digest from the stronger family, or than authentication with encryption.

queries.name: Authentication absent, disabled, cleartext or overridden
queries.short_description: The adjacency has no effective authentication - none configured, explicitly disabled, a cleartext password, or a weaker attachment overriding an area-wide profile.

queries.name: Authenticated with a weak digest
queries.short_description: The keyed digest uses an algorithm the vendor's own guidance elsewhere calls not secure.

queries.name: BGP peer with no enforced prefix ceiling
queries.short_description: The peer's prefix limit does not refuse the routes beyond it - no ceiling, a ceiling configured as unlimited, or one that only warns.

controls.name: Sanctioned SaaS Applications Tagged
controls.description:
Requires each enforcement point to record which cloud applications the business has approved, in the one mechanism the firewall itself reads: the predefined approval tag on an application. Policy can only separate corporate use of a SaaS application from personal use if the approved set is identified somewhere the firewall can act on, and this is that place.

THE CONTROL IS ABOUT WHETHER THE MECHANISM IS USED AT ALL, and that is a narrowing rather than a convenience. The firewall holds NO list of what the business approved - the marking IS the firewall's only record of it - so no reading can compare the marked set against an approved set, and a control claiming to do that would be asserting something no firewall read supports.

ZERO IS THE FINDING AND IT IS THE VENDOR'S OWN RULE THAT MAKES IT ONE: a partition that marks nothing treats every application as unsanctioned. The reading is a COUNT and not a presence test, because a partition can hold application entries that carry no marking at all - the collection is populated and the marked count is nil, and a truthiness test on the container splits those two the wrong way.

THE SECOND HALF ASKS WHETHER THE PARTITIONS AGREE, on an appliance that has more than one. It is reported separately at the same severity and it cannot say which partition is in force: precedence for this node across a virtual system, the firewall's shared namespace and a Panorama push has never been measured, so the finding reports that they diverge and stops there.

AND THE INVENTORY CANNOT BE CHECKED FROM THE SCREEN THAT SHOWS IT. The Objects > Applications grid renders the vendor's predefined application CHARACTERISTIC tags - Web App, Uploading, Deleting - in the same chips as the operator's approval markings, and its filter panel counts them. So that column is full on an appliance which marks nothing, and a reviewer who takes a populated Tags column for a marked inventory has refuted nothing.
controls.rationale: Tenant restrictions, unsanctioned-application controls and attribute-driven selections all need to know which applications are approved, and the firewall has one place to record that. Where the record is empty, every control that depends on it either catches the approved applications too or catches nothing - and the vendor's own rule is that an unmarked application is an unsanctioned one.
controls.audit: Objects > Applications, for the virtual system named in the finding: select an application and read Edit Tags. Do NOT read the grid's Tags column as the answer - it mixes the vendor's predefined characteristic tags with the operator's approval markings. Where the appliance runs several virtual systems, read the same screen in each one: the marking is per partition and the partitions can disagree.
controls.remediation: Apply the predefined approval tag to each cloud application the business has approved, in every virtual system that enforces policy for its users, and apply the same set in each one. The marking is a SET rather than a state - the device accepts an application marked approved and tolerated at once, and writing a tag MERGES into the member list - so removing a wrong marking is its own step and setting the right one does not replace it. An application group can hold the same inventory for policy reuse and CANNOT carry the marking: the device refuses a tag on a group outright, so a group is not a substitute. Where a marking is pushed from a Panorama device group it counts here and cannot be edited on the firewall; make the change in the device group instead.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: No application in this virtual system carries the predefined approval tag.

queries.name: Approval marking differs between virtual systems
queries.short_description: A multi-vsys appliance marks an application approved in one partition and not in another.

controls.name: HTTP Header Insertion Enforces Tenant Restrictions
controls.description:
Requires that for sanctioned applications which also have consumer or external tenants - Office 365, Google Workspace, Dropbox, Slack - a URL Filtering profile reachable from the enforcement point inserts a tenant-restriction header AND is carried by a security rule of that enforcement point, so only the corporate tenant is reachable.

IN FORCE AND NOT MERELY DEFINED, which is the whole of this control and is why it rests on a derived verdict rather than on the presence of a profile. The hop is rule to profile group to profile to header insertion, resolved across the virtual system, the firewall's own shared namespace and whatever Panorama pushed - and a clause compares one field to one literal.

A COUNT OF PROFILES CARRYING HEADER INSERTION COUNTS THE WRONG THING. One header-insertion entry carries exactly one type - the device refuses a second - so covering N applications takes N sibling entries, and the unit of coverage is the TYPE entry.

WHAT THIS CONTROL DOES NOT CLAIM. It does not report that a tenant identifier is wrong: the device stores whatever string it is given and cannot tell a correct identifier from a plausible wrong one, and for the Microsoft case the value comes from the customer's own cloud directory and from no firewall screen. What it does report is a header that names NO tenant at all, which reads as configured and restricts nothing. It also does not claim the header name is one the vendor offers - the enumeration is enforced at neither the write nor the commit, and an arbitrary header name commits.

AND IT DOES NOT ANSWER WHETHER THE REWRITING CAN HAPPEN ON THE SESSIONS IT COVERS. The vendor states that header insertion requires HTTP/1.x, which needs the protocol-negotiation extension stripped in a decryption profile and the QUIC application refused - both of which belong to other objects and neither of which is asserted here or anywhere in this catalogue. A passing verdict on this control is therefore not a statement that the restriction reaches the traffic.
controls.rationale: A sanctioned application reachable in any tenant is a sanctioned application through which data leaves the organisation: the same client, the same domain and the same App-ID serve a personal account as serve the corporate one, so nothing in an application-level decision separates them. The tenant-restriction header is the mechanism that does, and a header defined in a profile no rule carries changes nothing about any session.
controls.audit: Objects > Security Profiles > URL Filtering > (profile) > HTTP Header Insertion, for every profile reachable from the enforcement point named in the finding - the partition's own, the firewall's shared namespace and anything pushed from Panorama. Read the Type entry and the headers beneath it, then confirm in Policies > Security that a rule of that partition carries the profile, directly or through the profile group it names. A profile with header insertion that no rule carries is the state this control exists to catch.
controls.remediation: Add an HTTP Header Insertion entry of the vendor's tenant-restriction type to a URL Filtering profile, give each header the organisation's own account identifier as its value, and attach that profile to the security rules that carry the traffic for those applications. One type per header-insertion entry, so add a sibling entry per application rather than expecting one to cover several. Where the profile is PUSHED from Panorama the firewall will refuse the edit - make it in the device group or Shared instead. Where the platform supports a SaaS Tenant List, prefer it: it is referenced from the rule directly, and a list carrying no members commits and restricts nothing, so check the members rather than the reference.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: No URL Filtering profile reachable from this enforcement point inserts a tenant-restriction header into traffic one of its rules carries.

controls.name: Upload/Download/Share Function Controls per App
controls.description:
Requires that where App-ID resolves the upload, sharing and delete FUNCTIONS of a cloud application as applications of their own, the enforcement point's policy refuses those functions while leaving browsing and viewing permitted - cutting the path data leaves by without breaking casual use.

THE ASSERTION IS A RELATION BETWEEN TWO RULES and that is why it rests on a derived verdict: a refusal of the function child evaluated BEFORE the permission on the base application. Rule order is positional rather than a value, and the ordering spans scopes, because rules pushed from Panorama as pre-rules are evaluated before the firewall's own and post-rules after.

THE COMMONEST FAILING STATE IS THAT NO RULE NAMES THE FUNCTIONS AT ALL, which is an absence rather than a value: there is no action anywhere to read. It is reported at this control's own severity, because a policy that does not distinguish browsing an application from moving data into it permits both.

`deny` IS NOT THE ONLY REFUSAL. The action a rule carries has six values and four of them - drop and the three resets - are refusals in this control's sense while none of them is the word deny. A reading that matched the literal would report a compliant policy as failing.

WHAT ANY COUNT HERE CAN MEAN IS BOUNDED BY A CONTENT RELEASE. Which applications have function children is a property of the vendor's application catalogue, which content updates deliver and which changes with no configuration change - so a count of rules naming one is a LOWER BOUND over a namespace this assessment has not enumerated.

AND A DISABLED RULE COUNTS TOWARD THE REFUSAL, which is stated because the direction of that error is the unsafe one: a disabled rule that refuses an upload function reports a refusal no session will ever meet.
controls.rationale: Blocking a cloud application outright is usually refused by the business and permitting it outright leaves the upload path open, so the function-level App-IDs are the only setting that separates reading from writing. Where no rule names them the two are the same permission, and the policy shows no sign of the distinction anybody intended.
controls.audit: Policies > Security, for the enforcement point named in the finding, INCLUDING the pre-rules and post-rules pushed from Panorama - a decision made in a pre-rule is evaluated before anything local. Find the rules whose Application column names a function child App-ID (the indented children under an application in Objects > Applications - for example the uploading, downloading and delete entries beside a base application) and read the Action of the FIRST rule that matches each one in evaluation order. Treat drop and the three reset actions as refusals, not only deny.
controls.remediation: Add a rule that refuses the upload, sharing and delete function App-IDs of each cloud application the policy permits, and place it ABOVE the rule that permits the base application - in the same rulebase, or in a Panorama pre-rule so it is evaluated before the local rules. Any of deny, drop or the three reset actions satisfies this; which one to choose is a question about what the user sees, and the vendor notes the firewall may reset one application and silently drop another under the same action. Check that the rule is ENABLED: a disabled rule counts toward this assessment's reading and refuses nothing.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: A function child application this enforcement point's policy names is permitted by the first rule that matches it, or no rule names any of them.

controls.name: Unsanctioned SaaS Restricted by Category
controls.description:
Requires the enforcement point to restrict the web categories that carry consumer file storage and personal publishing - actively restricted, meaning interrupted, held behind a password or refused. These categories catch the long tail of unsanctioned cloud services that no explicit list will enumerate.

THE READING IS AN ENUMERATION OVER THE CATEGORY NAMESPACE AND NOT A MEMBERSHIP TEST, and that is the measured reason this control rests on a derived verdict. A predefined category explicitly set to permit is NEVER WRITTEN: the configuration holds the per-action member lists and the question is which categories appear in none of them. So a profile naming 29 of 90 categories and leaving 61 implicit passes any membership test and is exactly the configuration this control exists to catch - the vendor states its own default from the other side, that site access for all categories is Allow.

THE VERDICT IS THE WEAKEST LINK, twice over: the weakest treatment any reachable profile gives a category, because a permissive profile that also applies leaves the category reachable, and then the weakest across the categories themselves.

`alert` IS GRADED BELOW THE RESTRICTING VALUES AND ABOVE THE PERMITTING ONES, reported at LOW rather than at this control's own severity. The visit still happens; what exists is a record of it, so the exposure is unchanged and an investigation after the fact has something to read. The vendor's own floor for categories it calls necessary-but-risky is the interruption, which is why that value and the two above it produce no finding.

TWO RESTRICTING SURFACES ARE NOT IN THIS READING AND A CATEGORY REACHABLE ONLY THROUGH ONE OF THEM IS RESTRICTED IN FACT: the block-response list and remote browser isolation. Neither has a measured place in the restrictiveness order, so neither is counted, and the error runs toward reporting such a category as weaker than it is.

AND THE HALF THAT IS NOT HERE. This control also asks that the organisation's own approved applications be carved out BY NAME instead of the whole category being left open, and there is no object on the firewall for an exception that excludes a named approved application from a restricted web category. The only carve-out the firewall has is an application filter's exclusion list, which belongs to the application-attribute surface - a different subject, which this control cannot carry a query for.
controls.rationale: No list of unsanctioned cloud services stays current: a new consumer storage provider appears and the policy that names providers by hand does not know about it. The web category is the only surface that covers the ones nobody has heard of yet - and a category in no restricting list is permitted by the vendor's own default, which is indistinguishable in the configuration from a decision to permit it.
controls.audit: Objects > Security Profiles > URL Filtering > (profile) > Categories, for every profile reachable from the enforcement point named in the finding, and read the Site Access column for the consumer file storage and personal publishing categories. Read the categories you do NOT find as well: one left at its implicit value is permitted and is not written anywhere. Where several profiles are reachable, the weakest one decides. A security rule naming the category explicitly also counts as a restricting surface where its action refuses - the keyword `any` is not a naming.
controls.remediation: Set Site Access for the consumer file storage and personal publishing categories to Continue, Override or Block in every URL Filtering profile reachable from the enforcement point - not only in the one an engineer happens to open, because the weakest reachable profile decides. Alert is not enough: the visit happens and is merely recorded. Then carve the organisation's own approved applications out by name, on the application surface, so that restricting the category does not refuse the services the business approved. Where the profile is pushed from Panorama, make the change in the device group or in Shared.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: A web category carrying consumer file storage or personal publishing is not actively restricted at this enforcement point.

queries.name: Permitted and recorded rather than restricted
queries.short_description: The weakest treatment is `alert`: the visit happens and is recorded, so the exposure is unchanged and measurable.

controls.name: SaaS Security Inline / SSPM Adoption Documented
controls.description:
Requires that where the cloud application inspection subscription is bought, the App-ID Cloud Engine is actually working on the appliance. The engine is what delivers cloud-based App-IDs, and the policy recommendations the inline SaaS product produces reach the firewall through it.

THE CONFIGURATION AND THE ENGINE POINT OPPOSITE WAYS FROM ONE NODE AND THE CONFIGURATION IS THE REASSURING ONE. The key that switches the engine off is absent on an appliance nobody has touched, which reads as 'not deliberately disabled' - while the engine itself may be reporting a failed licence check, a failed cloud connection or a missing device certificate. So this control rests on the engine's own account of its condition and not on the configured key, and what the device does with that key absent is an inference rather than a measured vendor default.

THE DEVICE CERTIFICATE IS A SECOND PRECONDITION AND IT IS NOT IN THE LICENCE LISTING AT ALL, which is why the finding names the condition rather than the symptom: a remediation that buys a subscription and stops there still has no engine.

AN APPLIANCE WITH NO SUBSCRIPTION PRODUCES NO FINDING HERE, deliberately: the control was never about it, and the vendor states that an unlicensed firewall cannot use the cloud-delivered applications at all. So the ABSENCE of a finding on an appliance is not a statement that the engine is healthy - most often it is a statement that the licence check failed.

AND THE HALF THIS CONTROL CANNOT READ. Whether the recommendations are reviewed and taken into policy on a stated cadence is not on the firewall: the recommendation feed is operational only and lists what the cloud has OFFERED rather than what anybody imported, and an imported recommendation appears afterwards only as an ordinary security rule. Neither is the posture-management product's adoption: the firewall has no surface for it whatever. Both are the engineer's answer, and this control's finding says nothing about either.

THIS CONTROL IS A PREMISE UNDER THE OTHERS IN ITS DOMAIN. Rules and application filters naming cloud-delivered App-IDs stay VISIBLE in the policy while they stop enforcing, so a finding on the function-control or category controls rests on this engine working - and neither of those controls can read this row.
controls.rationale: A cloud-delivered App-ID that the engine cannot fetch stops matching traffic while the rule naming it still reads as policy, so the configuration looks correct and enforces nothing. The failure is silent, it has at least three independent causes, and only one of them is the subscription anybody thinks to check.
controls.audit: Device > Setup > Content-ID for the appliance named in the finding, to see whether the App-ID Cloud Engine is switched off - and then ask the engine itself, with `show cloud-appid connection-to-cloud`, which reports the licence check, the cloud connection and the device certificate as three separate conditions. The licence listing alone cannot answer this: it names the features present, so it can only report a missing subscription by what is absent from its list, and it does not mention the device certificate at all. `show system info` carries the certificate status beside it.
controls.remediation: Name the condition the finding reports and fix that one. For a failed licence check, install and activate the cloud application inspection subscription. For a missing or invalid device certificate, install it and confirm it has reached the daemons - a subscription without it buys nothing. For a failed cloud connection, check egress and name resolution for the engine's endpoint. For a configured disable, clear the checkbox in Device > Setup > Content-ID - and where the value comes from a Panorama template, clear it there, because the next push will set it again. Where the engine was never asked, issue the operational read before concluding anything: this finding then says only that nobody looked.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: The App-ID Cloud Engine is not working on an appliance whose failure is not the absence of the subscription.

controls.name: IoT Security Subscription Active Where IoT Present
controls.description:
Requires that where an estate carries equipment nobody administers - unmanaged or IoT devices - a named means of identifying it exists, is paid up, and is actually feeding the firewall.

TWO HALVES, AND THE SECOND IS NOT IMPLIED BY THE FIRST. One asks whether the entitlement for the vendor's device-identification service is in force on this appliance. The other asks whether the firewall is wired to that service at all - a subscription that nothing points at delivers nothing.

THE QUESTION IS ABOUT THE ABSENCE OF A LICENCE ROW AND NO PREDICATE CAN EXPRESS THAT. The vendor returns NO ROW for an entitlement an appliance does not hold - the licence table has no row saying 'no' - so a clause asking whether that row reports `expired` finds nothing to compare on exactly the appliances this control is about, and the row would be dropped in silence. The control therefore rests on a per-appliance verdict computed over the whole table.

AND 'NOT ENTITLED' IS INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM 'NOBODY ASKED'. An appliance holding nothing licensed answers the licence listing with an empty envelope, which is exactly what an appliance whose listing was never taken produces. Both states report, at the same severity, because one of them is a configuration defect and the other is a gap in what we looked at - and a reader has to be told which. An appliance can match both arms, and then the report shows two findings about it rather than one wrong one.

WHAT A POPULATED EDGE-SERVICE ADDRESS DOES AND DOES NOT PROVE. It proves the WIRING exists. It says nothing about whether anything answers: a hostname that cannot resolve commits clean on this platform, so the finding reports that the firewall is pointed at nothing and never that delivery was tested.

THE ONE INPUT NOBODY HAS MEASURED is the exact feature name the vendor uses for this entitlement in the licence listing. No appliance available to this project holds it, so the match is against a candidate set rather than a literal anybody has read. The failure direction is the safe one - a wrong name leaves the control REPORTING rather than passing - but it reports on every appliance in every estate until the name is right, so a first estate should confirm it before acting on a fleet.

AND THE HALF THIS CONTROL CANNOT READ. Whether the organisation has adopted this vendor's service as its chosen means of identifying equipment is on no firewall: nothing in a configuration says which means an organisation chose. So this fires on every appliance and the engineer's answer decides whether it is reported. Suppressing it instead would need an applicability clause on a column nothing fills, which would silence the control on every appliance in every estate - the worse of the two errors.
controls.rationale: Equipment nobody administers cannot be patched, cannot be logged into and is routinely shipped with credentials its owner never changes. A policy that cannot tell what a device IS can only name it by address, so it cannot be segmented from anything as the estate changes around it. The subscription is the vendor's answer to that, and an unlicensed or unwired firewall has no answer at all while the policy still reads as if it does.
controls.audit: Device > Licenses on the appliance named in the finding, to see whether a device-identification entitlement is present and in force - and read the absence carefully, because an entitlement an appliance does not hold appears as a missing row rather than as a row reporting expiry. Then Device > Setup > Management for the IoT edge-service address, which is what tells the firewall where to send its traffic records. Confirm with `request license info` and a configuration read of the edge-service node through the API if the screens disagree. Where the finding says the licence listing was never taken, the gap is in the collection and not on the appliance: issue the read before concluding anything.
controls.remediation: Where no entitlement is in force, buy and activate the device-identification subscription for this appliance - it is per serial, so an HA pair needs both members. Where the entitlement is in force and no edge-service address is set, set it, and confirm afterwards that records are actually reaching the service: a populated address proves only that the configuration exists, and an address that resolves to nothing commits without complaint. Where the value comes from a Panorama template, set it there, because the next push will otherwise overwrite a local edit. Where the finding reports that the licence listing was never taken, re-run the collection rather than changing anything on the device. And where this estate identifies its unmanaged equipment by some other means entirely, record that decision - this control cannot read it from any configuration and will keep reporting until a person says so.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: No in-force entitlement for the vendor's device-identification service exists on this appliance - the licence listing carries no unexpired row for that feature.

queries.name: Licence listing never taken
queries.short_description: The licence listing was never taken for this appliance, so whether it holds the entitlement is unknown rather than answered - an appliance with nothing licensed and one nobody asked give the same reply.

queries.name: No edge service address configured
queries.short_description: This appliance is pointed at no device-identification edge service, so it sends the service no traffic records and retrieves no device mappings from it.

controls.name: Device-ID Enabled on IoT-Hosting Zones
controls.description:
Requires that device identification is switched on in the zones that carry equipment nobody administers, and that it has not been narrowed away from that equipment afterwards.

TWO HALVES THAT CANNOT BOTH FIRE ON ONE ZONE. The first is about a zone where identification is off. The second is only about narrowing WITHIN a zone where it is on, so the first half's assertion is the second half's qualifying condition, inverted.

THE FIRING STATE OF THE SECOND HALF IS A POPULATED LIST, WHICH IS THE OPPOSITE OF WHAT A REVIEWER LOOKS FOR. With no device address list configured, the zone's Included Networks render as `any` and its Excluded Networks as `none`: identification applies to EVERY address in the zone. That is the most permissive reading and it is the COMPLIANT one here. The state that needs reporting is a list that LIMITS identification to named addresses, because equipment outside the list sits in an identified zone and is not itself identified. An absent list and an empty one are the same state - deleting the last member leaves PAN-OS dropping the container - so there is no third reading.

WHAT THE NARROWING HALF REPORTS IS NARROWING AND NOT A COVERAGE FAILURE. Whether the list still covers the equipment the zone was enabled for cannot be established from any configuration read: a member may be a literal address, a range, an address object or an address GROUP, and nothing on the firewall says what is plugged in. So the finding names the members and asks a reviewer to confirm them against the equipment. It does not claim anything is uncovered.

AN UNREAD LIST REPORTS RATHER THAN PASSING. An address list that was never read is stored as an empty one, and an empty list is exactly the value of a zone that identifies everything - the most compliant state there is. So a zone whose lists nobody collected would have read as correctly configured. A separate arm reports that the scope could not be established, which is a statement about our visibility rather than about the configuration.

THE REMEDIATION MAY BE ONE THIS FIREWALL REFUSES, AND THAT IS THE NORMAL CASE. Nothing stored about a zone records whether it was configured on the firewall or pushed to it from a template, so a finding on a pushed zone names a local zone while the setting can only be changed where it is defined. A reader has to check the source before acting.

AND THE QUESTION THIS CONTROL DOES NOT ASK. Which zones carry equipment nobody administers is not readable from a firewall, and it is deliberately NOT written as a qualifying condition: an unanswered question must leave the finding standing rather than suppress it. So this reports every zone with identification off - 48 of the 50 zones in the environment it was measured against - and the engineer's answer narrows the report rather than the query.
controls.rationale: A zone is where the traffic from unadministered equipment actually arrives, and identification is per zone rather than per device: switched off, nothing in that zone is identified by what it is, so the policy can only name it by address and a reader of the estate's own device reports sees nothing. Narrowing is the subtler failure of the two - the setting reads as on, the screen looks correct, and the equipment the zone was enabled for may be outside the list that was added later.
controls.audit: Network > Zones on the appliance and vsys named in the finding. The grid's Device-ID column shows whether identification is enabled; the zone's own Device-ID tab shows the Included and Excluded Networks. Read an EMPTY Included Networks as `any` rather than as nothing - the grid says so in those words, and it is the compliant state. Then check where the zone is configured: a zone pushed from a Panorama template cannot be edited on the firewall, and nothing in a finding on it can tell you that. Where the finding says the address lists were never read, the gap is in the collection rather than on the appliance.
controls.remediation: Where identification is off on a zone that carries equipment nobody administers, enable it - Network > Zones, the zone's Device-ID tab - and where the zone comes from a Panorama template, enable it in the template, because a local edit will be refused or overwritten. Where identification is narrowed, confirm the member list against what the zone actually carries and widen it, or remove the list entirely to identify everything in the zone; remember that a member may be an address group whose contents moved since somebody wrote it. Where the finding reports that the lists were never read, re-run the collection rather than changing the zone. And where a zone genuinely carries no unadministered equipment, record that: this control cannot read it and will keep reporting the zone until a person says so.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: Device identification is not enabled on this zone, so nothing in it is identified by what the equipment is and the policy can name it only by address.

queries.name: Identification narrowed to a device address list
queries.short_description: Device identification is enabled on this zone and has been limited to a named set of addresses rather than applied to everything in it, so equipment outside that set is in an identified zone and is not identified.

queries.name: Device-ID address lists never read
queries.short_description: Device identification is enabled on this zone and its address lists were never read, so whether it applies to the whole zone or to a narrow set of addresses could not be established.

controls.name: Device Dictionary Current
controls.description:
Requires that the device classification data installed on an appliance is current, so that equipment types the vendor has published can actually be recognised.

WHAT THIS MEASURES IS THE AGE OF WHAT IS INSTALLED, counted from the release date the appliance reports for it. It is NOT the distance behind the release the vendor is currently publishing, because nothing on a firewall carries that. The two coincide only while the vendor publishes continuously: during a quiet period a perfectly current appliance ages into this finding with nobody touching it, and that limit belongs to the measurement rather than to the estate.

GRADED IN TWO BANDS. More than a week behind is reported at the baseline tier - the usual cause is a missed delivery rather than a broken mechanism. More than a quarter behind is reported higher: whole classes of equipment published since then cannot be matched at all, so rules written for them are inert and the estate's own device reports understate what is on the network. Within a week of the current release is acceptable and is not reported, because equipment types published in the last few days are the only ones that can be unrecognised.

AN APPLIANCE THAT REPORTS NO RELEASE DATE IS REPORTED SEPARATELY AND NOT SILENTLY. A row with no computable age passes every staleness threshold that can be written over it, so without a second arm the appliances nobody could measure would read as the freshest in the estate. In the environment this control was measured against, two of four appliances reported no release date at all - and they were the two holding content 167 releases behind their siblings. The graded comparison therefore excludes them deliberately and the second arm reports that their currency could not be established.

TWO INSTRUMENTS DISAGREE ABOUT THIS AND ONLY ONE IS GRADED.
