queries.name: WildFire signatures are retrieved every minute
queries.short_description: Comfortably inside the floor and still short of streaming on a public-service deployment. The residual exposure is a minute, which is the lowest severity above informational this store can express.

controls.name: The GlobalProtect Content Schedules Are In Force And Apply What They Fetch
controls.description:
A firewall that does not retrieve the GlobalProtect data file or the clientless VPN content on a recurring schedule, or that retrieves either and never applies it. Two content types, one control, and one row per appliance.

THE SIGN IS INVERTED ON BOTH HALVES AND THAT CHANGES THE SHAPE OF THE QUERY. Stage 5 states each half as the PASSING condition - a recurrence that is not `none` AND an action that equals download-and-install - so the finding fires on the DISJUNCTION of those failing: no recurring schedule at all, OR a schedule that does not install. The baseline is therefore an `or` group rather than a conjunction, and it is the whole of the data file half.

ONE BASELINE AND THE SECOND HALF CARRIED BY FOUR DISJOINT QUERIES. A control has exactly one baseline, so the data file half is the baseline and the clientless VPN half is expressed as four queries that partition its failing set: no recurring schedule; scheduled but download-only; scheduled but taking no action; and scheduled but never read. They are disjoint by construction - the first excludes the other three on the recurrence column and those three are mutually exclusive equalities on a single-valued action column - and their union IS the half.

NO CADENCE FLOOR ON EITHER HALF, which is why any recurring value passes. Stage 3 names only `on a recurring schedule` for these two content types, so weekly, daily and hourly all pass and the single failing recurrence is `none`. That is a deliberately lower bar than the antivirus and Applications-and-Threats controls carry, and it is why this control's severity is medium rather than high.

THE DATA FILE HAS NO CONTROL ON ANY SCREEN AND THE CLIENTLESS VPN CONTENT DOES, which is the opposite way round from the vendor's own documentation and decides what a remediation can say. Stage 4 measured Device > Dynamic Updates as carrying six groups with NO GlobalProtect data file group at all - in the DOM over the whole document after scrolling, and confirmed in a screenshot - while the clientless VPN content has a group of its own. The vendor's Help inverts it, naming the data file in its opening sentence and never naming the clientless VPN content on that screen. So a remediation for the data file half must point at the API or the CLI, and one for the clientless VPN half can point at a panel.

`none` AND THE EMPTY STRING ARE DIFFERENT ANSWERS AND BOTH FIRE, on both halves - an absence that was read against an absence nobody read.

WHAT THIS CONTROL CANNOT SAY: how far behind the GlobalProtect data file actually is. Every other content type's installed version is readable across the estate in one call; this one has no such key in the reply at all, so a consumer computing content recency estate-wide silently returns nothing for it. That is recorded against the appliance-level control that owns content recency, not here - this control owns the configured cause and not the symptom.
controls.rationale: Both GlobalProtect content types feed decisions made about endpoints connecting from outside the perimeter, and neither is visible on the screens an operator checks after a change - one has no screen group at all. A schedule that never runs, or runs and never installs, leaves that content frozen with nothing on the appliance drawing attention to it.
controls.audit: `show config running` at `deviceconfig/system/update-schedule/global-protect-datafile/recurring` and at `.../global-protect-clientless-vpn/recurring` on the appliance the finding names. The clientless VPN content also has a group on Device > Dynamic Updates; THE DATA FILE HAS NONE, so do not conclude from that screen that the data file is unscheduled. Read the finding for which of the two content types failed and which half - cadence or action.
controls.remediation: Set each GlobalProtect content schedule to any recurring cadence and set its action to download and install. The clientless VPN content can be set on Device > Dynamic Updates; the GlobalProtect data file has no group on that screen and must be set through the API or the CLI. Where a schedule exists and takes no action, the fix is the action alone - the cadence is faultless.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: The GlobalProtect data file has no recurring schedule at all, or its scheduled run does not install what it fetches. An `or` group, because stage 5 states this half as the passing condition and the finding is its negation.

queries.name: The clientless VPN content has no recurring schedule
queries.short_description: No recurrence branch at all, or an explicit `none`: this content is never retrieved automatically. Also the value held by a firewall with no `update-schedule` node.

queries.name: The clientless VPN content is downloaded without being installed
queries.short_description: A recurring schedule exists and its action is `download-only`, so the content is retrieved and never applied.

queries.name: The clientless VPN content schedule takes no action when it runs
queries.short_description: A recurring schedule exists and the in-force branch carries no `action` key at all, which the screen renders as `None`. Read as taking neither action.

queries.name: The clientless VPN content schedule's action could not be read
queries.short_description: A recurrence is present and the action is empty, which is the appliance's `deviceconfig/system` node having come back empty. An unknown fires rather than passing.

controls.name: Malicious URL Categories Blocked
controls.description:
A URL filtering profile that does not refuse all three of the confirmed-hostile categories - command-and-control, malware and phishing - outright. Anything short of the refusal permits a connection to infrastructure that is hostile by definition.

GRADED BY THE WEAKEST ACTION ANY OF THE THREE HOLDS, not by which category is weak. The refusal is the asserted state and compiles to no query at all - a query for it would report the most compliant profile in the estate. The four permitting actions are ranked by what still stands between the user and the site: a password prompt, a warning page, a log entry, or nothing.

THE CRITICAL RANK IS THE STATE AN UNTOUCHED PROFILE IS IN, which is why it is ranked above a logged permit rather than beside it. A predefined category named in none of the profile's member lists resolves to the permit that writes no log entry, measured - so a profile nobody has edited reaches the worst rank on this control, and neither the connection nor the absence of any record of it is visible afterwards.

THE PERMIT SET IS NOT IN THE PROFILE. Which categories a profile refuses is the device's own catalogue of 88-to-90 names MINUS the profile's member lists, so the verdict is computed at normalization and no clause here can be written over a member list.

WHAT IS NOT ASSERTED: the vendor names eleven categories as dangerous enough to refuse and this control asserts three, which is a scope decision taken deliberately upstream. The override password itself is configured per vsys on another screen and no column here holds it, so a profile at the password-prompt rank is ranked on the prompt existing and not on the password being set.

ONE ACTION IS DELIBERATELY UNRANKED AND A PROFILE HOLDING IT STILL REPORTS. The isolation action was ruled out of scope upstream as absent from the vendor's own list and configurable on one platform only. Measured, it is worse than out of scope: a category can be put at isolation by API, the interface then renders it as the bare permit, and no screen shows otherwise. So such a profile fails this control's assertion and is reported at this control's own severity, neither escalated nor softened, and ranking it is a decision for a person rather than a value this catalogue may invent.
controls.rationale: A category that is malicious by definition has no legitimate destination in it, so every session the profile permits there reaches an attacker's infrastructure. Where the action also writes no log entry, the firewall holds no record that the connection happened at all.
controls.audit: Objects > Security Profiles > URL Filtering. Open the profile the finding names, at the scope the finding names, and read the Categories tab: find command-and-control, malware and phishing and read the Site Access column on each. The finding names the weakest of the three. A category that appears in no list at all takes the device's own default for a predefined category, which is the permit - so read the three rows explicitly rather than looking for them among the entries somebody added.
controls.remediation: Set Site Access to the refusal on command-and-control, malware and phishing in the profile the finding names. Where the profile is pushed from a management station, change it at the scope it is defined at rather than overriding it on the firewall. A category left at the isolation action must be changed too: the interface renders it as the bare permit and it is not a restriction.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: URL filtering profiles that do not refuse all three confirmed-hostile categories.

queries.name: Hostile categories permitted behind a password prompt
queries.short_description: The weakest action on a confirmed-hostile category permits the session once a password is given.

queries.name: Hostile categories permitted behind a warning page
queries.short_description: The weakest action on a confirmed-hostile category permits the session once the user dismisses a warning page.

queries.name: Hostile categories permitted and logged
queries.short_description: The weakest action on a confirmed-hostile category permits the session in full and writes a log entry, so the only product is a record.

queries.name: Hostile categories permitted with no log entry
queries.short_description: The weakest action on a confirmed-hostile category permits the session and writes no log entry. This is the state an unedited profile is in.

controls.name: No URL Category Reachable Without Logging
controls.description:
A URL filtering profile that leaves at least one category reachable and unlogged. The permit that writes no log entry and the permit that logs behave identically for the user and differently for everyone investigating afterwards, so a permitted category should be at the logging action or stronger.

GRADED BY THE WORST CATEGORY LEFT UNLOGGED, over the device's own catalogue minus the three categories the hostile-category control owns. A refused category is not reachable; a custom category at the inert action matches nothing and is not reachable either.

SIX OF THE CATALOGUE'S NAMES ARE PLACED AND THE REST TAKE THIS CONTROL'S OWN SEVERITY. The member set is the device's catalogue of 88-to-90 names, moving with the content release, so placing all of them would write one release's content into a contract. An unplaced category is returned as the device gave it and matches no rank query, which is what makes this control's own severity the right answer for it.

THE ISOLATION ACTION COUNTS AS UNLOGGED HERE, and that is a measurement rather than a reading of the vendor's table: the interface renders an isolated category as the bare permit and no screen shows otherwise, so it cannot be treated as a restriction.

WHAT IS NOT ASSERTED: the lookup timeout, and whether a request is held while the lookup runs, are device-wide settings that no column of this subject holds. The category this control reports as worst is the worst one left unlogged and not necessarily the one carrying the most traffic.
controls.rationale: Web activity that is permitted and unlogged cannot be reconstructed, so an investigation into a compromise reaches the firewall and finds no record that the session took place. The firewall's own logs are usually the only place that record would have existed.
controls.audit: Objects > Security Profiles > URL Filtering. Open the profile the finding names and read the Site Access column across the Categories tab: the finding names the worst category left at a permit that writes no log entry. Categories in no member list take the device's own default for a predefined category, so the unlogged set is usually larger than the entries somebody added.
controls.remediation: Move every permitted category to the logging action or stronger in the profile the finding names, which permits the session exactly as before and writes a log entry. Where the finding names a category the organisation means to refuse outright, refuse it instead.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: URL filtering profiles leaving at least one category reachable with no log entry written.

queries.name: A closely-associated-with-malicious category is unlogged
queries.short_description: The worst unlogged category is the tier the vendor describes as not confirmed malicious but closely associated with malicious sites.

queries.name: An uncategorised category is unlogged
queries.short_description: The worst unlogged category is the one the URL database cannot categorise at all, which is the broadest unlogged route a profile can leave open.

queries.name: A medium-risk category is unlogged
queries.short_description: The worst unlogged category is the tier the vendor pairs with high-risk in the same instruction, with the same remedies named.

queries.name: A newly-registered-domain category is unlogged
queries.short_description: The worst unlogged category is the one that exists because throwaway infrastructure is new, so this is an unlogged permit to the domains with no history.

queries.name: A category whose lookup did not resolve is unlogged
queries.short_description: The worst unlogged category is where a lookup lands when it times out, so the record of every site the firewall could not classify in time is lost.

queries.name: A benign category is unlogged
queries.short_description: The worst unlogged category is the benign tier. Still unlogged, which is this control's point, but the least of these.

queries.name: The category population behind this verdict was never established
queries.short_description: The device's own category catalogue was not read for this profile's appliance and scope, so the denominator this verdict is computed against was never established.

controls.name: Credential Phishing Prevention Enabled
controls.description:
A URL filtering profile that does not stop a corporate credential being submitted to an external site. TWO WAYS TO FAIL AND THE QUERIES KEEP THEM APART, because the remediation differs: a profile with no detection method at all detects nothing, and a profile with a method but no per-category decision detects and permits.

THE TWO HALVES ARE MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE BY CONSTRUCTION, which is what makes reporting both from one control safe. The first applies only where no detection method is selected and the second only where one is, so no profile is reported twice and no profile falls between them. The detection mode materialises the disabled value on a committed profile carrying no credential node at all - measured on three appliances across two major versions - which is what makes the first half reachable from the configuration rather than from an absence.

GRADED BY THE WORST CATEGORY THAT WILL STILL ACCEPT A CREDENTIAL, over the categories the profile permits. Three of the catalogue's names are placed and the rest take this control's own severity, for the same reason as the unlogged-category control: the member set is the device's own catalogue and moves with the content release.

A CATEGORY THE PROFILE REFUSES IS NOT IN THIS SET AT ALL. The device refuses its credentials automatically, so whether it is in the credential list says nothing about this control and everything about the hostile-category one.

WHAT IS NOT ASSERTED, AND IT IS THE LARGEST GAP ON THIS CONTROL: whether the firewall decrypts the traffic a detection method would have to inspect. The vendor states credentials cannot be monitored in traffic the firewall does not decrypt, so a profile with a method selected on a firewall that decrypts nothing detects nothing - and this control reports it as compliant with its first half. No column of this subject holds that fact.
controls.rationale: Credential harvesting works by collecting a password that is still valid everywhere else, so the damage is done at submission and not at the visit. A profile that detects the submission and permits it anyway records the theft without preventing it.
controls.audit: Objects > Security Profiles > URL Filtering, then the URL Filtering Settings tab for the detection method and the Categories tab for the User Credential Submission column. Where the finding says no method is selected, the Mode control reads as disabled. Where it names a category, read that category's User Credential Submission column: the finding names the worst one that will still accept a credential.
controls.remediation: Select a credential detection method appropriate to the deployment, then set User Credential Submission to the refusal on every category the profile permits - starting with the uncategorised and high-risk tiers, which the vendor names specifically. Confirm the firewall decrypts the traffic the method has to inspect, because neither setting has any effect on traffic that is not decrypted.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: Profiles with a credential detection method that still permit a corporate credential on at least one category they allow.

queries.name: No corporate credential detection method is selected
queries.short_description: The profile selects no credential detection method at all, so no credential submission is detected and no per-category decision can take effect.

queries.name: An uncategorised category accepts corporate credentials
queries.short_description: The worst category still accepting a corporate credential is the one the URL database cannot categorise, where a new phishing page lands before anyone classifies it.

queries.name: A closely-associated-with-malicious category accepts corporate credentials
queries.short_description: The worst category still accepting a corporate credential is the tier the vendor instructs the reader to refuse credentials on, in two separate places.

queries.name: A medium-risk category accepts corporate credentials
queries.short_description: The worst category still accepting a corporate credential is the tier the vendor names in the same instruction as high-risk, in both places.

queries.name: The category population behind this verdict was never established
queries.short_description: The device's own category catalogue was not read for this profile's appliance and scope, so this verdict rests on a population nobody established.

controls.name: HTTP Header Logging Enabled
controls.description:
A URL filtering profile that does not record all three of the request headers the device offers at this object. The headers are what turn a URL log line into something an investigator can reconstruct an incident from.

GRADED BY THE WORST HEADER LEFT UNRECORDED, and the whole set is placed: the device offers these three and no more at this object on every platform read. The forwarded-for header is ranked above the other two because it is the only one that recovers the originating address where a proxy or a source translation has replaced it, so losing it loses attribution rather than context.

THIS IS THE ONE VERDICT ON THIS SUBJECT THAT NEEDS NO CATEGORY CATALOGUE. Its three inputs are the profile's own keys and are never unknown, so unlike every other control over this object it is answered on every row and has no companion question about whether the population behind it was established.

TWO OF THE THREE DEFAULTS ARE INFERENCES AND THE FINDING SAYS SO. The referring-page and forwarded-for keys rest on an assumed default rather than a measured one, so a profile that carries neither key is reported on an inference about what their absence means. One write per key settles it.

WHAT IS NOT ASSERTED: a later major release replaces these three with a different field set, so this control's derivation is not established there and a grading over values a release does not have would read as coverage it does not have.
controls.rationale: A URL log line without the client identification says a request happened and not who made it or what sent them. Behind a proxy or a source translation the forwarded-for header is the only record of the originating address, so without it every session in the estate attributes to the proxy.
controls.audit: Objects > Security Profiles > URL Filtering > URL Filtering Settings, in the HTTP Header Logging section. Open the profile the finding names and read the three checkboxes; the finding names the worst one left clear. A profile carrying none of the three keys shows all three clear.
controls.remediation: Enable all three HTTP header logging options on the profile the finding names. None of the three changes what the firewall permits or refuses - they change only what the log line carries - so the change is safe to make on a profile already in production.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: URL filtering profiles that do not record all three HTTP request headers.

queries.name: The forwarded-for header is not recorded
queries.short_description: The worst unrecorded header is the one that recovers the originating address where a proxy or source translation has replaced it, so losing it loses attribution.

queries.name: The client software header is not recorded
queries.short_description: The worst unrecorded header identifies the client software, which is how an investigator separates a person driving a browser from an automated client using the same credentials.

queries.name: The referring page header is not recorded
queries.short_description: The worst unrecorded header names the page that sent the user, which is the link between the delivery of a phishing message and the visit it produced.

controls.name: Advanced URL Filtering Inline Categorization Enabled
controls.description:
A URL filtering profile that does not have real-time page analysis working on every site it permits. THREE WAYS TO FAIL AND THEY ARE INDEPENDENT, so a profile can fail any one alone: the cloud-side engine is off, the on-box engine is off, or a list of custom categories is exempted from analysis altogether.

GRADED BY THE BROADEST EXEMPTION IN FORCE. An exemption that targets sites by category membership is ranked above one that lists them, because its reach grows whenever the URL database reclassifies a site into the combination rather than only when somebody edits a list. Which kind an exemption is cannot be seen in the profile at all - only the custom category's own stored type says - which is why this is a stored conclusion and not a clause over the exemption list.

A PASSING ROW DOES NOT MEAN ANALYSIS IS HAPPENING, and this is the claim a reader must not take from this control. The cloud-side engine is gated on both a subscription and a device certificate, and no appliance in the lab this control was built against held both: the licensed appliance had no device certificate and the appliance holding the only certificate had neither the licence nor an unexpired certificate. So the cloud setting being on means configured and never means working.

THE ON-BOX HALF OVER-REPORTS ON ONE PLATFORM FAMILY AND THE FINDING SAYS WHICH. An absent on-box key means the engine is ON on one platform family and OFF on another, measured on both, and the stored verdict takes the reporting direction - so that half is a false positive on every profile of the first family that stores nothing. The column recording that doubt is true on exactly those rows and is presented beside the finding. A finding raised on a healthy appliance is checkable in a minute; the alternative would report an engine as running on an appliance whose own interface says it is off.

WHAT IS NOT ASSERTED: the device-wide setting that widens a listed exemption by trailing token, and whether an external dynamic list can appear at the exemption field at all - the device offered no such name there on any build read, so it has no rank here rather than a guessed one.
controls.rationale: Real-time analysis is what catches a phishing kit or a cloaked page in the window before the URL database has categorised it, which is exactly the window an attacker uses. An exemption removes that protection for the sites it covers, and a category-matching exemption removes it for sites nobody listed.
controls.audit: Objects > Security Profiles > URL Filtering > URL Filtering Settings for the two inline categorization checkboxes, and the same tab's inline-analysis exemption list for the exemptions. Where the finding names an exemption, read the stored type of each custom category it names at Objects > Custom Objects > URL Category: the member list of the profile does not show which kind it is. Check the subscription and the device certificate before concluding the cloud-side engine is working.
controls.remediation: Enable both inline categorization options on the profile the finding names, and remove the inline-analysis exemptions the finding names unless each is still justified. Where an exemption must stay, prefer one that lists the sites over one that matches on category membership, whose reach changes without anyone editing it. For the cloud-side engine, confirm the subscription is licensed and the device certificate is installed and unexpired.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: URL filtering profiles exempting at least one custom category from real-time page analysis.

queries.name: An exemption matches on category membership
queries.short_description: The broadest exemption in force targets sites by category membership, so its reach grows as the URL database reclassifies sites into the combination.

queries.name: An exemption lists the sites it covers
queries.short_description: The broadest exemption in force covers the entries it holds, so its reach is what somebody typed - auditable, and still an exemption.

queries.name: Cloud-side inline categorization is switched off
queries.short_description: The profile does not send never-before-seen URLs for cloud-side real-time analysis, so a page is categorised only once the URL database has seen it.

queries.name: On-box inline categorization is switched off
queries.short_description: The profile does not run the on-box real-time analysis engine. Where the key is absent this reading depends on the platform family, and the column recording that doubt is presented beside the finding.

queries.name: The exemption list behind this verdict was never read
queries.short_description: This profile's inline-analysis exemption list was not read and counted, so the count beside it is a migration default rather than a reading and an exemption would not be reported.

controls.name: Unused Custom URL Categories (Hygiene)
controls.description:
A custom URL category that nothing this assessment read points at. An object nobody references is a permissive configuration already written, already reviewed and no longer watched, so putting it into service later is one edit that grants an exception nobody re-approves.

A LIST OF CANDIDATES FOR REVIEW AND NEVER A REMOVAL INSTRUCTION, and that bound is part of the control rather than a caveat on it. Every error this reading makes is in the direction of calling a live object unreferenced: the vendor documents four rulebases that can match on a URL category and this assessment reads two of them. The surfaces actually searched are recorded on every finding so that the word unreferenced is never printed without its denominator.

GRADED BY WHAT KIND OF OBJECT IS LEFT UNREFERENCED, read from the category's own stored type. A category that matches on category membership is a readier instrument than a list of named sites, because it needs no entries added to it to have reach. Measured, and it narrows the claim: such a category targets the INTERSECTION of the categories it names rather than their union, so it cannot wrap a whole predefined category and the indirect route is narrower than it first appears.

THERE IS NO ACCEPTABLE VALUE OF THE GRADED FIELD, because the passing state is that the object is referenced or deliberately kept, which is not a value either field holds. So every category this control reports is reported, and the rank says how much reach it already has.

THE UNDER-REPORTING HAZARD IS NOT AT THE ROW LEVEL AND NO COLUMN CAN CARRY IT. Absence is this object's passing answer - no category, nothing to clean up - and on every appliance this control was built against the firewall's own container was absent while the live categories were in force through the pushed view. So an assessment that does not read the pushed view reports zero rows here and reads as a clean estate.

THE PROFILE HALF OF THIS CONTROL IS NOT BUILT, and a reader comparing this entry with the control's own description should know why rather than assume an omission. The unreferenced URL filtering PROFILE is the other object the control's description names, it lives on a different model, and the two models have no relation in either direction - the only paths run through shared ancestors, every one to-many and every one leaving a scope field unconstrained, which would attach a finding to the wrong row. A control id targets one model, so this entry is the category half. The profile half is recorded as unbuilt rather than quietly dropped, and the grading is why this half is the one that ships: the rank is read from a category's stored type and a profile carries no such field, so the profile half could never report above this control's own severity.
controls.rationale: A permissive object nothing uses is an exception that has already been written and approved and that nobody is watching, so putting it into service is one edit rather than a request. A category that matches on membership is worse: its reach grows as the URL database reclassifies sites, with no edit at all.
controls.audit: Objects > Custom Objects > URL Category, at the scope the finding names. Read the category's Type column for the rank the finding gives it, then search the configuration for its name before acting: this assessment reads the security rulebase and the profile action lists, and the vendor documents two further rulebases that can match on a URL category. The finding records which surfaces were searched.
controls.remediation: Confirm the category is genuinely unused - including in the rulebases this assessment does not read - and then either remove it or record why it is kept. To remove one, set it to the inert action in every profile that names it first: the vendor documents that as the precondition for deleting it. Do not delete one on the strength of this finding alone; a category in use by a rulebase this assessment did not read reads exactly the same way.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: Custom URL categories that nothing this assessment read points at.

queries.name: An unreferenced category matches on category membership
queries.short_description: The unreferenced category targets sites by category membership, so it is a prepared way to act on predefined categories and its reach grows as the database reclassifies sites.

queries.name: An unreferenced category lists the sites it covers
queries.short_description: The unreferenced category reaches only the entries it holds, so it is as broad as whoever last typed into it and no broader.

controls.name: User-ID Enabled Only on Trusted Internal Zones
controls.description:
Requires that User-ID is switched on only in zones carrying the organisation's own user populations, and is off in every zone carrying traffic from a network the customer does not control.

WHAT THE SWITCH DOES AND WHY ITS DIRECTION IS THE FINDING. With User-ID enabled on a zone, the firewall maps usernames to the addresses it sees there and those mappings become names in policy, in the traffic log and in every report that reads from them. On an untrusted or Internet-facing zone that leaks internal identity outward and can be probed to enumerate it. So the state this control reports is the switch being ON, which is the opposite direction from the Device-ID control over the same object.

THE QUESTION THIS CONTROL DOES NOT ASK. Which side of the firewall a zone faces is not readable from a firewall, and it is deliberately NOT written as a qualifying condition: an unanswered question must leave the finding standing rather than suppress it. So this reports every zone with the switch on, and the engineer's answer narrows the report rather than the query.

THE PER-ZONE ADDRESS LISTS ARE CONTEXT AND NOT JUDGED HERE. A zone carries its own User-ID include and exclude lists, and the finding prints them, but what bounds User-ID discovery for a vsys is a different object with its own control. Both are JSON columns reachable from no query in this language, so neither is clausued.

THE REMEDIATION MAY BE ONE THIS FIREWALL REFUSES, AND THAT IS THE NORMAL CASE. Nothing stored about a zone records whether it was configured on the firewall or pushed to it from a template, so a finding on a pushed zone names a local zone while the switch can only be changed where the zone is defined.
controls.rationale: Identity is only as trustworthy as the zone it was learned in. A username-to-address mapping gathered on a zone the customer does not control is an attacker-supplied fact that the policy then enforces on and the log then attributes traffic to, and the same switch that gathers it is what makes the zone probeable for identity data. Switching it off on those zones costs nothing, because no user population lives there.
controls.audit: Network > Zones on the appliance and vsys named in the finding. The grid's User Identification column shows whether the switch is on; the zone's own tab shows the User-ID Include and Exclude address lists. Confirm against the site's addressing which zones carry the organisation's own user populations - that is the judgement this control cannot make and does not claim to have made.
controls.remediation: Where User-ID is on in a zone that carries traffic from a network the customer does not control, switch it off - Network > Zones, the zone's User Identification setting. Where the zone comes from a Panorama template, change it in the template, because a local edit will be refused or overwritten. Where the zone does carry the organisation's own users, leave the switch on and bound what it discovers, which is the discovery include/exclude list on that vsys and is a separate control.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: User-ID is enabled on this zone, so the firewall maps usernames to the addresses it sees here and those mappings reach policy, the traffic log and every report reading from them.

controls.name: User-ID Include/Exclude Networks Scoped
controls.description:
Requires that the User-ID discovery include/exclude list bounds which subnets the collector will map, so that guest, server and external ranges are not mapped even where a zone is misconfigured.

THE SUBJECT IS A VERDICT OVER THE WHOLE LIST AND THE COMMONEST FAILURE IS AN EMPTY ONE. A collector with no in-force entry performs discovery in ALL subnetworks, so every address reachable through a monitored server is eligible to become a named user in policy and in the log. A control keyed on a list ENTRY would have had nothing to report in exactly that case, so the row is one per vsys and the conclusion is a stored shape.

FOUR SHAPES, THREE DIFFERENT FAULTS, AND THE RANKS ARE NOT ORDERED THE WAY A READER EXPECTS. An in-force include list is the acceptable state and raises nothing. No in-force entry is the vendor default and the baseline failure. An EXCLUDE-ONLY list is the opposite fault and is graded BELOW the baseline: an exclude-only list excludes every subnetwork rather than only the ones it names, so user mapping stops entirely and identity enforcement matches nobody rather than the wrong body - a functional fault rather than an exposure. An include entry naming a PUBLIC range is graded ABOVE the baseline, because the collector excludes public addresses from probing by default and naming a public subnetwork with Discovery set to Include is what re-enables credentialed probing of it.

AN UNCOLLECTED LIST REPORTS RATHER THAN PASSING, which is the opposite of what an unknown normally does. This control's assertion is inverted - it fires on every shape that is not an in-force include list - and a vsys whose list was never read carries no shape at all, which is not an in-force include list either. So it is reported, and the finding says that the bound could not be established rather than describing a shape nobody saw.

WHAT THIS CONTROL CANNOT SAY. Whether an include list that exists bounds discovery to the RIGHT subnets is site-specific, and nothing on the firewall says which subnets carry the organisation's user population. An in-force include list therefore passes, and the finding prints its members for a reviewer to confirm against the site's addressing.
controls.rationale: The zone switch decides where identity is gathered and this list decides which addresses within reach are eligible at all, so it is the second and independent bound on how much identity the firewall invents. Unbounded, it maps guest and server ranges as though they were user populations and aims credentialed probes at whatever a monitored server can reach. The two failures at the ends of the scale are opposite in effect, which is why they do not share a severity.
controls.audit: Device > User Identification > User Mapping, the Include/Exclude Networks tab on the vsys named in the finding. Read an entry carrying Disabled as ABSENT - a disabled entry bounds nothing, and the finding counts in-force entries only. Check whether any included range is publicly routable, which is the state graded above the baseline, and whether the list holds excludes with no include, which stops mapping altogether.
controls.remediation: Add an explicit include list naming the subnets that carry the organisation's own user populations, so everything else is implicitly excluded, and remove any publicly routable range from it. Where the list holds excludes and no include, add the include entries: shortening the exclude list will not restore mapping, because an exclude-only list excludes every subnetwork. Where the finding says the bound could not be established, the configuration was not collected and the remedy is a collection one rather than a device change.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: The discovery include/exclude list on this vsys is not an in-force include list, so nothing bounds which subnets the collector may map - the empty, exclude-only and public-range shapes and an unread list all report here.

queries.name: No in-force include or exclude entry
queries.short_description: No in-force entry bounds discovery on this vsys, which is the vendor default: the collector performs discovery in all subnetworks, so every address reachable through a monitored server may become a named user.

queries.name: Exclude entries only, which stops user mapping entirely
queries.short_description: This list holds excludes and no include. An exclude-only list excludes every subnetwork rather than only those named, so the collector maps nobody and identity-based policy on this vsys matches nobody.

queries.name: An include entry names a public address range
queries.short_description: An include entry on this vsys names a publicly routable range, which re-enables credentialed probing of it: the collector excludes public addresses by default and naming one with Discovery set to Include is what turns that off.

controls.name: WMI Client Probing Disabled
controls.description:
Requires that WMI/NetBIOS client probing is switched off on the PAN-OS integrated User-ID agent.

WHAT PROBING DOES. With probing on, the agent sends its own credentials to endpoints to ask who is logged in. Anyone positioned on a probed segment can capture and relay those credentials, which is a documented lateral-movement primitive rather than a theoretical exposure, and the vendor itself recommends disabling the feature.

THE SEVERITY IS ABOUT THE CREDENTIAL AND NOT ABOUT THE MAPPING. What this control reports is not that identity data is imprecise; it is that the firewall is distributing an authenticated service account's credentials onto every segment it probes. Identity sourced from GlobalProtect, the Cloud Identity Engine or authentication logs needs no probe and carries no credential onto the probed segment.

A SECOND HALF OF THIS ASSERTION IS NOT A CONFIGURATION QUESTION. Whether the environment has an alternative identity source in place, so that probing can be switched off without losing coverage, is the engineer's answer rather than a stored value, and it decides how the finding is reported rather than whether it fires.

AN ABSENT SETTINGS NODE IS NOT A PASS AND IS NOT REPORTED EITHER. The agent settings node does not exist on an unconfigured vsys; the row carries the vendor implicit, which has probing off, so a vsys that configures nothing passes. A vsys whose configuration was never collected has no row at all and is reported by nothing, which is a collection question rather than a compliance one.
controls.rationale: Every other User-ID weakness costs accuracy. This one hands out credentials. The agent authenticates as a directory account in order to read who is logged in, and probing is the one feature that takes that account's credentials off the firewall and onto an arbitrary endpoint, where an attacker who controls or merely observes the endpoint can relay them. That is why it is graded above the rest of this domain.
controls.audit: Device > User Identification > User Mapping, the Palo Alto Networks User-ID Agent Setup dialog on the vsys named in the finding, Client Probing tab. Confirm Enable Probing is unticked. Where it is ticked, establish what identity sources the site has besides probing before planning the change, because switching it off without one loses mappings.
controls.remediation: Untick Enable Probing - Device > User Identification > User Mapping, the agent setup dialog on the vsys named, Client Probing tab - and commit. Where probing is the site's only identity source, put an alternative in place first: GlobalProtect, the Cloud Identity Engine, or server monitoring reading the security logs, none of which puts the agent's credentials on a probed segment.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: WMI/NetBIOS client probing is enabled on this vsys, so the User-ID agent sends its own credentials to endpoints and anyone on a probed segment can capture and relay them.

controls.name: User-ID Service Account Least Privilege
controls.description:
Requires that the directory account the firewall uses for server monitoring is a minimal-rights service account: event-log reader rights and no more, no domain or enterprise admin, no interactive logon.

WHAT THIS CONTROL CAN AND CANNOT ESTABLISH, which is the whole of how to read its findings. The firewall stores the principal it authenticates as and NOTHING about the rights that principal holds, because group memberships live in the directory. So the configuration half of this assertion is that a directory account IS configured for server monitoring, and the finding names it for a reviewer to check directory-side. It does not claim the account is over-privileged, and a finding here is a prompt to verify rather than a defect in itself.

THE SECOND HALF IS THE PRIVILEGE THAT MAKES THE RIGHTS MATTER. Session reading enumerates user sessions on the monitored servers rather than only reading their security logs, which needs more of the account than log reading does. It is reported at the same severity because it is the same exposure read from the other end: an account with wide rights matters most where the firewall is using them.

THE DIRECTORY-SIDE VERIFICATION IS NOT A CONFIGURATION READ AND IS NOT OPTIONAL. Whether the account is a domain admin, whether its password is rotated and whether interactive logon is denied are answers from the directory, not from the firewall, and this control exists to put the question in front of somebody who can answer it.
controls.rationale: Server monitoring is the identity source the vendor recommends in place of probing, and it works by authenticating to every monitored server as one account. That account is therefore a credential with reach across the estate's servers, held on a network device, and used continuously. Event-log reader rights are sufficient for what it does; anything more converts a monitoring integration into a standing lateral-movement path, and nothing on the firewall will ever report that it happened.
controls.audit: Device > User Identification > User Mapping, the Palo Alto Networks User-ID Agent Setup dialog on the vsys named in the finding, Server Monitor Account tab, which shows the configured principal. Then verify the account IN THE DIRECTORY: group memberships, interactive and remote-desktop logon rights, and password rotation. The firewall cannot answer any of those. The WMI Authentication and Server Monitor tabs show whether session reading is enabled.
controls.remediation: Replace a privileged principal with a dedicated minimal-rights account - a group-managed service account or a vaulted account with Event Log Readers membership only - and deny it interactive and remote-desktop logon. Where session reading is enabled and the site does not need session enumeration, switch it off and leave security-log reading in place, which needs less of the account.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: A directory account is configured for server monitoring on this vsys. The firewall stores the principal and nothing about its rights, so the account is named here for directory-side verification rather than reported as over-privileged.

queries.name: Session reading enabled on the monitored servers
queries.short_description: Session reading is enabled on this vsys, so the firewall enumerates user sessions on the monitored servers rather than only reading their security logs - the privilege that makes the service account's rights matter.

controls.name: Syslog User Mapping from Authenticated Senders Only
controls.description:
Requires that no management surface permits the unauthenticated UDP syslog identity listener.

WHAT THE LISTENER IS. Syslog-based identity mapping accepts username-to-address bindings from external systems. The UDP listener is connectionless and unauthenticated, so anyone who can reach the port can forge identity mappings and impersonate users in policy. The vendor's own guidance is explicit that a sender list is not a defence here, because the source address can be spoofed, and that SSL should always be used instead.

TWO SURFACES, ONE ASSERTION. A management plane - the MGT port and, on the platforms that have them, the auxiliary ports - carries the listener as a negated switch under the device's own service node. A traffic-carrying interface carries it through an interface management profile bound to it. Those are opposite key polarities over the same fact, and the stored column resolves both, so one assertion spells both halves and the finding names whichever surface it found.

A PROFILE BOUND TO NOTHING PERMITS NOTHING, which is why the dataplane half reports surfaces rather than profiles. A row for a traffic-carrying interface exists only because a profile is bound to it, so a profile that is merely defined produces no row and raises nothing.

AN UNCOLLECTED SURFACE READS AS COMPLIANT UNLESS SOMETHING ASKS, so something does. An absent service record matches no membership test and SQL drops the row, which means a surface nobody collected would pass the listener question silently. A second query reports that the listener state could not be established, and it fires on the measured case: auxiliary planes whose service node exists with the listener keys absent, where the project's own read does not cover them.

WHAT THIS CONTROL DOES NOT JUDGE. Whether the segment a management plane sits on is dedicated to management and reachable only by administrative hosts is not readable from the firewall; it decides how the finding is reported rather than whether it fires. The permitted-source list on these same surfaces is a separate control, so a surface with the listener up and no source restriction appears in both. The encrypted listener's own protocol floor, and the per-sender transport each configured sender uses, are also not judged here - the second is a different object that this control cannot reach.
controls.rationale: Every other control in this domain bounds identity the firewall gathers for itself. This one is about identity the firewall ACCEPTS from elsewhere, with no authentication on the path. A forged mapping is not a gap in coverage; it is an attacker choosing which username the firewall attributes their traffic to, which turns identity-based policy from a control into an instrument. The listener is also not an administrative service, so the control that reports administrative exposure on these surfaces deliberately does not cover it, and the judgement was unowned until this control.
controls.audit: For a management plane: Device > Setup > Management, the Management Interface Settings services list on the appliance named in the finding, and the same list on each auxiliary interface the platform has. For a traffic-carrying interface: Network > Network Profiles > Interface Mgmt, the profile named in the finding, and Network > Interfaces to see what it is bound to. Where the finding says the listener state could not be established, the service node for that plane was not covered by the read rather than found permissive.
controls.remediation: Disable the UDP syslog listener on the surface named - for a management plane, untick the User-ID syslog listener (UDP) service; for a traffic-carrying interface, untick it in the bound interface management profile, or unbind the profile where the interface does not need it. Where syslog identity mapping is needed, enable the SSL listener instead and give it a certificate profile, which is the vendor's own instruction. Leave it enabled only on the interface the firewall collects mappings on, and restrict the permitted sources on that surface.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: A management plane on this appliance permits the unauthenticated UDP syslog identity listener, so anyone able to reach the port can forge username-to-address bindings and impersonate users in policy.

queries.name: A traffic-carrying interface permits the listener
queries.short_description: An interface management profile bound to a traffic-carrying interface permits the unauthenticated UDP syslog identity listener, so the forgery path is reachable from the traffic side rather than only from the management network.

queries.name: Listener state on a management plane could not be established
queries.short_description: The User-ID listener state of a management plane on this appliance was never established, so its listener question is unanswered rather than answered compliant - the measured case is an auxiliary plane the read does not cover.

queries.name: Listener state on a traffic-carrying interface could not be established
queries.short_description: The User-ID listener state of a traffic-carrying surface was never established. This should match nothing, so a row here means the bound profile's service node was not collected, which is a collection fault rather than a device setting.

controls.name: User Mapping Timeout Bounded
controls.description:
Requires that IP-to-user mappings expire, and that the lifetime they expire after is bounded.

TWO HALVES THAT CANNOT BOTH FIRE ON ONE ROW, and the first is the worse of them. The first half is about expiry being switched off, so a mapping never expires at all. The second is only about the lifetime WITHIN a vsys where expiry is in force, so the first half's assertion is the second half's qualifying condition, inverted.

A STORED TIMEOUT VALUE BESIDE EXPIRY SWITCHED OFF IS NOT A MITIGATION, and it is the thing most likely to mislead a reader of the row. The lifetime column holds a number whether or not expiry is on, so a vsys with expiry off and a thirty-minute lifetime stored looks bounded and is not: the value is inert. The finding states the value and says so.

THE NEVER-EXPIRE STATE IS NOT A ZERO. The shape of a timeout field invites reading zero as the never-expire value and it is not that: the device refuses zero at the write gate, so no stored row can hold it. Never-expire is the sibling switch being off, which is this control's first half.

WHY THE SECOND HALF REPORTS BELOW THE FIRST. Expiry switched off means identity never stops being attributed. A lifetime above the bound means identity outlives the lease that justified it by some margin, which is a degree of the same harm rather than the whole of it. The band is graded as one rank deliberately: a day-long mapping and a sixty-one-minute one differ in degree, and splitting them would be a decision about the control taken where nobody is reviewing the control.
controls.rationale: An IP-to-user mapping is a claim that an address belongs to a person, and DHCP makes that claim expire whether the firewall agrees or not. A mapping that outlives its lease attributes one person's traffic to another in policy and in the audit trail, so the failure is not that enforcement stops - it is that enforcement and logging keep working confidently on a fact that stopped being true. That makes it a data-integrity problem in the record the customer will later rely on.
controls.audit: Device > User Identification > User Mapping, the Palo Alto Networks User-ID Agent Setup dialog on the vsys named in the finding, Cache tab. Confirm Enable User Identification Timeout is ticked and read the timeout beside it. Where the finding reports expiry off, read the stored timeout as inert rather than as the effective lifetime. Compare the lifetime against the site's DHCP lease time rather than against the default.
controls.remediation: Tick Enable User Identification Timeout where it is off - Device > User Identification > User Mapping, the agent setup dialog on the vsys named, Cache tab - and set the timeout to sixty minutes or less. Where expiry is already in force and the lifetime is above the bound, reduce it; tuning it to the site's typical DHCP lease time, rather than to the bound, is what keeps identity accurate.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: IP-to-user mapping expiry is switched off on this vsys, so a mapping never expires and traffic keeps being attributed to a user after DHCP has reassigned the address. Any stored timeout beside it is inert.

queries.name: Mapping lifetime above the bound
queries.short_description: Mappings on this vsys expire, but only after more than sixty minutes, so identity outlives the DHCP lease that justified it by a margin nobody at the site has justified.

controls.name: Decryption Profile Protocol Version Range
controls.description:
A decryption profile that lets the sessions it governs negotiate a protocol version below TLS 1.2, or that caps them below the newest version the appliance implements.

TWO ASSERTIONS OVER ONE OBJECT, AND THE CEILING IS THE ONE A READER DOES NOT EXPECT. The floor half is the familiar one: a deprecated protocol version left negotiable makes the firewall's own decryption path the weakest link on the connection, so an attacker who can influence the handshake gets a session whose confidentiality is broken by published attacks while the traffic still reads, to the user and in the logs, as protected and inspected. The ceiling half reports the opposite shape: a cap below what both ends support discards the newer protocol's protections on every session the profile touches, and a cap set below the same profile's own floor leaves the two settings contradicting each other, so whichever one the firewall honours is not the one the configuration appears to state and nobody reviewing it can tell which.

THE TWO LEAVES DO NOT SHARE A VALUE SET AND NEITHER IS COMPARED AS A STRING. The floor offers five members and the ceiling six, the extra one being the literal that means no maximum - which the device refuses at the floor outright. Lexicographic order happens to be right for the floor and is INVERTED for the ceiling, where that literal sorts first while meaning the strongest setting available, so the assertion rests on two stored verdicts and each rank is an equality on one member.

THE CEILING IS RESOLVED BEFORE IT IS JUDGED. Two appliances storing the no-maximum literal can negotiate different ceilings, and an appliance upgraded between two collections changes what that literal means without the stored value moving - so the verdict is computed against the version that appliance's own build implements, and a build the resolution does not cover leaves the verdict firing rather than passing.

WHY A WEAKER PROFILE IS NOT AUTOMATICALLY A FINDING. The vendor recommends applying a separate, weaker profile by rule to the specific destinations that demonstrably require it, so a control asserting the floor over every profile unconditionally would report the vendor's own remediation. The floor half therefore applies only where no decryption rule naming the profile narrows its destination to a named set. Which destinations the business actually requires is not in the configuration and is an engineer's answer.

THE CEILING HALF CARRIES NO SUCH EXCEPTION, deliberately: the vendor's one named reason for a capped ceiling is certificate-pinned mobile applications, which nothing on the firewall records, so that exception is graded rather than claused - a ceiling of TLS 1.2 reports at LOW while a ceiling below the asserted floor reports at HIGH.
controls.rationale: Both halves are invisible on the session record. A session negotiated down to TLS 1.0 and a session negotiated at TLS 1.3 are both logged as decrypted and inspected, and an assessor reading the policy cannot see which versions the profile behind a rule permits without opening every profile. The ceiling is worse again, because nothing presents the stored literal beside what that literal means on that appliance's build.
controls.audit: Objects > Decryption Profile, the SSL Protocol Settings tab of the profile the finding names, at the scope the finding names. Min Version is the floor and Max Version the ceiling; the finding prints both, and prints what the ceiling resolved to on that appliance where the stored value is the no-maximum literal.
controls.remediation: Set Min Version to TLSv1.2 or better and Max Version to Max. Where an application cannot tolerate the newer version, do not cap this profile: build a second profile with the narrower range and attach it by rule to just those destinations, which is the vendor's own recommendation and is what this control's applicability clause exists to respect. Record which destinations those are and who owns them, because nothing in the configuration distinguishes a deliberate cap from a forgotten one.

queries.name: The protocol floor is TLS 1.0
queries.short_description: The configured floor is TLS 1.0, deprecated by RFC 8996. It is also the value an unconfigured profile materialises, so a profile storing no floor at all reports here.

queries.name: The protocol floor is TLS 1.1
queries.short_description: The configured floor is TLS 1.1, deprecated by RFC 8996 alongside TLS 1.0 and graded level with it.

queries.name: The protocol ceiling is SSLv3
queries.short_description: The ceiling forces every session this profile governs onto a broken protocol, and contradicts any floor above it.

queries.name: The protocol ceiling is TLS 1.0
queries.short_description: The ceiling is below the floor this control's other half asserts, so the two settings on one profile contradict each other.

queries.name: The protocol ceiling is TLS 1.1
queries.short_description: The ceiling is below the floor this control's other half asserts, so the two settings on one profile contradict each other.

queries.name: The protocol ceiling is TLS 1.2
queries.short_description: The newest protocol version is unreachable on every session this profile governs. LOW because the vendor recommends exactly this ceiling where certificate-pinned mobile applications are in scope - and it is the value an unconfigured profile materialises.

controls.name: Decryption Profile Negotiable Primitives
controls.description:
A decryption profile that still leaves a broken encryption or authentication primitive negotiable, or that still permits a key exchange without forward secrecy or a cipher mode that does not authenticate what it encrypts.

TWO ASSERTIONS AND TWO SEVERITIES. A cipher or hash with a practical attack against it means the firewall will complete, inspect, re-encrypt and record as clean a session whose contents can be recovered or whose integrity can be forged - so the inspection the organisation paid for is performed on a channel an adversary can rewrite underneath it. That half is HIGH. The second half is MEDIUM and is about a different kind of loss: without a throwaway secret per session, one disclosure of the server's long-term key retrospectively decrypts every session an adversary has been recording under it, so the exposure is not the traffic after the breach but all the traffic before it; and a cipher mode that does not authenticate its own output leaves open the padding and record-splitting attacks the authenticated modes were introduced to end.

EACH HALF IS ONE COMPOSED VERDICT AND NOT A LIST OF SWITCHES. The assertion is a disjunction - any one of four primitives permitted is the finding - and a query clause list is one conjunction with no OR, so each half rests on a stored column holding the WORST member its class still leaves negotiable, with `none` as the only compliant value. That is also what carries the severity ordering the grading needs.

THE COLLAPSE COSTS SOMETHING AND THE FINDING SAYS SO. Where two broken primitives are permitted the column holds only the worse, so a finding naming RC4 is silent about SHA-1 on the same profile. The seven per-primitive switches are presented beside the verdict for exactly that reason.

SHA-1 IS GRADED BELOW ITS NEIGHBOURS because the vendor's own instruction for it is conditional where theirs are unconditional - block it if no necessary site uses it - and the block-chaining modes are graded below the broken primitives because the primitive is not broken and the mode is weaker. The larger-key block-chaining mode is graded with the smaller one although no corpus names it.

WHAT THIS CONTROL CANNOT SEE, AND IT IS A FALSE-POSITIVE DIRECTION. The vendor states that the firewall blocks two of these primitives of its own accord once the profile's protocol floor is TLS 1.2 or better. Nothing stored records the effective primitive set, so on a profile whose floor already meets PAN-DCP-001 this reports a weakness the device may not have. The switches really do say permitted and the column really does hold the value; what is missing is a measurement of the vendor's rule.
controls.rationale: Every one of these is a checkbox on a tab an assessor has to open per profile, and the defaults are the permissive side on six of the seven - so an unconfigured profile permits RC4, 3DES, SHA-1 and a static RSA key exchange without anybody having chosen any of them. Nothing in the session record shows which primitive was negotiated.
controls.audit: Objects > Decryption Profile, the SSL Protocol Settings tab of the profile the finding names. The finding names the worst member of each class that is still permitted; the seven individual switches are printed beside it, because the verdict holds only the worst and a profile may be permitting more than one.
controls.remediation: Clear the algorithm checkboxes the finding names. Where a necessary destination still requires one of them, do not loosen this profile: build a second profile and attach it by rule to just those destinations, which is the vendor's own recommendation and what this control's applicability clause respects. Raising the profile's protocol floor to TLS 1.2 or better is worth doing first in any case - the vendor states the firewall then blocks two of these primitives whatever their own switches hold.

queries.name: RC4 is still negotiable

queries.name: 3DES is still negotiable
queries.short_description: The worst broken primitive this profile permits is 3DES, a 64-bit block cipher with a practical birthday bound.

queries.name: MD5 is still negotiable
